sources.title: How v0 aims to create 100 million builders: Rauch on AI, taste and exposure hours
sources.originalTitle: Everyone’s an engineer now: Inside v0’s mission to create 100 million builders | Guillermo Rauch
sources.summary: Guillermo Rauch explains why v0 exists (growing the pool of product builders from ~20M JavaScript developers to 100M), how specialist "translation tasks" are being absorbed by AI, and how to build taste through exposure hours. He also covers tight in-product feedback loops, escape hatches, and how Vercel's teams ship with AI.

principles.text: Size your market by who aspires to build, not who can code: 100M product builders vs ~20M JS developers.
principles.quote: how many product builders or people with aspirations of building products exist my back of the napkin like minimum calculation is 100 million

principles.text: Bet on open source early: your tools end up in model training data, so AI is natively good at your stack.
principles.quote: our tools are already in the training data of the internet and so that long-term bet and vision and open source really paid off

principles.text: Tasks that are really translation (design to code) get automated; knowing how things work remains valuable for steering the model.
principles.quote: Knowing those tokens is going to be very important for you because you're going to be able to influence the model and make it follow your intention a lot better.

principles.text: Taste is a learnable skill: quantify and increase the hours you spend watching people use products.
principles.quote: Try to quantify how much time you expose yourself to watching how people use your products.

principles.text: Build many in-product feedback channels from day one; AI products create a constant stream that improves each iteration.
principles.quote: create a lot of opportunities for people to give you feedback inside the product.

principles.text: Great products need creative restraint: every feature is like adopting a puppy, so say no far more than yes.
principles.quote: the best product builders will say nine nos for every yes because when you say yes is like adopting a puppy.

sources.title: Guillermo Rauch on saying no, picking battles, and designing products for the AI era
sources.originalTitle: Guillermo Rauch: Why Great Companies are Defined by How Many Things They Say No To | E1069
sources.summary: Vercel's CEO explains why great companies are defined by what they reject, how a high quality bar can coexist with speed, and why product simplicity depends on stage. He also covers hiring on tangible output and why AI interfaces often need more UI, not less.

principles.text: Great companies are defined by how many attractive ideas they reject before shipping the one that earns a place in the lineup.
principles.quote: what makes a company good is how much they reject over time how many things they say no to how many attract seemingly attractive on the surface ideas they rule out before they say yes

principles.text: Pick your battles. Being right beats being first, and this matters more as a company matures.
principles.quote: you don't always have to be first you have to be right and and that's what I think companies over time optimize more around how do you pick your battles

principles.text: A high bar isn't slow. Shrink the blast radius of experiments so you ship broadly only with strong evidence.
principles.quote: you can find the ways of reducing the blast radius of your experimentation such that when it's the time that you bring the product to everybody you've accumulated enough evidence of success

principles.text: Product simplicity is stage-dependent. What works from zero to one won't work from one to two or later.
principles.quote: the Simplicity of your product from zero to one might not be the Simplicity of your product from one to two and two to three

principles.text: Hire on tangible output. Look at what candidates have shipped and shared, not just brand-name resumes.
principles.quote: what are they putting out into the world that is tangible what can I use what what hyperlinks Have you shared with the World by your creations

principles.text: AI products are probabilistic, so good AI interfaces often give users more choices and UI, not less.
principles.quote: it's actually giving you more UI not less because it's uncertain about what it is that you actually want so it needs to give you more choices

sources.title: How Vercel found extreme product-market fit by simplifying and focusing on the frontend cloud
sources.originalTitle: How Vercel found extreme product-market fit by focusing on simplification | Guillermo Rauch (CEO)
sources.summary: Guillermo Rauch explains how Vercel and Next.js reached very fast product-market fit: he narrowed from "deploy everything" to frontend, dogfooded a framework, and integrated with existing tools. He also covers open source monetization, early positioning, pricing, and where AI is taking engineering.

principles.text: Simplify and focus: stop trying to serve everything. Narrowing to the frontend was a catalyst for product-market fit.
principles.quote: one of the catalysts for that joint product Market fit was us simplifying the offering

principles.text: Enterprises distrust products that promise to solve everything; saying what you don't solve builds credibility.
principles.quote: it's much better to say we do not solve that set of problems in fact we integrate into solutions

principles.text: Your strength can be what you don't build. Invest heavily in the quality of integrations with tools customers already use.
principles.quote: I would call it the unreasonable effectiveness of building a lot of your engineering into the quality of the integration

principles.text: A strong demand signal is other serious organizations building the same thing and reaching out after you launch.
principles.quote: when something is really needed there's lots of very intelligent people at other organizations probably building a version of it

principles.text: Align open source value creation with the business's value creation. Users want to see continuous investment in the project.
principles.quote: we have to align the value creation of Open Source with the value creation of the business that supports that open source project

principles.text: Early on, position in relatable terms; earn the right to a lofty category name later.
principles.quote: in the early days I think your priority should be to make yourself relatable to what already exists

sources.title: Guillermo Rauch: Vercel's AI cloud, v0, and building for agents as customers
sources.originalTitle: Guillermo Rauch: Why Software Development Will Never Be the Same
sources.outlet: The MAD Podcast with Matt Turck
sources.summary: Rauch explains how v0 doubled Vercel's user base in under a year, why vibe coding and agentic engineering coexist, and how Vercel is rebuilding the cloud around agents, MCP and tokens. He also covers taste, designing from the model forward, doubling down on users who say it's life-changing, and his personal operating principles.

principles.text: Double down on the users who say the product is life-changing, not on everyone who finds it okay.
principles.quote: we doubled down on the people that were telling us this is life-changing.

principles.text: Design from the model forward: build for where models will be in six months, not science fiction.
principles.quote: you have to design from the model forward. If you go too far into a world of science fiction you actually might not have a working product.

principles.text: Treat agents as a customer alongside developers: serve them raw signal like markdown and text, plus CLIs.
principles.quote: you need to be thinking about agents as your customer and developers as your customer.

principles.text: Exposing your data and capabilities through an MCP server is a minimum viable AI product and the new business development.
principles.quote: expressing your capabilities and data through MCB is a way of participating in the AI economy.

principles.text: Every pixel is a liability: remove surface area, features and words to keep products simple and clear.
principles.quote: every pixel is a liability. Every little feature, button, text link, etc. is a huge liability.

principles.text: Encode your expertise into the product (model, context, best practices) so it scales beyond you, as Next.js and the v0 model did.
principles.quote: the vzero model is essentially my brain into tokens and my team's brain and the community's brain

sources.title: Recursive Founder Mode: how Vercel scales ownership with product leads, an internal agent, and build-to-interview hiring
sources.originalTitle: Inside Vercel's AI-era playbook: "Recursive Founder Mode" | Guillermo Rauch (CEO)
sources.summary: Guillermo Rauch explains how Vercel scales founder-style ownership through autonomous product leads, an internal omni-agent ("V"), open-sourced skills, and work-prompt interviews. He argues platforms beat bespoke SaaS in the agent era, quality comes from raising the floor, and the human edge is taste, capital allocation, energy and grind.

principles.text: Founder mode doesn't scale alone; create pockets of autonomy where product leads act as CEOs of their own product.
principles.quote: He's almost like the CEO of his own product. And over the years, we've been very fortunate to identify a handful of these people that what I've seen is that these are the people you want as you're scaling your company.

principles.text: Build the machine that builds the product: shift from working on the output to working on the factory that produces it.
principles.quote: we're leaning into this shift of I work on the output to I work on the machine that produces the output.

principles.text: Interview by having candidates build; hire for proof of work and for extrapolating where things are headed in 6 to 12 months.
principles.quote: There is an element of proof of work that I look for when I recruit or when I reach out to people. But there's also this futurebased mindset like are you able to extrapolate and position yourself in the future?

principles.text: Keep velocity by removing blockers: no one has veto power, only a few carefully designed choke points exist.
principles.quote: No one at Verscell has a right to veto sorry to block things

principles.text: Taste and AI are not opposed: raise the quality floor with platform primitives and encode institutional taste into skills and agents.
principles.quote: You know what's tasteless is grabbing the model and having it output as it is.

principles.text: Platforms win as software gets easier to build; bespoke products may not survive outside a broader platform with distribution.
principles.quote: I do think that platforms are going to do extraordinarily well in this world Maybe some of the bespoke pieces of software that you could put into that platform do not survive outside of it

sources.title: How Guillermo Rauch built Vercel: ship fast, find asymmetries, and AI platform ideas
sources.originalTitle: This Opportunity Won’t Exist In 5 Years - $3B Founder
sources.summary: Guillermo Rauch explains how teaching and open source took him from Argentina to Vercel, why iteration velocity is the one thing he optimizes for, and why small, simple products that evolve beat complete ones. He then shares free AI startup ideas built as opinionated vertical platforms that combine software 1.0 and 2.0.

principles.text: Bootstrap a career by teaching anything online; open source contributions turn into reputation and job offers.
principles.quote: When I advise young people on like how to bootstrap their careers, I say start by teaching anything.

principles.text: Success comes from finding asymmetries or unfair advantages, often in things that look like toys.
principles.quote: you always arrive to success by finding asymmetries or finding alpha or finding unfair advantages

principles.text: Ship the minimum surface that evolution can build on, rather than aiming for a complete first version.
principles.quote: what is the minimum surface that you can ship on top of which evolution can be bootstrapped. I think that's much better than trying to aim for completeness of that initial version.

principles.text: Optimize iteration velocity first: shorten the path from idea to a shareable URL.
principles.quote: The pattern throughout my career has been iteration velocity is the most important thing to optimize for.

principles.text: Early companies find focus by simplifying the offering, not by changing markets.
principles.quote: we didn't pivot in the sense of going into a different space but we simplified the offering way way way significantly.

principles.text: Entrepreneurs don't need to train models; they can combine existing ones into opinionated vertical workflows.
principles.quote: entrepreneurs don't need to like go and train foundation models. They just need to go in and put the pieces together into opinionated workflows.

sources.title: Guillermo Rauch on building Vercel: niche focus, brand permission, and designing for LLMs
sources.originalTitle: A conversation with Vercel's Guillermo Rauch
sources.summary: Guillermo Rauch explains how Vercel paired open-source Next.js with a cloud business, why he narrowed to a niche instead of pleasing everyone, and how he decides when to expand. He also covers pricing for the AI era, treating the LLM as a customer, and agentic commerce.

principles.text: Keep ambition unbounded but meet it with realism: dominate a niche first, then expand.
principles.quote: your ambition for a venture-backed business that will reach global scale should be pretty much unbounded.

principles.text: Trying to please everyone spreads you thin; a thousand customers who love you beat a million mediocre ones.
principles.quote: You might get into a situation of what some call it like, you know, having a million mediocre customers versus a thousand customers that really love you.

principles.text: Expand only into adjacencies where your brand has permission and that sit next to your core competence.
principles.quote: if Vercel tomorrow launched a washer and dryer product, even if it's slick and black and beautiful, you'd be like, that's a little strange.

principles.text: Look for platform shifts and the unmet need in the market; Vercel solved the framework gap that cloud providers left to developers.
principles.quote: I always encourage people to think about platform shifts very closely.

principles.text: Use progressive disclosure of complexity: meet each customer at their level and reveal sophistication only as needed, even as you scale up-market.
principles.quote: you still should present yourself where you meet the the needs and and complexity and and experience of that customer that comes in through the door. And then over time, if needed, you reveal your more complex self.

principles.text: Design pricing for fast iteration and transparency, with hybrid usage plus seat models, and experiment heavily.
principles.quote: optimizing for high iteration velocity, not just of your product, but your pricing and packaging and the way you bill.

sources.title: Guillermo Rauch on AI code generation: ship outcomes, build agents for results, and work backwards from the end user
sources.originalTitle: The Future of Code Generation | Guillermo Rauch, CEO of Vercel | Ep. 20
sources.summary: Vercel's CEO explains why code generation is nearly solved but review and shipping are the new bottleneck. He argues for constrained vertical agents, measuring business outcomes instead of code, and blending first-principles vision with close customer listening.

principles.text: Define 'shipping' as achieving a tangible business result, not just deploying code.
principles.quote: بل وأفضل من ذلك، الإطلاق يعني أنك حققت نتيجة تجارية ملموسة.

principles.text: Work backwards from the pixels on a user's screen to the business outcome.
principles.quote: ومجدداً، هذا ينبع من مبدأ العمل دائماً بطريقة عكسية، بدءاً من وجود بكسلات على شاشة شخص ما تؤدي في النهاية إلى نتيجة تجارية ما.

principles.text: A great developer experience alone is incomplete; platforms must deliver measurable business results to justify migration.
principles.quote: وأدركتُ أن منح الناس تجربة تطوير رائعة دون تحقيق نتائج أعمال، سيظل معادلة غير مكتملة.

principles.text: Expect specialized, constrained agent tools per problem type rather than one general tool, so quality is near-guaranteed.
principles.quote: وأعتقد أن هذا هو السبب في أن العالم سيستمر في الانقسام أكثر فأكثر إلى أدوات متخصصة للغاية لكل نوع من المشكلات.

principles.text: Move products from surfacing problems to delivering solutions (a fix, a PR), not raw error data.
principles.quote: لأننا نعمل بأساس ما أسميه الانتقال من المشاكل إلى الحلول.

principles.text: Combine customer listening with a first-principles vision of the future, or you miss the next platform shift.
principles.quote: ولكن يجب أن يمتزج ذلك برؤية للمستقبل، وإلا فلن ترى التحول القادم في المنصات.

sources.title: Guillermo Rauch on v0, Software 2.0, and why open source wins
sources.originalTitle: Vercel CEO Guillermo Rauch on v0, AI-Powered Coding, and Software 2.0
sources.summary: Rauch explains how Vercel's iteration-velocity philosophy and front-end cloud led to v0, and why every product will gain AI. He covers practical AI-skill building, when to build your own AI product versus a GPT, and why open source and startups win the Software 2.0 wave.

principles.text: Optimize for iteration velocity (speed with direction), not just deploy speed; pair fast shipping with continuous feedback data.
principles.quote: it's not iteration speed because if you just like do something fast and it's not what the customer wants you're not going to make progress if you implement iteration velocity or if you optimize for iteration velocity it's speed with a Direction

principles.text: Win bottoms-up by earning developer love; the tools that feel best get adopted, even inside the largest enterprises.
principles.quote: developers choose the products that feel the best

principles.text: Don't hand your customer relationship to a platform; build your own AI experience, though often the answer is both own site and marketplace.
principles.quote: do you want to retain the direct connection to your customer or do you want to be a product in somebody else's shelf

principles.text: Every product will become an AI product; incorporate assistants into your own product rather than waiting on ChatGPT.
principles.quote: every product in the planet is going to become an AI product in some capacity

principles.text: Re-evaluate your assumptions about AI every week because models, context windows and economics keep changing.
principles.quote: every week you have to re re-evaluate your assumptions that's the best operating model right now

principles.text: Never underestimate open source: it starts weak but compounds through ecosystem, and business development happens via git clone.
principles.quote: business development is not done with phone calls and meetings and contracts it's done by doing a get clone of our repository

sources.title: Guillermo Rauch: Why front-end-first building and instant preview URLs bring design and engineering together
sources.originalTitle: The shape of future builders: from design to deploy - Guillermo Rauch (Config 2023)
sources.summary: Rauch argues the next web will be built design-first: start from the front end, rely on off-the-shelf or legacy backends, and ship every iteration as a shareable URL. He ties speed and personalization to conversion, and shows how comments, draft mode and visual editing pull non-engineers into the shipping process.

principles.text: Start with the front end and design intent, not infrastructure. Connect off-the-shelf or legacy backends behind it.
principles.quote: you don't start by saying okay what kind of you know underlying bits do I need a provision you don't start with AWS you don't start with Google Cloud you start with designing your application

principles.text: Speed is a business lever: mobile-era latency improvements lifted conversion far more than the old desktop findings.
principles.quote: instead of 100 milliseconds of improving one percent it lifted conversion by eight percent it's actually extremely dramatic across lots of different Industries

principles.text: Ship every iteration as a live URL so others can see the real product, not a diff, and you iterate toward the right direction.
principles.quote: instead of just giving you a hyperlink to the code like the git systems do you get a hyperlink to the product and you can share that with everybody

principles.text: Test in real-world conditions (Safari quirks, in-app browsers, mobile) as early as possible, with production infrastructure rather than screenshots.
principles.quote: let's get to testing in the real world as soon as possible and as I mentioned uh from the 100 millisecond eight percent thing the real world is also mobile web

principles.text: Pull non-engineers into the release process: feedback attached to real components can file issues and even block a merge.
principles.quote: when I leave that comment it actually blocks the merging of the pr in the software development life cycle so this is what we you know is getting a taste of how can we invite non-engineers into actually building real world software

principles.text: Components give design and engineering a shared vocabulary; build on headless UI libraries rather than re-inventing accessibility and interactions per project.
principles.quote: you conceive your design in figma and then you take one of this base Baseline component libraries and then you adapt and you adapt Your Design to those rather than starting over from rediscovering a lot of those you know painful Parts on on accessibility

sources.title: How Vercel's v0 reached 3,200 merged PRs a day by bringing git workflow to vibe coding
sources.originalTitle: Guillermo Rauch: Vercel CEO on how v0 hit 3,200 PRs merged per day (and lets anyone ship)
sources.summary: Guillermo Rauch demos v0's new git-native workflow (branches, previews, PRs) using skills.sh. He argues vibe coding is easy at zero-to-one but hard at scale, and that production rigor lets non-engineers ship, collapsing prioritization friction.

principles.text: Vibe coding's real test is iterating and deploying safely at scale, not the zero-to-one demo.
principles.quote: It's really easy to go from zero to one. Like I think we've all seen the demos of I prom thing and it's cool and I think what's harder is to iterate on a project at scale and to deploy changes safely.

principles.text: Give AI-built changes real engineering process: branches, previews, code review, merge.
principles.quote: we always work on branches and we take advantage of branch previews and then we code review and then we merge them.

principles.text: Let non-engineers prototype and hand off as a PR, so ideas stop living in prototype land.
principles.quote: until I had this mechanism to hand it off as a pull request to the engineering team then I was kind of like playing in La La Lands.

principles.text: Lowering the friction to get something live shifts debate from prioritizing hypotheses to judging real ideas.
principles.quote: the humiliation ritual of prioritization goes away and you can actually focus your time on defending the merits of an idea

principles.text: Hold internal products to the same bar as external launches so you know people will adopt them.
principles.quote: when we cook on a on a project or a product internally, we hold ourselves to the same sort of high bar as if you had launched a product externally

principles.text: Use a 'customer zero' (yourselves) plus 'customer one' (close design partners) to validate what to build.
principles.quote: There's a customer zero and a customer one. Customer zero, we like to to be ourselves.

sources.title: Guillermo Rauch on Vercel: simplicity, focus, and building a strong core before adjacencies
sources.originalTitle: Guillermo Rauch at Founders in Arms Live: Simplicity, Focus, and the Bet That Built Vercel
sources.summary: Rauch recounts how Vercel went from many open-source bets to focus on Next.js and deployment, then to repeatable use cases like e-commerce. He argues for simplicity, solving your own pain, entering big markets via a wedge, marketing with real customer results, and saying no often.

principles.text: Simplicity and ease of use win markets, even when investors say the problem is already solved by existing tools.
principles.quote: I do think that so much of the world is won by the people that bring simplicity and ease of use.

principles.text: Build what solves your own pain; the best products came from internal problems proven before going to market.
principles.quote: the things that have always worked the best and I teach the company still is the things that were uh solving our own pain points.

principles.text: Play in enormous markets and enter through a narrow wedge that expands into a much larger category.
principles.quote: Next.js became a wedge into what has now become the entirety of the cloud for us

principles.text: Market with concrete customer results and substance, not logo walls; start from one happy customer with measured ROI.
principles.quote: And so you need substance. Okay, sometimes I ask an entrepreneur, just tell me about one happy customer. Just one.

principles.text: Build a very strong core first, then expand only into smart adjacencies of that core.
principles.quote: the way to succeed is by building really smart adjacencies to that strong core.

principles.text: Saying no, to many things, is core to the job, even when the company is praised for shipping fast.
principles.quote: I think saying no to a lot of things, to the right things, and to a lot of things is also part of the job

sources.title: Next.js Conf 25 keynote: Vercel's bets on composition, Turbopack and cache components
sources.originalTitle: Next.js Conf 25: Opening Keynote
sources.summary: Guillermo Rauch reviews Vercel's App Router bets, arguing that composition and co-location win while global, implicit caching failed. He announces Turbopack as default in Next.js 16, an open benchmark for AI agents on Next.js, and a deployment adapters API. Cache components were presented by Sam and Jimmy.

principles.text: Design APIs for LLMs and humans together: what is easier for people is easier for agents.
principles.quote: An LLM's context window is even shorter than a human's attention span. So, if we make an API that's confusing for anyone in this room, the LLMs stand no chance. The easier we make the developer experience for humans, the better we make it for agents.

principles.text: Treat product strategy as a portfolio of bets: review which paid off and openly revisit the ones that didn't.
principles.quote: So, with all of this in mind, let's take a closer look at our bets and see which ones paid off and which ones we're revisiting.

principles.text: Composition and co-location are the common trait of winning features; global, implicit APIs cause spooky action at a distance.
principles.quote: Composition and co-location. Our best features really embrace these qualities, right? So, you have this ability to reason locally.

principles.text: Composition beats separation of technology, and it matters even more now because it is essential for LLMs.
principles.quote: Because it's not only better for humans, it's essential for our friends, the LLMs. [...] So, composition wins over separation of technology every single time.

principles.text: Speed investments compound in the agent era: millisecond gains that humans barely feel matter in agent loops.
principles.quote: But for an agent loop, every millisecond counts.

principles.text: Keep models current on your framework's best practices, and publish a public benchmark to improve AI's skill with your product.
principles.quote: we're open-sourcing Next.js Next.js is a public benchmark that tracks how well the latest models in coding agents can build with Next.js. This is an investment into the ecosystem. The better AI gets at Next.js, the better everyone's developer experience will become.

sources.title: Guillermo Rauch on Vercel's AI strategy: AI-native apps, front-end, and copy-paste over packages
sources.originalTitle: No Priors Ep. 30 | With Vercel CEO Guillermo Rauch
sources.outlet: No Priors: AI, Machine Learning, Tech, & Startups
sources.summary: Vercel's CEO explains why foundation models are "Cloud 2.0" backends, why integration and product design matter more than training models, and why dogfooding drives better products. He also covers abuse of AI endpoints, SEO for retrieval engines, the swing back to copy-paste, and taste-driven AI-assisted UI building.

principles.text: You don't need to train or fine-tune a model to build a genuinely useful AI product; the last mile of integration holds the value.
principles.quote: I do believe that you don't have to train or fine tune a new model in order to create a legitimately useful product

principles.text: Design AI-native products from the problem up instead of bolting AI onto an existing product.
principles.quote: what would it look like to solve it if now I have ai as sort of my input in the design space and I think that's a radically different way of thinking compared to I'm going to add AI to an existing product

principles.text: Avoid checkbox AI; ship products that are actually useful.
principles.quote: I'm not for random acts of AI like just like you know checking a box but creating really useful products

principles.text: Be customer zero of your own products to build the best ones.
principles.quote: we're going to build the best possible products if we're customer zero of our own products

principles.text: Foundation models are the new backend; expect many AI-native companies built on them, as SaaS was built on cloud.
principles.quote: there's going to be a lot of great AI native companies that are built on top of this new infrastructure let's call it like Cloud 2.0

principles.text: Front end is where you meet the customer, so it drives conversion and sales; focus on the last mile of user experience.
principles.quote: front end is the most important thing that your company has because that's where you meet your customer that's where you can accelerate your website or drive more conversion more science more sales

sources.title: Guillermo Rauch on building Vercel as agentic infrastructure: open source, blocks, and tokens
sources.originalTitle: Stanford MS&E435 Economics of the AI Supercycle | Spring 2026 | Applications, Coding AI
sources.summary: Vercel's founder explains how betting on open source, composable "blocks" and developer experience made Vercel the default deploy target for coding agents. He covers agentic infrastructure (sandboxes, AI gateway), why software is becoming free and tailored, and why consumption pricing with no rate limits wins.

principles.text: Deploying and running code, not just writing it, is what makes you win; learning starts when users hit the running version.
principles.quote: the people that will win the world are the ones that don't just write software, they deploy it and they run it.

sources.title: How Vercel's Guillermo Rauch is rebuilding the internet for agents, not humans
sources.originalTitle: Vercel CEO Guillermo Rauch on Building the Internet for Agents
sources.summary: Rauch explains Vercel's shift from human developer experience to agent experience, with agents now making 60% of deployments. He covers publishing agent-readable content and protocols, why custom software beats SaaS, open-source distribution, non-gameable retention metrics, and what he hires for.

principles.text: Build interfaces for agents: give them direct, accurate information instead of polished human UI.
principles.quote: الوكيل لا يهتم، بل يريد معلومات مباشرة.

principles.text: Code is now free, so build custom software with coding agents instead of buying generic SaaS.
principles.quote: أنا شركة "نعم لكتابة الكود" لأنني أقول الآن إن وكلاء البرمجة يجعلون الكود مجانيًا.

principles.text: Open-sourcing everything made Vercel the default choice for coding agents, because models learn from public information.
principles.quote: عندما يتم تدريب النماذج، كلما زادت المعلومات المتاحة عنك، وكلما زادت قدرتها على الوصول إلى محتواك والقواعد التي تحددها، كان ذلك أفضل لهذا الوكيل.

principles.text: Track non-gameable metrics like long-term retention, not marketing stunts or ad-driven signups.
principles.quote: أنصح دائماً المؤسسين الشباب بالتركيز على المقاييس غير القابلة للغش في أعمالهم.

principles.text: In fast-moving markets, optimize for speed of iteration rather than raw speed, and stay open to new tools.
principles.quote: ما أقوله دائمًا لعملائنا هو أن القيمة الأساسية التي تقدمها Verscell لأعمالك هي سرعة التكرار، وليس السرعة.

principles.text: Hire people who can orchestrate teams of agents, with strong technical fluency and human communication.
principles.quote: بل أبحث عن قدرتك على بناء فرق من العملاء والاستفادة القصوى من هذا النظام البيئي الجديد.

sources.title: Redefining developer experience in the age of AI: ship more, raise quality
sources.originalTitle: Redefining Developer Experience In The Age Of AI | BUILD 2025 Luminary Talk
sources.summary: Guillermo Rauch argues the cloud, interfaces and who can build software are all changing as the web moves from pages to agents. Coding is one skill among many; the durable meta skill is shipping end to end with taste. AI should serve quality, not only productivity.

principles.text: Shipping, not coding, is the meta skill: build end to end, including messaging, QA, marketing, selling and iterating.
principles.quote: Shipping is a distinct skill from coding. Shipping is the meta skill. Shipping is first about building end to end.

principles.text: Don't get attached to individual skills like coding; machines can replicate them. Focus on what problems are worth solving.
principles.quote: Don't get too attached to your individual skills.

principles.text: AI must serve quality, not just productivity. Move fast and raise quality; productivity without quality is noise.
principles.quote: Productivity without quality is just noise. And quality without productivity means you're probably getting left behind.

principles.text: Taste is a learnable skill: spend time watching people use your product and other products to build the muscle.
principles.quote: People think of taste as this inaccessible thing that this person was born with taste or not with taste, but I see it as a skill that you can develop.

principles.text: Clarity of intent is the new barrier to building. Prompting is the new literacy, so anyone can build software.
principles.quote: The barrier isn't technical knowledge. It's clarity of intent.

principles.text: Put agents where users already work (Slack, Zoom, Teams) to cut friction and widen who can build and use software.
principles.quote: Agents are meeting users where they work and talk, dramatically reducing friction.

sources.title: 7 Principles of Rich Web Applications: minimizing time-to-data with JavaScript
sources.originalTitle: 7 Principles of Rich Web Applications
sources.summary: Guillermo Rauch argues that JavaScript on the web should be judged purely by user experience, especially how fast users get the data they want. He gives seven principles: pre-render pages, act instantly on input, push data and code updates, control data exchange, respect history, and predict behavior. This dissolves the website vs web app divide.

principles.text: Pre-rendering is a performance requirement, not just SEO; avoid SPAs that need extra roundtrips before showing data.
principles.quote: Pre-rendering is not (just) about SEO, it’s about performance. Consider the additional roundtrips to get scripts, styles, and subsequent API requests.

principles.text: Latency, not bandwidth, is the bottleneck, so minimize network roundtrips needed to show information.
principles.quote: The bandwidth capacity of your users' connections might improve noticeably, as it steadily has, but the latency needle won't move much at all.

principles.text: Mask network latency by acting optimistically on user input; defer spinners until the response no longer feels immediate.
principles.quote: JavaScript allows us to mask network latency altogether. Applying this as a design principle should even remove most spinners or “loading” messages from your applications.

principles.text: Make the UI self-updating: push data changes to clients and handle reconnection and state reconciliation.
principles.quote: When data changes on the server, let the clients know without asking.

principles.text: Push code updates alongside data, ideally via modular hot reloading, so long-lived sessions never hit stale-client errors.
principles.quote: Pushing data without pushing code is insufficient. If your data updates automatically, so should your code.

principles.text: Predict user intent (hover prefetch, mouse trajectory) to approach negative latency.
principles.quote: Starting to fetch data when you hover a hyperlink so that it's ready when it's clicked is a straightforward example.

sources.title: Pure UI: designing and building UI as a pure function of application state
sources.originalTitle: Pure UI
sources.summary: Guillermo Rauch explains how defining a UI as a pure function of state (as in React) lets designers and programmers share one protocol. By rendering every state as a visible artboard, you can measure completeness, discover missing states, and improve estimates.

principles.text: Define the UI as a pure function of application state; describe each state, not the transitions between them.
principles.quote: The fundamental idea I want to discuss is the definition of an application’s UI as **a pure function of application state**.

principles.text: Describe what state A and state B look like instead of scripting how to get from A to B.
principles.quote: No need to specify how to go from **A** to **B**: just describe what **A** looks like and what **B** looks like, in a discrete way.

principles.text: Underestimating the size of the state space is easy, which explains poor software estimates.
principles.quote: The main issue, however, is that underestimating the size of the state space is actually very easy.

principles.text: Separate design (representing known data) from discovery (uncovering new states while building); expect both to interleave.
principles.quote: Discovery is about the transformation (usually expansion) of that input. It’s the evolution of the design. The uncovering of new states and new ideas throughout the process itself.

principles.text: Render every state as a visible artboard so completeness is measurable: 10 of 20 states rendered means 50% done.
principles.quote: If you think up and hand out 20 distinct states in which your application can behave, then you should be able to clearly see them rendered on a screen as HTML. If only 10 are done, then the implementation is only 50% done.

principles.text: Map the app's states to track complexity and scoping; late-discovered map areas signal a project that was misunderstood and explain delays.
principles.quote: If much of the map is discovered later on, it could mean that the project was improperly scoped or understood, and it can explain why it’s taking longer to ship.

sources.title: Guillermo Rauch's 2016 in review: ZEIT, Now, Next.js, Hyper and the ideas shaping his thinking
sources.originalTitle: 2016 in Review
sources.summary: Rauch recaps his first year building ZEIT: Now (immutable one-command deploys), World (free DNS), Hyper (an extensible terminal) and Next.js. He explains the product philosophy behind each, plus ideas on accessibility, universal code style and being wrong about reactions.

principles.text: Make deployment a single command and let every deploy be immutable with its own URL, so dev, staging and production are one system.
principles.quote: One is that the same system gives you development, staging and production all in one. You can deploy to build, test and iterate during development. You can _stage_ by simply sharing these links to your co-workers or clients, before you make them live.

principles.text: Remove dependencies on a specific person or team for infrastructure chores like DNS and SSL; they kill productivity and become invisible barriers.
principles.quote: Processes like that kill productivity and create invisible barriers for product engineers. Worse yet, after a while you just get used to it.

principles.text: Build for composable, focused tools: CLIs resist bloat because they do one thing well, compose, and are easy to replace; text is fast and searchable.
principles.quote: Most CLI programs adhere to the [Unix Philosophy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unix_philosophy). Unlike most apps and websites, it's hard for these programs to bloat. They tend to do one thing well. They compose. They are easy to replace.

principles.text: Bring back good old ideas (zero setup, filesystem routing, pre-rendered HTML) and generalize across paradigms rather than choosing between site and app.
principles.quote: Websites tend to _pre-render markup_ and download code _lazily_. Apps tend to download _everything_ in advance, and therefore tend to feel faster afterwards. Now we're showing you can do both.

principles.text: Make errors actionable by attaching a URL to every error message, pointing users to a resource you can update over time instead of making them Google it.
principles.quote: Instead of having our users Google error messages or codes, we can point them to a resource we can update over time and others can comment on!

principles.text: Hedge the risk of a startup by founding it with people you love and respect; adopt universal code style tools to stop wasting time debating style.
principles.quote: If there's a way to [hedge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hedge_(finance)) the risky personal investment of launching a startup company, it surely must be to do it with people you love and respect.

sources.title: Why efficiency is the one thing you can't forego: Guillermo Rauch on tradeoffs and efficient systems
sources.originalTitle: It's Hard to Forego Efficiency
sources.summary: Rauch argues that building anything means accepting tradeoffs and letting things drop (design, docs, tests), but efficiency is the exception. Once people experience a faster workflow or system, going back is nearly impossible, and even knowing a faster option exists creates an inexorable pull. He illustrates this with fast search, deploys in seconds, and his own experience as an immigrant.

principles.text: Progress means accepting tradeoffs: you can't optimize everything at once, so learn to let some things drop.
principles.quote: In order to make progress in any system, we learn to be ok with juggling many things and letting some drop to the ground.

principles.text: Early on, it's fine to forego polish like design, docs, comments and tests to ship.
principles.quote: When you start coding a new app, you might not document your APIs, thoroughly comment your code or write lots of tests.

principles.text: Efficiency is the one thing you can't forego once users or teams have gotten used to it.
principles.quote: once you’ve grown accustomed to a certain level of efficiency when performing a task, or a certain level of efficiency provided by the system or environment you are in, it’s extraordinarily difficult to forego it.

principles.text: Speed regressions in daily-use tasks are nearly impossible to justify to users, so protect performance.
principles.quote: It would be almost impossible to justify such a backwards change in your daily routine.

principles.text: Merely knowing a faster alternative exists pulls people toward it, so competitors with better efficiency create pressure on you.
principles.quote: Even knowing greener and more efficient grass is out there does the same.

principles.text: Efficiency is a quality worth fighting to preserve above others, in products and in the systems around them.
principles.quote: If there is a quality worth fighting to preserve, this one is at the top.

sources.title: 2019 in Review: Rauch on static-first Jamstack, deploy previews, and engineering quality
sources.originalTitle: 2019 in Review
sources.summary: Rauch's year-end essay argues static-first (Jamstack) architecture wins on speed, availability and safety, and that deploy-per-push preview URLs are replacing code review as the center of team collaboration and QA. It also collects product and engineering heuristics: resist settings, treat slowness and flakiness as signs of being wrong, demo often, and optimize team velocity.

principles.text: Precompute pages statically so servers leave the hot path, improving speed, availability and backend load.
principles.quote: Instead of putting a server in between the user's request and the response, we compute the response ahead of time.

principles.text: Share a live preview URL for every push; seeing the real site beats reviewing code alone.
principles.quote: nothing beats teams collaborating by sharing URLs to the _actual_ sites that are being worked on and experiencing them directly.

principles.text: Don't add settings until a product has substantial evidence of success without them.
principles.quote: absolutely resist adding options until **substantial evidence of success without them** exists.

principles.text: Test the real production-like deployment instead of a mocked environment.
principles.quote: instead of running tests that make all kinds of assumptions about the environment (like mocking it), we can instead test the _real thing_.

principles.text: Microservices add network hops and reduce availability; statically bind dependencies per function instead.
principles.quote: Not only are microservices harder to _manage_ than, say, a static blob of code together with its dependencies inside a function or container, but odds are they are also **less available**.

principles.text: Optimize for whole-team speed, not individual developer speed, and give frequent demos.
principles.quote: At Google, we optimize for the speed at which a team of developers can produce a product together**, as opposed to optimizing for the speed at which an individual developer can write code.

sources.title: Develop, Preview, Test: why end-to-end tests on every deploy beat the testing pyramid
sources.originalTitle: Develop, Preview, Test
sources.summary: Guillermo Rauch argues that testing is an investment judged by return and risk, and that modern infrastructure now makes E2E tests the best return. Per-push preview deployments plus headless browsers on serverless compute make prod-like staging and fast, cheap tests possible. He demos a Vercel, Checkly and GitHub workflow set up in minutes.

principles.text: Treat writing tests as an investment: weigh return and risk, including opportunity cost versus shipping features.
principles.quote: Writing tests is an **investment**, and like any other investment, it has to be evaluated in terms of its **return** and **risks**

principles.text: Prioritize E2E tests on the critical parts of your app; they reduce risk and give the best return.
principles.quote: I want to make the case that **prioritizing end-to-end (E2E) testing** for the critical parts of your app will reduce risk and give you the best return.

principles.text: Focus on the customer first: it is the best way to run a business and to judge software quality.
principles.quote: is the best way to run a business, but also the best way to ascertain software quality.

principles.text: Quality is more than correctness: it includes reliability over time and performance.
principles.quote: (whether your program stays working correctly over time)

principles.text: Give every push its own prod-like preview URL instead of one shared staging server, so tests run against real production infrastructure.
principles.quote: Instead of thinking about a single staging server that end-to-end tests are run against, now you can have millions of concurrent "staging" environments.

principles.text: Keep testing continuously the way users experience your product to tame the chaos of complex, ever-changing dependencies.
principles.quote: continuously testing just like our users do is our best bet to tame the chaos.

sources.title: Next for Vercel: why a frontend-focused, hybrid, everywhere-computing platform won its Series B
sources.originalTitle: Next for Vercel
sources.summary: Rauch explains Vercel's $40M Series B and the seven tailwinds behind its growth: obsessive customer focus on the frontend, hybrid SSR/SSG, running code everywhere, measuring real user experience via Core Web Vitals, collaborative previews, and openness beyond Next.js.

principles.text: Center the business on obsessive customer focus; for web, that means the frontend, where every customer interaction happens.
principles.quote: Applying this to web development, focusing on the frontend is the most customer-obsessive way to build your products.

principles.text: Invest where differentiation lives: frontend is a space for technological and artistic edge while the backend commoditizes.
principles.quote: What's more, frontend is an area of **technological and [artistic](https://www.fastcompany.com/90521691/first-look-kanye-wests-new-website-turns-shopping-into-art) differentiation**, while backend becomes increasingly commoditized, turnkey and undifferentiated.

principles.text: Serve two customers at once: delight the developer and give them the platform to delight their own customer.
principles.quote: For Vercel, being customer focused represents a unique challenge: to delight our developer customer, and to give them the tools and platform to delight **their customer**.

principles.text: Don't be dogmatic: meet customers where they are, enable incremental adoption, and give per-page choice instead of one pure approach.
principles.quote: A key ingredient of being customer focused is not being dogmatic, meeting the customer where they are and [enabling incremental adoption](https://nextjs.org/blog/incremental-adoption) of the promising new technology.

principles.text: Measure what reflects actual user outcomes, not proxies like CDN latency; real-user metrics tell you what to optimize.
principles.quote: Measuring how good your pages are has been, until recently, a daunting task because we didn't know what to measure, and therefore, what to optimize.

principles.text: Stay open and agnostic: use a flagship framework as a lighthouse, but make platform capabilities available to any framework.
principles.quote: While we consider Next.js to be our lighthouse framework, Vercel is designed to be completely agnostic to it.

sources.title: Vercel rebrand: why preview URLs, components and speed define frontend DX
sources.originalTitle: Vercel
sources.summary: Guillermo Rauch announces the Vercel rebrand and $21M raise, and explains the thesis behind it: the backend is commoditized, so value has moved to the frontend. He lays out three bets: components as the primitive, deploy-preview URLs as the collaboration primitive, and speed by default.

principles.text: When the backend is commoditized, the valuable opportunity moves to the layer that creates products and content users see.
principles.quote: Today the most interesting new opportunities for modernization have shifted to the frontend. That’s where the value is for most enterprises - creating new products and content that attract users and drive revenue.

principles.text: Make the preview deploy URL the unit of collaboration so every team can review the real thing.
principles.quote: Vercel made a huge breakthrough with the realization that the preview deploy URL was a superior abstraction for frontend teams.

principles.text: Shared working URLs let non-engineers (marketing, sales, legal) give feedback early and remove the staging step.
principles.quote: The most obvious immediate benefit of the URL for deploy review is making it much easier to collaborate across any organization, from marketing and sales to legal and engineering.

principles.text: Replace stitched-together CI/CD, CDN and tooling with one integrated workflow that triggers on every git push.
principles.quote: Too many cycles are spent configuring your own CI/CD pipeline, setting up Jenkins, finding your optimal vendor for CI, finding your optimal vendor for CDN, and so on.

principles.text: Ship performance by default so customers get great results without thinking about infrastructure.
principles.quote: Vercel operates a global edge network and gives you a perfect Lighthouse score out of the box every time you deploy.

principles.text: Be a platform that supports every framework rather than locking users to your own; meet teams at whatever component technology they adopted.
principles.quote: Vercel as a platform wants to support them all!

sources.title: Static hoisting: pushing pre-computed results to the edge, not just hosting and caching them
sources.originalTitle: Static Hoisting
sources.summary: Guillermo Rauch explains why Jamstack on an edge network differs from a server with a CDN on top: framework builds can hoist the results of computation to the edge. Pre-render as much as possible once at build time, share it across all users, and let the framework pick the optimal output per page.

principles.text: Pre-render as much as possible: move computation from request time to build time and share the result with every user.
principles.quote: A core tenet of Jamstack has been to **pre-render (pre-compute) as much as possible**, which has given prominence to static site generation.

principles.text: Hoist the results of computation to the edge, next to visitors, rather than only hosting and caching static files.
principles.quote: What Jamstack as a software architecture has now made possible, however, is to **hoisting the results of computation to the edge**, right next to where your visitors are.

principles.text: Compute once at build, serve to many: shifting work out of the request timeline makes it a shared, one-time cost.
principles.quote: computation that would have happened later on, in the request's timeline, has now been shifted to the build phase, performed once and made available for all users to share.

principles.text: Frameworks should choose the optimal output per page automatically, so developers get static, SSG, or serverless by how they fetch data.
principles.quote: the next build process has started automatically outputting the optimal asset on a per-page (entrypoint) basis.

principles.text: Even highly dynamic apps can ship as static HTML that fetches data client-side, keeping the shell on the edge.
principles.quote: Our [dashboard](https://vercel.com/dashboard), despite being super dynamic in nature, is a static HTML page that queries data securely using [React Hooks](https://swr.now.sh) from the client side.

principles.text: Traditional CDNs treat the origin as a black box; the advantage comes from designing frameworks that push content directly to the network.
principles.quote: CDNs have been treating the "origin" as an opaque black box. It's now possible, instead, to push content directly **to the network** and design frameworks that optimize for this capability.

sources.title: Making the Web. Faster.: Vercel's $102M Series C and the case for an SDK for the Web
sources.originalTitle: Making the Web. Faster.
sources.summary: Guillermo Rauch announces Vercel's $102M Series C and lays out three priorities: build an SDK for the Web around React and Next.js, lower the barrier to collaboration, and focus on the end-user. The core lesson for platform and tooling builders is that you serve two users, and the end-customer's experience is the ultimate fitness function.

principles.text: Platform and tooling companies have two users: the tool's user and the user of what the tool produces. Optimize for both.
principles.quote: A particularly interesting challenge of building a platform and tooling company is that you have **two users** (whether it's acknowledged or not):

principles.text: Measure success by your customers' success, not by adoption stats. The customer is king.
principles.quote: No matter how many downloads Next.js gets, or how delightful and realtime the development experience, a universal truth remains: **the customer is king**.

principles.text: Make end-user performance a design principle baked into everything, and aim to be invisible: the product feels fast and delightful.
principles.quote: Our primary fitness function is your success for your customers.

principles.text: Measure what the end-user actually experiences (per-device Real Experience Score) instead of vanity traffic stats or server-side latency.
principles.quote: Vercel Analytics prioritized giving you a Real Experience Score calculated by each device, rather than just listing traffic stats or TTFB latencies.

principles.text: Give developers a meaningful starting point on a durable abstraction, and open source the lessons learned from the biggest players. Growth comes organically from developers recommending it.
principles.quote: Next.js builds on this formidable foundation to give developers and companies a meaningful starting point to build great pages, open sourcing the lessons learned from the giants of the Web.

principles.text: Remove friction from collaboration so everyone, from new designers to experienced developers, can contribute to the product.
principles.quote: With Next.js Live, we want to build a Web that everyone can contribute to.

sources.title: The AI Cloud: Why Vercel is moving from pages to agents, problems to solutions, closed to open
sources.originalTitle: The AI Cloud
sources.summary: Guillermo Rauch lays out Vercel's strategy for the next decade: infrastructure should be an output of frameworks, the web is shifting from pages to agents, and the cloud should deliver solutions (PRs, fixes) instead of alerts. He argues the AI web must stay open, with model choice and open protocols rather than one closed mega-app.

principles.text: Make infrastructure an output of the developer's code, not something they configure by hand.
principles.quote: We set out to make Vercel the _React of the Cloud_, where the hyperscaler primitives are outputs not to be directly manipulated, or jQueryed.

principles.text: Lead with developer experience; time spent on configs is time stolen from product and customers.
principles.quote: The time you should have spent on the pixels... was spent on the configs. The jobs you could have devoted to product and customers, were devoted to the setup of clusters and machines.

principles.text: Page speed drives conversion and SEO, creating a flywheel of business, conversion and organic traffic.
principles.quote: One of the key unlocks of this first wave of the web was that page speed correlated closely with conversion. Google rewards page speed with higher rankings, which creates a flywheel of more business, more conversion, more organic traffic.

principles.text: The next wave of software is agents: async, generative, able to write their own code and tools, so the cloud must be rebuilt around them.
principles.quote: Unlike pages, agents are not usually synchronous. They're never static. They can think for seconds, minutes, hours.

principles.text: An AI cloud should deliver solutions (PRs, recommendations, automated actions), not a stream of alerts and dashboards.
principles.quote: Fundamentally, we believe an AI Cloud shouldn't give you problem after problem (alerts, 5xx errors, latency spikes, traffic anomalies...). It should give you solutions: pull requests, recommendations, and automated actions.

principles.text: Keep the AI web open: model choice, a web of agents and open protocols instead of closed SDKs and one mega-app.
principles.quote: Instead of a single agentic interface, we should have a web of agents. Instead of a single model SDK, we should embrace model choice.

sources.title: How Guillermo Rauch learned to code: hacking games, open source and code golf
sources.originalTitle: An Ode to Code Golf
sources.summary: Rauch argues learning to code is a messy, discontinuous process, sped up by open source, online communities and hacking competitions. Using Izhal and code golf as examples, he shows these games teach transferable problem-solving (reverse engineering, debugging blind, trial and error, perseverance), and he recommends learning through fun and friendly competition.

principles.text: Learning to code is a messy, discontinuous process, not a single breakthrough moment.
principles.quote: there wasn't a particular instant, or month, or year, or flow state I got in where I finally learned to code. It was more of a _discontinuous_ process full of ups, downs, impostor syndrome, months of voracious learning

principles.text: Open source, online communities and competitions are decisive accelerants for learning to code.
principles.quote: there were many decisive contributing factors that clearly helped: exposure to open-source (Linux), being involved in online communities (IRC and forums) and **hacking competitions**.

principles.text: Game-like challenges teach transferable problem-solving (reverse engineering, debugging with little info) faster than tutorials.
principles.quote: It taught me skills that are essential to problem solving, rather than coding itself, like reverse engineering a system and [unusually effective debugging](http://carlos.bueno.org/2013/09/effective-debugging.html) with very little information. And it did so very quickly.

principles.text: Seeing what others have demonstrably achieved (a public leaderboard) pushes you past what looks like the limit.
principles.quote: Once again, just like back in the day in the programming forums, I was driven to succeed inspired by what other had demonstrably accomplished.

principles.text: Programming skill is largely navigating unfamiliar systems: try several search strategies, back the promising one, iterate, persevere.
principles.quote: figuring out unfamiliar environments and systems without a manual, applying multiple "search" strategies and selecting the most promising one, iterating and dealing with trial-and-error, and perseverance.

principles.text: Learn by having fun, overcoming obstacles and competing with friends, rather than relying only on courses and bootcamps.
principles.quote: Whether it's with code golfing or hacking tournaments, I suggest giving a try to the alternative of learning by having fun, overcoming obstacles and a healthy dose of competition with your friends.

sources.title: Guillermo Rauch's 5 lessons for AI-era founders: open source, focus, and discernment
sources.originalTitle: Guillermo Rauch's 5 Lessons for Founders Building in the AI Era
sources.summary: Takeaways from Rauch's a16z speedrun fireside chat. Open source is a fast test of product-market fit, early focus beats unbounded ambition, and in the AI era choosing what to build (and what to dismiss) is the real edge. He also covers hiring for proof of work and communication, and cutting distractions from your product's story.

principles.text: Treat open source as a speedrun to product-market fit: if people won't use it free and easy, work on something else.
principles.quote: I’ve always thought of open source as a speedrun to product-market fit, because if people don’t use it when it’s free, when it’s easy to consume, when the code is available, then you probably should be working on something else.

principles.text: Don't let fear of the future stall you; you likely don't even have product-market fit yet.
principles.quote: What stops entrepreneurs in their tracks is that they worry too much about what’s going to happen in the future. In reality, they don’t even have product-market fit yet.

principles.text: Keep unbounded long-term vision but ruthless early focus; with three people, building everything is a mistake.
principles.quote: When you’re getting started and you’re three people, if all you do every day is unbounded ambition and building two hundred million different features, then you’ve fucked up.

principles.text: Be truly excellent at one problem class; buyers want the best of each category, not second-best.
principles.quote: If I had continued doing everything, I would have made a company that made zero dollars. Literally zero dollars. Discerning buyers want the best of each class of problem. They don’t settle for the second-best solution.

principles.text: When AI makes everything buildable, discerning which problems are worth solving is a key differentiator.
principles.quote: A bunch of you are probably already over-building massively because you notice that you can just prompt it and it’ll do it. But the discernment of what problems are worth solving could be one of your biggest differentiators.

principles.text: Remove everything that isn't your thing from your product story; clutter gives people an excuse to get distracted.
principles.quote: Delete all the things that are not your thing, because they’re an excuse for people to get distracted.

sources.title: Guillermo Rauch on building v0 and the generative web: reliability, agents as users, ephemeral software
sources.originalTitle: Training Data: Building the Generative Web with AI
sources.summary: Guillermo Rauch explains how v0 reached 3M builders by obsessing over reliability, how AI products ship with built-in metrics, and why ChatGPT became a top signup source for Vercel. He argues customers are increasingly agents, and that the web is moving from dynamic to generative, ephemeral software.

principles.text: AI products come with built-in success metrics, giving a compass for iteration.
principles.quote: AI products have that kind of built in, which is amazing, right? Like, if you look at the first coding AI product, which is Copilot... the acceptance rate of the completion.

principles.text: For AI coding tools, reliability is everything; invest in custom models so a generation always works.
principles.quote: We trained our own custom code application model that sits in front of the frontier model, all in the service of reliability. You want to come in, you create a generation, it has to work.

principles.text: Open the top of funnel beyond developers: designers, marketers, anyone with a keyboard can now build.
principles.quote: AI coding tools that are now attracting what I would call dev-adjacent profiles, like designers, marketers, basically anybody with a keyboard

principles.text: Dev tools have two customers: the developer and the developer's end user. Optimize for the end user, resisting short-term developer delight.
principles.quote: remember that you have two customers. You have your direct customer who's the developer, but then you have to be thinking about what is that developer trying to create? What is their customer?

principles.text: Design products for agents as the customer; LLM strengths and weaknesses will shape APIs, runtimes and frameworks.
principles.quote: Your customer is the agent that the developer or non-developer is wielding. That is actually a pretty significant change.

principles.text: LLMs are a new marketing channel: ChatGPT recommendations drive signups, so write LLM-first, question-style content and still rank in search.
principles.quote: people would come to our booth and tell them that they'd learned of Vercel because ChatGPT told them to use Vercel. This kind of changes how marketing is done, right?

sources.title: How Vercel built a front-end cloud, a framework, and v0: Guillermo Rauch on Acquired ACQ2
sources.originalTitle: ACQ2: Building Web Apps with Just English and AI
sources.summary: Guillermo Rauch explains how Vercel dominated one niche (front-end) before expanding, why Next.js stays open source while the infrastructure is the business, and how v0 turned English prompts into apps and hit $4M ARR in about 11 months. He also covers staying hands-on as a technical CEO and why teams will get smaller.

principles.text: Be world-class at one narrow thing first, then expand outward as customers pull more product out of you.
principles.quote: My number one priority is to be excellent at one thing. I want to be world-class at one thing. People call it dominating a niche.

principles.text: Don't match your product's first version to the size of your ambition; start small and excellent, then let customers pull the rest.
principles.quote: That I think is something a lot of entrepreneurs miss, which is they feel the initial presentation of their product has to match one-to-one the size of their ambition.

principles.text: Open source the programming model for adoption; monetize the operational infrastructure customers don't want to run, with usage-based pricing.
principles.quote: If an application on Vercel is small, then you don't pay a lot. If an application takes over the world, you pay more. It's a very fair deal to developers and they understand exactly what they're paying for.

principles.text: Open source projects like AI SDK are built for adoption, feedback and brand, not direct revenue; deployment revenue follows.
principles.quote: There's actually no direct business model for it. We want developer adoption. We want their feedback on their community. We want to get our brand out.

principles.text: Make the shortest path from code to a live, shareable URL; it unlocks collaboration with non-developers and shortens sales cycles.
principles.quote: What I underestimated, and it's been a wonderful gift for our business, is that companies value even more the ability for their developers to collaborate with other personas in the organization.

principles.text: Dogfood your platform with a tiny team and forbid special help, so you prove customers won't outgrow the product.
principles.quote: They're not allowed to cheat. They're not allowed to go to the infra team and say, oh I'm having a million requests per second right now.

sources.title: How Vercel moved from developer love to enterprise deals: Guillermo Rauch on DX plus enterprise sales
sources.originalTitle: Blend Developer Experience and Enterprise Sales
sources.summary: Guillermo Rauch explains how Vercel grew from a developer-first open source framework into an enterprise platform. He covers building beyond the developer champion, starting sales from customer success, closing deals before features like SSO existed, and using security as a differentiator.

principles.text: Design for the developer's stakeholders, not just the developer; think two layers beyond your early adopter.
principles.quote: my tool has a early adopter who's a developer, but that developer has stakeholders and, and users beyond that. So if you just think one layer in you're going to get stuck, most likely you have to think one layer in and then two layers deeper

principles.text: Go enterprise or stay stuck at one team: seat expansion inside big companies needs enterprise features.
principles.quote: in order for it to be rolled out to as many seats as possible within the company, we have to have that enterprise approach. Otherwise, you might get stuck at just one team within a company.

principles.text: Build sales on top of customer success: support reveals customer tiers, then AEs sell the long-term vision.
principles.quote: It started with customer success. So, it started with our support team, recognizing that there were basically different categories of clients

principles.text: Developers dislike sales, but the company buying wants a human and predictable pricing.
principles.quote: developers don't want to talk to sales, but the company as a whole wants to talk to sales. They want to understand who they're partnering with.

principles.text: Win enterprise deals with missing features by aligning your roadmap with the customer's security team and champions.
principles.quote: we worked as much as we could with their security teams, with our champions, within those companies to sort of align our roadmaps.

principles.text: Interview procurement, security and CSO stakeholders early, even before they buy, to build scalable products.
principles.quote: just talk to the person that works on procurement, on security, questionnaires on the CSO.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Guillermo Rauch explains why v0 exists (growing the pool of product builders from ~20M JavaScript developers to 100M), how specialist "translation tasks" are being absorbed by AI, and how to build taste through exposure hours. He also covers tight in-product feedback loops, escape hatches, and how Vercel's teams ship with AI.

chunks.heading: v0's mission and the 100 million builders thesis
chunks.text:
Guillermo frames v0 as the next step in the same mission as Vercel: "to enable the world to build and ship the best products." His estimate of the opportunity:
- About 5 million React developers and maybe 20 million JavaScript developers exist today.
- His "back of the napkin like minimum calculation" for people with aspirations of building products is 100 million.
- He anchors that number on Slack's roughly 100 million monthly active users, many of whom talk about products they want to see built. v0 lets them "yap into the computer and see something happen": a prototype, a demo, a full-stack product, shipped.

He calls this expanding the addressable market of people who actually ship software. He describes v0 as "social product building", an evolution of GitHub's "social coding" that no longer requires knowing how to code.

chunks.heading: Why v0 exists and why LLMs are good at it
chunks.text:
- Origin: when ChatGPT launched, it was already good at JavaScript, Tailwind and Next.js. Vercel's open source tools were already in the training data, so "that long-term bet and vision and open source really paid off."
- The idea was "a ChatGPT for building web products." The first v0 prototype may have predated ChatGPT; it ran on GPT-3.5.
- v0 uses a pipeline of models (OpenAI, Gemini, Claude), with different models specializing in different tasks and handing off work to one another.
- Files and components help: Next.js routes from a file, similar to PHP. LLMs struggle with massive codebases, but they do well when a task is scoped to one component or file.

chunks.heading: Scale, community and the fork flywheel
chunks.text:
Figures at recording time:
- Over 1.3 million users had interacted with v0.
- It was setting new daily usage records and was one of the biggest customers of most cloud providers, hitting limits across GPU and LLM infrastructure.
- v0 Community launched less than a month earlier and already had 20,000 submissions. Some showed 1,200, 1,500 and 6,000 forks, and a Luma Labs recruiting site got 2,000 forks in a day.

His reasoning:
- A blank prompt box causes writer's block, so forkable community projects give users a starting point.
- Sharing and forking compounds, like open source: someone shares, someone else improves it.
- A git commit summarizes intent after the work. In v0 the intent comes first and the code is the output. Git commit support was coming within days.

chunks.heading: Retention, feedback loops and building AI products
chunks.text:
- v0 is "a very retentive product" compared to other AI products he has built. People use it daily and get jittery when they hit a bug.
- His top advice to startup founders: "create a lot of opportunities for people to give you feedback inside the product." He took the idea from Stripe.
- Early Vercel had an inline feedback button with four emojis that routed straight into Slack. Early on this meant a few to hundreds of messages a day.
- AI products produce a constant stream of feedback through thumbs up/down and bug reports. The next model, prompt, fine-tune or RAG setup improves from it, and he says it is hard to compete with a product that has such a tight loop.
- Showing the model's thinking was inspired by DeepSeek. Users can see where the AI went wrong and correct it, and some report exactly that.
- Vercel open sourced much of what makes v0 work: chat templates at vercel.com/templates and the AI SDK, which connects any model and generates UI, not just text. He calls this generative UI.
- He expects vertical AI tools to win, such as GetGC for legal, OpenEvidence for doctors, chatPRD for PRDs and X-ray tooling. His reason is that a founder who obsesses over one domain and carries a point of view is hard to beat. He also doubts AI will fully replace human direction, since "AI doesn't always know exactly what we want or what we need."

chunks.heading: How product teams and roles change
chunks.text:
- Conversations between builders and customers get mediated by artifacts, such as v0 links. A PM can write a "live PRD": last night a v0 spec of the deploy-to-Vercel flow showed the error, success and slow-stream states, animated and interactive.
- People become more full stack: a designer shipping a baked product, a PM prototyping and shipping to production, a backend engineer finishing the end-to-end vision.
- Vercel has about 600 people, of whom about 150 write code by trade. His claim is that "now we have 600 engineers." Some of the best v0 creations came from marketing, sales and product.
- Examples: a designer built an interactive explainer of Vercel's compute infrastructure that became one of his most viral posts, and the VP of sales engineering built a prospect-education tool.
- Ritual: "Demo Fridays" give people permission to step out of their lane and build.
- His frame: AI is becoming synonymous with software. "We build software and we use software to build software."

chunks.heading: Skills that keep their value
chunks.text:
- Translation work is disappearing. Turning a design, screenshot or intent into React and CSS is a translation task. A test he runs on each new model, rebuilding his own website, took 10-15 prompts once and two prompts with the latest model. The model also produced more accessible code than he wrote.
- Knowing how things work under the hood still matters. Naming CSS, layout, styles and animation terms lets you steer the model. One designer used the word "turbulence" to get a specific animation effect.
- He expects specialists to need less depth, for example no longer memorizing every CSS property. That frees people for more ambitious work.
- Foundational infrastructure engineering will stay valuable for decades. LLMs orchestrate existing tools; they do not write a compiler, a cloud or a framework from scratch.
- For his five kids he pushes math, eloquence (the "wordcel" and "shape rotator" sides), and presenting and putting yourself out there. He takes them to hackathons. In a world where software gets cheaper to produce, he says you need to build an audience and a signature brand.
- If someone wants to go deep into code, he says JavaScript is "the English of programming languages," reaching billions of devices.

chunks.heading: Tips for getting results with v0
chunks.text:
- Be as ambitious as you want and steer toward inspiration. If you lack ideas, fork from the community.
- Stay open-minded: the tool may know things you don't. Focus on describing the product and the user experience rather than the implementation.
- Iterate like you would with an agency or a stuck engineer. Even "just try something else" often unsticks it, and he compares this to giving the tool a one-on-one performance review.
- Use evocative style tokens such as neo-brutalist, minimalist, newspaper-like, vintage, telegram, or "make it pop." A bank CIO improved a print brochure design in a couple of prompts this way.
