- He sees three core skills when building with AI: figuring out what to build, making it look good, and getting it unstuck. Escape hatches help here: you can view and edit the Next.js code, or paste it into another model. A Luma Labs engineer unstuck a ~100-iteration project by giving the code to OpenAI's o1.
- He cites React's "escape hatch" principle (for example dangerouslySetInnerHTML) as a systems design lesson. He also cites Facebook's principle of getting unblocked rather than staying blocked.
- Bring screenshots of your own artboards, Slack posts and designs, not just other sites. You can also ask v0 to center a div with the inline refinement tool.

chunks.heading: Taste, quality and product craft
chunks.text:
- Taste is a skill, not an inborn trait. Vercel's operating principle is "increasing exposure hours": quantify the time you spend watching people use your product and other products.
- He says teams tend to overrate how well their product works. Hand it to someone and "expose yourself to the pain of reality."
- His own habits: calendar-color customer meetings (about a third of his meetings that week), use the product during customer calls instead of thinking about internals, and invite customers to demo live to the exec team or company. These sessions surface pain nobody knew about.
- Detail example: Grok defaults Enter to a new line on mobile and to submit on desktop, because that matches user habits. He rebuilt a Grok-style chat UI in v0 to capture such details.
- "A great product is made up of a thousand little details," and the best product builders say nine nos for every yes: "a feature is like adopting a puppy." He admires Midjourney's mobile web and says that level of quality takes restraint, obsession and heavy dogfooding.
- Vercel and v0 are built using themselves.

chunks.heading: v0 demos, limits and roadmap
chunks.text:
- Flight radar example: on a poor in-flight connection from Tokyo, he built his own flight tracker in under two hours on his $20 plan. It used Mapbox, Leaflet and a flight data API, then a canvas layer to render tens of thousands of flights, with a dashed route line that accounted for Earth's curvature. He estimates the work would take weeks and tens of thousands of dollars with engineers. His working style is experience-first: front end first, then performance, then full stack.
- He keeps a fitness function in mind: find the thing v0 can't build. The product's commitment is real quality and performance. One user called v0 "a super genius five-year-old PhD with ADHD."
- Users have shipped real things: an enterprise customer builds all products and client communications in v0, someone sold a client website, and others used it for an engagement site.
- Limits he names:
  - Errors still happen; the agentic setup tries to fix runtime errors itself.
  - Very large codebases are harder.
- Roadmap mentioned:
  - Zip import now, Git coming soon.
  - Tighter Vercel Marketplace integrations that auto-install databases, search and AI models.
- On scale: the combined v0 and Vercel path lets one person go from prompt to a site that can reach 100 million people. Ramp had 43x traffic from a Super Bowl ad with 100% uptime, built by an engineer who only learned Next.js.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Vercel's CEO explains why great companies are defined by what they reject, how a high quality bar can coexist with speed, and why product simplicity depends on stage. He also covers hiring on tangible output and why AI interfaces often need more UI, not less.

chunks.heading: Starting from a narrow wedge, then sequencing the product
chunks.text:
- Guillermo says there is no universal truth on whether great products are "deceptively simple." It depends on stage and market.
- Early on he likes a simple interface that hides huge complexity. Examples: Google search, Auth0 (he invested), and Stripe (he admired it but did not invest). He calls Stripe "a simple API call that hides a tremendous amount of complexity."
- He thinks in terms of "sequencing." Seed, A, B, C and D are arbitrary, but they give a common language for pressure-testing frameworks.
- What gets you to Series A is not what gets you from D to IPO. The simplicity of your product from zero to one is not the simplicity from one to two.
- Companies become multi-product over time. AWS looks complex now, but a competitor will not win by copying it. They will bring a simplification, then re-evaluate their priors as the market changes.
- He cites a conversation with Snowflake's original CEO, whose view was that open source solves a zero-to-one problem (market positioning and awareness) but not the one-to-one-million problem.
- Guillermo is himself deeply open source (node.js since 0.1, Mongoose), and agrees that GitLab, Hashi and others succeeded on more than open source alone.

chunks.heading: Picking battles and saying no
chunks.text:
- "Great companies are defined by how many things they say no to."
- His own job is to build a few of the best products in his category, not to solve every problem a customer has. Compare a VC, whose job is to find a handful of the best companies in the world.
- Options for not solving a problem right now:
  - Push solutions to user space.
  - Skip entering a market.
  - Wait and hold. "Sometimes you're better off waiting" and letting the truth emerge from the experiments being run.
- He holds up Apple as a model: it does not react to every trend, it picks its battles.
- This matters more as the company matures: "you don't always have to be first, you have to be right."
- He says a good designer or product person is defined by how much they have rejected over time, and what survives many rounds of yes and no earns its place in the product lineup.
- Faster iteration loops that turn things down can be healthy if the system learns from each rejection. He uses Rick Rubin as the reference: Rubin's value is telling artists what he likes and does not like, not knowing how to play an instrument.

chunks.heading: Shipping fast with a high quality bar
chunks.text:
- Culturally, Vercel goes deeper into what counts as complete than most people are willing to. It spends a lot of time on internal testing before a product reaches the market.
- He separates a high bar from being slow. A founder told him his customers complained he was breaking their stuff too often while he was trying to move fast. His advice: reduce the blast radius of experimentation, so that by the time you bring a product to everybody you have enough evidence of success to have overwhelming confidence.
- He compares this to Boeing bending the wings of an airplane in the factory beyond what turbulence could realistically do, so millions of flights a year are safe. "You've gone above and beyond to certify and sign off."
- On whether the bar costs speed: if the process is rigorous, frequent and part of the culture, people carry the approach into their own work. He is not applying it to every project himself. He sets the bar, shares techniques, and tells stories.
- The stories matter because "moving fast and shipping with high quality" otherwise sounds contradictory. He points to how they did it for Next.js 1.0 and for the new deployment infrastructure.

chunks.heading: Hiring: judge by what people have put into the world
chunks.text:
- Guillermo works backwards from what outstanding products look like. This is why Vercel bet that front end matters, though it was overlooked for years. His own dad asked why he was wasting time on JavaScript instead of hardcore back-end languages.
- His main hiring signal, for people and for acquisitions, is what they have made that is tangible. What can he use? What hyperlinks have they shared? "You're communicating your capability through your creations."
- He admits this is not a silver bullet, since some people contribute more theoretically.
- Writing is another signal: whether they follow through, and the quality of how they present themselves. So are the stories they tell about their work.
- For candidates from big companies where attribution is hard (e.g. "I was at Apple for 25 years"), he wants a narrative of where they moved the needle. How did that contribution reach the business or make an end user's or developer's experience better?
- To separate depth from storytelling, he goes into the details:
  - how they implemented something, down to the syscall
  - which cloud infrastructure they used
  - what alternatives and vendors they were aware of
  - for a paper, what other papers they looked at
- He wants conceptual understanding. A candidate does not need to know how to write a custom Linux kernel module, but should be able to explain how the parts fit together.
- His biggest hiring mistake was overweighting a resume that was "a stellar list of awesome brands" (Apple, Google, Amazon, Netflix). Four strong companies in a row cannot all be wrong, but he now treats that with curiosity about what the person actually brings. He says the same trap exists with universities.
- On second-time founders, he agrees they are a good heuristic but warns the pool is constrained. His reasoning: "You don't have to get every single opportunity right. You just have to get a few great ones."
- His own edge as a founder was seeing decisions at an early-stage startup where he "would have chosen the exact opposite," then setting up hiring, product development and speed differently. He sold his first startup in a moderately successful exit and built his second on those learnings.

chunks.heading: AI changes interface design, and more UI is needed
chunks.text:
- Guillermo expects UI to change, not disappear. The jobs people have to do (decisions, data, communication) stay, but how they get done is profoundly transformed.
- When designing software in the past 10 years, AI was not in the design space. Now you can invoke reasoning machines on demand, so a next Notion, Superhuman or Figma would look completely different.
- He says design instinct is like a go player's pattern matching (the Lee Sedol versus AlphaGo reference). The board has shifted, so software 1.0 designers have to update.
- Startups have no legacy software to retrofit AI onto. Incumbents can say "I added AI, ship it" and increase their TAM, but they are also exposed to someone producing a completely different design.
- Vercel's own products are moving the same way. What used to be dragging, dropping and long editing is increasingly typing in English, and Vercel's job is to help developers create the new kinds of interfaces.
- He pushes back on "UI matters less":
  - Software 1.0 is deterministic: input a, b, c, get d every time.
  - AI is probabilistic, so "you actually have to create UIs that tame the craziness of the machine."
  - Midjourney is the example: a text prompt returns four choices. "It's actually giving you more UI, not less, because it's uncertain about what it is that you actually want."
  - The choices also feed data back into the system.
- On the paradox of choice: more options suit the creative stage of a workflow. The best assistant has rich context about what you like and proposes better variations over time, but should not be too absolutist.
- Successful AI products so far are suggestive, not authoritative: Copilot, Gmail Smart Compose, Notion AI. Agents acting alone with no supervision have not produced many successful products.
- He expects agents to arrive, but with a close feedback loop. His metaphor is the editor in a newsroom: agents bring ideas, you say "nope, go back to the drawing board," and you set the creative direction. He calls this the healthiest AI future, because the alternative, with AI calling the shots, is what scares people.
- Against a view that "selling the work, not the tools" will leave incumbents winning only an intermediary phase, he says it may be true over a long timeline but gives no practical advice for the next few quarters.
  - The iPhone's OS came from retrofitting Mac OS, not a fresh codebase. The first killer app was shrinking websites onto a small screen, and native-only apps came later.
  - He expects AI and traditional software to co-evolve the same way, so chat-type interfaces will meet customers where they are, and "it's still all UIs all the way down."

chunks.heading: Incumbents versus new entrants in AI
chunks.text:
- Guillermo's example: Microsoft Word shipped a thick toolbar exposing every option, a fully additive approach where adding utilities gets you promoted. Notion did less. It offers 8 or 16 text colors and no custom hex input, which he reads as a focus decision.
- A hypothetical next entrant might do even less, because AI can do exactly what you want without the menus, icons and blocks. The incumbent then faces "holy crap, we have to delete everything" after crafting every icon, menu, doc and training video.
- When challenged that today's incumbents are stronger and faster than ever (Notion, Adobe), he agrees they can be underestimated in both directions.
  - He gives Microsoft credit for telling the company years ago to focus on AI.
  - He praises Adobe's Firefly additions as high quality and considered.
  - But the interface itself can shift. Midjourney is a place where Photoshop's drag-and-drop, magic wand, selection tool and color switcher "just don't exist."
- His desktop-to-mobile analogy: the right call for Meta was not to delete desktop software but to go where the growth and user minutes were going and "almost start over." Desktop still exists, like AM and FM radio, but the growth is elsewhere. Most incumbents historically do not manage this.

chunks.heading: Pricing: hybrid seat plus consumption
chunks.text:
- Vercel offers two things: front-end hosting with infrastructure that scales autonomously (a consumption, pay-for-what-you-use model like Snowflake), and iteration velocity and agility, similar to Google Docs or Figma, via collaboration with shared links across the organization.
- His claim: businesses that sell only one half of that equation will become less popular. Buyers want a comprehensive platform for business problems, "like an operating system for my organization," especially at scale.
- Vercel combines SaaS priced per seat, for platform capabilities, with infrastructure that grows when visitors use the software.
- AI accelerates what cloud already started. AI products cost more to serve the more they are used (GPU cycles, "expensive outsourced intelligence"), so a flat $20 to $30 a month does not model it.
- He expects more hybrid models: a baseline of utility, plus the ability to burst and use more of what you can automate for me.

chunks.heading: Open versus closed AI, and his framework for betting
chunks.text:
- He says he has no firm prediction, but gives his framework from how past platform wars resolved.
  - Kubernetes won because every company decided it was the standard to build an ecosystem on.
  - React won "the hearts and minds" of the ecosystem, and developers talk about "React brain."
  - Linux brain: the ecosystem value of everyone who learned Linux overcame proprietary alternatives, even when it benchmarked worse.
  - On this basis, "Llama becomes Linux." It is not as good as GPT-4 now ("not even close"), but ecosystem commitment (researchers, hardware budgets, documentation, user-space tools like LlamaIndex and LangChain) can make it better.
- The counter-thesis is a Jeff Bezos line about why AWS pulled ahead: even a two-year technology advantage can be lethal, five years is exponential, and ten is nearly impossible to catch.
- He applies this to Vercel's own bets. When others bet on static rendering, Vercel bet on dynamic front-end rendering, which was less popular among VCs in the Valley at a few crucial points.
- On the AI funding question, he disagrees that 99% of cash going into AI companies goes to zero. He compares it to Web 2.0 (mobile and social produced Uber, Airbnb, Facebook), and would bet about 20% of investments are productive, including companies that get acquired. He mentions Vercel might buy an AI company.

chunks.heading: Angel investing lessons
chunks.text:
- Many of his best angel investments were problems he would have loved to work on himself but lacked the time and bandwidth for. Scale AI is an example, and he says he got lucky choosing the right horse.
- Founders should be uniquely positioned, but not necessarily by existing expertise. He says "it's about the slope," meaning how fast people can learn, which is also his hiring philosophy.
- Judge the problem and market separately from the solution. "It's all about people's willingness to buy a certain thing." Be open-minded, because he can be bad at judging solutions.
- On Auth0, he was skeptical about outsourcing auth to a three-person startup ("chicken and egg"), but invested because he knew implementing auth is "freaking hell."
- The same pattern shows up with Slack. People knew the problem (collaboration over chat) but the solution space was odd, including IRC-as-a-service and a Slack IRC proxy. When he sold his first company to WordPress and Matt said to install Slack and deprecate IRC, his first reaction was the same hesitation about trusting a company with all their communication.
- His rule of thumb: when the problem is very painful and your only hesitation is whether you can offload it to someone else, there may be a huge opportunity.
- He also notes that people overestimate their capacity to solve problems excellently themselves, as when he used to set up IRC servers for teams.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Guillermo Rauch explains how Vercel and Next.js reached very fast product-market fit: he narrowed from "deploy everything" to frontend, dogfooded a framework, and integrated with existing tools. He also covers open source monetization, early positioning, pricing, and where AI is taking engineering.

chunks.heading: Simplify first: the cloudup lesson behind Vercel
chunks.text:
- At his first startup (edtech) Guillermo tried to "boil the ocean" with a very broad platform. Users kept latching onto one feature, file sharing used for lesson plans.
- He pivoted to cloudup: drag and drop a file or folder from the menu bar and get back a URL. The product was reliable, took 30 seconds to demo, and needed no storytelling.
- Folders of HTML files got fast static hosting. Cloudup was sold to Automattic (WordPress) in 2013, before it opened to the public.
- His takeaway is the "unreasonable effectiveness of URLs": a shareable link is embeddable anywhere. Vercel's preview URL for every change is the same idea, much as Google Docs did for word processing and Figma for design.
- On company building, he says focus matters most early, and it is easy to slowly let go and overbuild. Returning to the simplicity of cloudup is what produced the exit.

chunks.heading: How Vercel started: a founder's own pain, dogfooded
chunks.text:
- As an early AWS user he loved the idea of hardware becoming software, but found that doing anything in the cloud was "so freaking hard".
- At WordPress he saw millions invested in hosting one application, wordpress.com, while every new app or feature stayed hard. The industry was moving from monoliths to microservices.
- He left to make deploying software "completely instantaneous" and give that power back to the developer. His rule was to dogfood from day one: build a tool he would use every day to improve itself.
- His first task was a company website with a production-grade stack, using React and a deployment platform on top of Kubernetes. Four weeks of struggling confirmed his hypothesis.
- If he struggled, he reasoned, the next 100,000 companies going through digital transformation would too, especially e-commerce players moving from brick and mortar.
- Selling to successful companies at WordPress gave him a view of highly qualified Enterprise buyers who have the capital to buy innovative technology.

chunks.heading: Next.js: a high bar, a customer zero, and a "seven principles" master plan
chunks.text:
- In 2014 he wrote an essay, "the seven principles of Rich web applications", before he had any framework. He calls it a Tesla-style master plan for what became Next.js and Vercel.
- He reverse engineered how Google Search, Facebook and amazon.com were built. His bar was that Next.js should have no compromises: it could build a small website but also the next Amazon or Google. Most of his original code is now deleted, but the bar gave direction.
- He told himself he would put out a deployment platform prototype in 3 months, publicly, to get feedback.
- The platform needed a dynamic web app for logs and orchestration, so he started the framework internally (called N4) with the deployment platform as customer zero. He compares this to Rust, whose early customer zero was Mozilla's Servo rendering engine.
- React was "a great engine" that needed "a car". After about six months of internal use he open sourced it.
- It felt like an overnight success, he says, but it came after a long internal battle. He had been thinking about the principles for two years or more.

chunks.heading: Reading product-market fit signals
chunks.text:
- Fast growth right out of the gate is a sign the product solves a huge pain, though it can be hard to see.
- A strong signal is that smart people at other companies are building the same thing. Right after launch, someone from Redfin reached out saying they were building it, and a week later Trulia did. Companies running businesses at scale were building or about to staff a version.
- He already had a following from MooTools, Socket.io and Bongo, so developers would look. The corresponding interest from large organizations is what made him "extremely bullish".
- Signals were mixed for a couple of years. Server rendering ran against the popular narrative of rendering everything on the client, and some developers preferred competing alternatives. He says he had to navigate the market and competition for quite a few years.

chunks.heading: Balancing developer experience and user experience
chunks.text:
- He says "developer experience at all costs" doesn't work. Developers (himself included) sometimes choose what is easier for them at the expense of end users.
- Many developers assumed the user side would figure itself out. Years later it hadn't, and Next.js invested in a balance.
- He distinguishes a "simplistic" solution from a "simple" one. A project can promise the world on your laptop but ignore a million users, deployment and scaling. Real global systems are often in a partial state of constantly recovering.
- Internally he frames this as "day one versus day 1000": it has to be good at day one but never at the expense of day 1000, which has to be secure, debuggable and global.
- The opposite myth is that systems built for huge scale must be hard to use. He cites Redpanda: faster than Kafka, a single statically linked C++ binary, lower memory footprint, and no ZooKeeper, so it has both good DX and business value.

chunks.heading: Focus on the front end, and win through integrations
chunks.text:
- His early deployment platform tried to deploy absolutely everything, so its complexity equalled the hardest thing deployable (his example was a Java Docker container needing 20 GB of memory).
- Their "finding ourselves" moment: their earliest customers and design partners were in e-commerce and storefronts. So they simplified to the frontend, building the "front-end cloud" instead of "the cloud".
- It resonated with customers because enterprises tune out vendors who promise to solve every problem. He says it's better to say what you do not solve and integrate with what they already bought. Enterprises buy about a thousand SaaS products on average, so "your strength can be in what you don't build".
- He underestimated the value of excellent integrations. Their GitHub and GitLab integrations took probably tens of thousands of developer hours of tuning. Users link a repo, and every commit builds and returns a URL.
- He warns that Founders fall into the trap of saying "please use our hosting too" instead of integrating.
- The frontend cloud's shift is from static to dynamic. Teams cache everything in a CDN under load or attack and lose personalization, even whether a user is logged in. Vercel offers an incremental path: modernize the front end and keep the back end.
- He says ChatGPT is built on Next.js, and that many generative AI companies bet on Vercel for dynamism.
- Services integrate by shipping a React component, the "Lego bricks for adults". Examples he gives: Clerk (auth), Frigade (product tours and onboarding), Resend (email).
- Backends were built first as foundations. Newer companies succeed by going higher up the stack, for example not making you rebuild your login screen for the thousandth time.

chunks.heading: From open source to business, and pricing
chunks.text:
- His framework is to align the value creation of the open source project with that of the business behind it. Users want continuous investment (commit activity, green tests) and a bet that lasts 10 years.
- Business paths he lists: open core (limit features), licensing that constrains deployment, or an infrastructure business. Vercel took the infrastructure route, outsourcing "a team's worth of responsibility". A Japanese customer presented how many engineers moved from platform engineering to product engineering and data science.
- Open source is "the global Maxima": a company supporting it automates undifferentiated work, while the customer keeps the option to take the workload on-prem. He would do it the same way again and keep the product as free and available as possible.
- Pricing began with metering every infrastructure resource. It later expanded to a hybrid reflecting platform value beyond hosting: collaboration, pre-production, QA and iteration speed. He compares it to GitHub's value plus Snowflake's infrastructure value.
- Customers use it differently. Some use all of it, and some in highly regulated environments use Vercel only pre-production for faster iteration.

chunks.heading: Positioning, multi-product, and AI
chunks.text:
- Early on, be relatable to what already exists. A lofty category name hurts a small team with three landing pages. He once told the team to change a landing page hero that made no sense, and Vercel's deployment history let them laugh at an oversimplified old version like "faster websites made easier".
- You earn the right to define a category later. Partners (Shopify headless, Algolia, CMS vendors) help by teaching their customers that their product makes sense with a front-end-as-a-service. Sales engineers use Vercel to demo their back ends.
- He cites Stripe: its first code snippet (curl and an API call) made it instantly understandable. Today the higher-level entry is often a React component, like a checkout, because back-end complexity has accumulated.
- Vercel's products: managed infrastructure, the DX platform (iteration speed, even for on-prem users), and v0, which he calls "generative UI". v0 turns a plain-English prompt into React and Tailwind code with taste and accessibility.
- v0's catalyst was noticing developers still spend lots of time copying and pasting. Frontend quality is judged visually, so he says code is becoming less interesting.
- On AI: it is an accelerator of human potential. He frames it as removing tedium.
- His product heuristics:
  - Anytime you start from blank (an email reply, a support ticket), give the user a starting draft.
  - Help users before they file a support case, with co-pilots and contextual docs.
  - Anytime you show an error, suggest the solution.
  - Quoting Elon, "all user input is error"; ask whether the input was necessary.
- Domain-expert AI beats general chatbots. He cites finance reporting tool thin tool.com and a legal AI proof of concept for redlining. He doesn't think chat text will be the only interaction mode.
- He predicts that in 10 to 20 years engineers write very little code by hand, much like not thinking about compiler instructions today. Engineers shift toward creativity, curation and feedback, and AI helps legacy customers migrate incrementally.

chunks.heading: Advice: velocity, saying no, raising the bar
chunks.text:
- Focus on iteration velocity, not speed. Velocity is speed with a direction. Sometimes the answer is to build less, or to talk to a prospect and find their real pain.
- Customers can be too nice, so do the work to discover what is behind feedback or a metric that isn't moving.
- Say no to more things. When launching Next.js he launched two other successful open source projects at once and says there was no need. Seven years later he is still improving Next.js.
- He invokes Steve Jobs: saying no "has to hurt" because the ideas you turn down are genuinely interesting.
- Be honest with yourself and the team about whether you meet the quality bar and iteration velocity you are chasing. "We're here to raise the bar", especially leaders.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Rauch explains how v0 doubled Vercel's user base in under a year, why vibe coding and agentic engineering coexist, and how Vercel is rebuilding the cloud around agents, MCP and tokens. He also covers taste, designing from the model forward, doubling down on users who say it's life-changing, and his personal operating principles.

chunks.heading: Why Vzero exists and how it started
chunks.text:
- Guillermo describes Vzero as converting text or an idea into an application. It speaks to an audience Vercel hadn't reached before: "basically everybody with a job or even everybody without a job."
- Vercel's original product required engineering skills. Vzero only requires an idea.
- Traction he cites as of the interview (Oct 2025): over 100 million generated applications, about 7 app generations per second, and a user base that more than doubled Vercel's entire base in under a year (Vercel had been around almost 10 years).
- It began as a small skunkworks team (about four people, with Guillermo doing QA at launch; about 10 now). The reason was to prove the AI cloud infrastructure with a "patient zero" application that embodies the transformation he expects every company to go through.
- As of the previous week, Vzero runs a "GM model": a general manager acts as CEO of Vzero and is a customer of the Vercel platform. He compares it to a microservice architecture for people, with Vzero as amazon.com and Vercel as the AWS underneath.
- Vercel also hosts many Vzero competitors. He believes there will be billions of agents and wants Vercel to be the platform they are built on.

chunks.heading: Vibe coding, agentic engineering, and where each fits
chunks.text:
- Vibe coding (Karpathy's term): you don't pay attention to the code; you give requirements, watch what gets built, and give feedback on the product, not the code.
- Agentic engineering (a term from the Zed team): you pay close attention to everything the agent generates. He wants Vercel's mission-critical infrastructure people (e.g. fluid compute, which just hit a trillion function invocations) working this way.
- His split: low-level and mission-critical work leans agentic engineering; apps, interfaces, demos, prototypes, specs, and slide decks lean vibe coding. Both have a place.
- Market size logic: an IDE-based tool still requires being a coder (downloading tools, setting up dev servers, SDKs). A web product like Vzero has a TAM of "everyone with a computer," because you open a website and start.
- The two worlds connect. Vzero has a git integration, so a vibe-coded project can be handed to professional coders. He also made the Vzero model available inside code editors like Cursor, VS Code, and open code.
- Why use the Vzero model over a stock model: it carries up-to-date Next.js and React knowledge, library knowledge (e.g. the AI SDK), design patterns, taste, and best practices.

chunks.heading: Encoding expertise into a model
chunks.text:
- Origin of Next.js: after a talk at BrazilJS where he presented "seven principles of rich web applications," he realized he couldn't scale himself by going to every conference. So he built a framework that embeds the best practices. "It was literally an essay to web framework pipeline."
- Next.js today has 1.4 million monthly active developers and powers sites like Midjourney, Walmart, and Nike.
- The Vzero model is the next step: "my brain into tokens," plus his team's and the community's (CTO ex-Google 11 years, CPO ex-Meta who created React, 13 years). He aims to scale from 1.4 million developers toward 100 million or a billion.
- He argues every company will go through the same process: turning its expertise from ad hoc work or SaaS into tokens. He cites Jensen Huang's "token factory" idea.
- Vercel's own support runs on the Vzero model at vercel.com/help. Human support became "customer support engineers" handling only frontier problems that AI can't solve, and they use Vzero to suggest product fixes that remove whole ticket categories. He was initially skeptical about AI support for a technical audience, but customers responded warmly.
- He tracks "disengagement" events (borrowing the self-driving term) to see where the product leaks and the model needs work.

chunks.heading: Building for agents as customers
chunks.text:
- Agents are given tools, context, and a prompt, and they wield the tools. Tools used to be drawn in front of a human's face. His point: agents removed the GUI by using the tools themselves and returning results.
- Developer workflow reality: developers constantly hit errors, alt-tab to Google, and paste errors. Vzero now hands that loop to the agent, and sometimes doesn't even render the error because the agent will probably fix it.
- Developer tools now have two audiences. Humans want visual context in errors and docs. Agents want "pure signal, no noise": raw text, `llm.txt`, or raw markdown. He expects dual output: HTML for humans, text for agents.
- Vercel started as a simple command-line tool (type `vercel` and enter to deploy). He was repeatedly told to move beyond the CLI for broader appeal, but now when Claude Code deploys something, it uses Vercel: "we accidentally created the perfect tool for an agent to deploy."
- His summary: "you need to be thinking about agents as your customer and developers as your customer."

chunks.heading: MCP and the generative web
chunks.text:
- He explains MCP as "the HTTP for AIs": a protocol that lets AIs talk to other AIs and call tools over the internet.
- Vercel reduced deploying an MCP server to about five lines of code. Zapier hosts MCP servers on Vercel, and he says some run significant volume.
- Why a company should do it: an MCP server is your "minimum viable AI product." If you're Target, exposing inventory via MCP makes you interoperable with ChatGPT and with Vzero (internal teams can build tools against it in plain English). Not doing it means excluding yourself from that economy.
- He thinks MCP "will be the new business development, but at 100 times the speed," with agents meeting instead of people.
- His historical analogy: Amazon Web Services was named for the Web 2.0 "mashup" idea. Mashups didn't take off then, but he thinks they're relevant again with MCP, producing cross-pollination between products and a "fully generative" internet with no rigid fixed interface.
- Security: new needs include observing which MCP tools are called, harmful context, and prompt injection. His example: hiding a prompt injection in an image that a human can't see but a model reads, triggering a tool call that exfiltrates data. Vercel's AI security team works on new primitives beyond a traditional firewall.
- Commerce: he expects hyper-personalized experiences for returning customers, using memory (extracting about five key facts like preferences and location from an event log) to improve later visits.

chunks.heading: The AI cloud: pixels to tokens
chunks.text:
- His framing: a transition "from pixels to tokens." Pixels still matter (fast, beautiful), but much more will happen agentically by serving tokens.
- Core idea: a traditional cloud showers operators with problems (alerts, 500 errors). "An AI cloud should have agents that automatically produce solutions rather than give you problems."
- Vercel sees every request end to end (CDN, firewall, rendering, backend), so a Vercel agent can investigate anomalies and open pull requests. He wants to say to a customer like OpenAI, "I've cooked on what I believe to be 95% or in many cases actually 100% of the solution." Humans stay in the loop.
- Three problem areas: attacks (e.g. bots doing credit-card stuffing and scraping on a sneaker site; the agent investigates anomalies like a 100x traffic spike from one country and decodes spoofed user agents); outages (attributing the cause, e.g. a failed upstream dependency, during the Google Cloud outage); and optimization (e.g. unoptimized images on mobile, delivered as pull requests).
- Fluid compute: AI workloads such as a model "thinking" for 15 minutes don't fit short-burst serverless. Fluid only bills for actual CPU cycles used, not idle waiting time. He says the compute work already existed and the change was the billing model.
- Other pieces announced: AI Gateway (beta), Vercel Sandbox (secure place to run model-generated code, "the Amazon EC2 of AI"), the Vercel agent, and a marketplace of partner products (Braintrust for evals, Browserbase and Browser Use for agent browsers).
- He stresses data-driven evals as non-optional for AI products, e.g. tracking the acceptance rate of changes an agent proposes.

chunks.heading: Product and business decisions at Vercel
chunks.text:
- Persona focus: he "doubled down where there was the light," citing Bezos. Vzero is usable by everyone, but the people who said it was life-changing were dev-adjacent people at companies (outside the dev room but working daily with developers).
- Design from the model forward: the first Vzero UI was too ambitious (three generations per prompt, hard to get into an agentic conversation). Rebuilding for what models could actually do was labeled "V1" internally, and traction improved "by 100x." Still leave room for the sci-fi future, and design for where models will be in six months.
- Economics: he says Vzero has positive gross margins that are improving. He attributes healthy retention to an enduring business persona: at work "you're forced to be creative," and there is an economic equation attached. He wants to add ways for individuals to make money (in-app payments, subscriptions), inspired by Apple's app store and by WordPress, which he saw through his previous company's sale.
- Growth: he cites roughly $100M revenue last year and around $180M at the start of this year (the host's figures, which he didn't dispute) and says it comes from "all of the above" including AI. A lot of it is Vzero.
- Leaning into AI trends early: he defended "ChatGPT wrappers" ("everything's always been a wrapper of a wrapper") and built the AI SDK, which he says is the second largest AI module in the TypeScript ecosystem behind OpenAI's, and a chat SDK.
- Earlier tailwinds: product-market fit "accidentally" in e-commerce (accelerated by COVID) and crypto.
- Churn view: Vzero is "a mind virus." Users may cancel and return months later when they need a prototype because "you can't forgo efficiency."
- Distribution tactics for Vzero: a community of one-click clonable examples (compared to Notion templates), starting from a screenshot, diagram, or photographed napkin sketch, and an "enhance prompt" button.

chunks.heading: Taste, communication, and principles
chunks.text:
- On taste: you need a vision, must be able to articulate it, and must give and receive feedback. He builds taste through "exposure hours": understand how people actually use your product, and use many other products so crossovers become new ideas.
- He wants AI creators to "set the bar" so AI doesn't produce slop (the way TikTok could have set a different bar), by embedding instructions and context.
- "Sweat every pixel": every pixel, button, or feature is a liability (surface area that can confuse users or go wrong). He contrasts ChatGPT's simple UI with Google's crowded one.
- He posts on X first to himself and his team (almost 700 Vercel employees), and to the builder community. He applies the same minimalism to words, calling prompting and communicating "practice," and believes "there is a positive correlation between prompting and success."
- On criticism: stay positive, don't post meanness, use negativity sparingly, and assume good faith. "There's a kernel of truth in everything a customer says"; the customer is always right. "I'm not here to create fans of Rauch G. I'm here to create amazing products."
- Competition mindset: whatever your size, you're competing with "the vibe coder in a garage."

chunks.heading: Advice for a young developer
chunks.text:
- Focus on learning everything available in the new world; don't chase high-status old paths. He bet on JavaScript when it was considered a toy language, and was being recruited by Facebook at 17.
- Coding will be done by agents, so learn enough to tell an agent what you want and to understand system limits (hardware, services, LLMs).
- He supports companies screening for AI literacy (naming Shopify and Zapier): prompting is a proxy for curiosity.
- "The world makes progress one deployment at a time, not one line of code at a time." Code needs to run to be useful; abstraction keeps rising.
- Keep learning math (systems thinking) and language and writing (pitches, storytelling). He recommends reading high-quality literature and says AI isn't yet at Borges level.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Guillermo Rauch explains how Vercel scales founder-style ownership through autonomous product leads, an internal omni-agent ("V"), open-sourced skills, and work-prompt interviews. He argues platforms beat bespoke SaaS in the agent era, quality comes from raising the floor, and the human edge is taste, capital allocation, energy and grind.

chunks.heading: Recursive founder mode: how Guillermo structures Vercel's product organization
chunks.text:
Guillermo's response to Paul Graham's founder mode essay (September 2024) is "recursive founder mode": founder mode doesn't scale on its own, so he builds "the machine that builds the machine."

- Vercel started by hosting frontends, then expanded to backends, agents, and the whole agentic software development life cycle. That meant growing the product portfolio and the team.
- He keeps the founder traits (pioneering spirit, being the voice of the customer, pride over every detail) but spreads them across a handful of product owners, each acting as "the CEO of his own product."
- Examples: Lars Grahammer (AI SDK, a seasoned engineer with a strong point of view who joined Vercel); Tom Leonard (Fluid Compute, an acquired one-man company who did marketing, comms, product design and a low-level Rust runtime); and the founder of Vercel's feature flags product, now one of its fastest-growing products.
- His job is to set the organizational framework, the values, and the KPIs and north stars with his executive team. He then creates "pools of autonomy" because the best people could otherwise start their own companies.
- Many new Vercel products are bootstrapped on the Vercel platform itself: "we have millions of companies building on Vercel and now we also have companies within Vercel."
- Why talent stays: some acquired products didn't do as well standalone but thrive "as part of a broader platform." The feature flags founder found distribution and channel inside Vercel.
- His "love language" is seeing someone take full ownership of the end-to-end business. He expects AI to force this, since models can already do a narrow job like writing Rust.
- On retention, he's explicit in interviews that the work "is going to take at least a decade" with insane hours and a lot of fun. He avoids "jitter" in the organization and is supportive of people who want to start companies.

chunks.heading: Hiring in the AI era: work prompts and proof of work
chunks.text:
Guillermo says the requirements change weekly, and his interviews now center on building.

- He screens for a mindset that extrapolates: where will things be in 6 or 12 months? "We are in the middle of an exponential." He wants proof of work, and asks candidates what they would ship next week.
- Interviews include a "work prompt": candidates build something, produce an artifact, and talk through it. He values the side quests they take, such as features they found missing or where they got stuck. One candidate delivered a beautiful output but noted she wasted an hour on something Vercel could fix, which signaled a point of view on improving the platform.
- This applies to non-technical hires too. Marketers are expected to build agents that produce marketing artifacts instead of filing Jira tickets or begging for engineering or agency resources: "You solve that problem."
- Vercel is nearly 800 people. He doesn't meet every hire, but hiring agents keep him posted on interview loops, with his requirements embedded in the candidate-summary prompts. He still reviews work and profiles, and sometimes asks for async revisions.
- Candidate experience matters even for rejections: "we think of you as a customer."
- He takes each hire seriously because he expects people to stick around for a decade.

chunks.heading: Moving fast without blocking: iterative greatness and choke points
chunks.text:
- One of Vercel's values is "iterative greatness" (ITG). "No one at Vercel has the right to block things." He uses a Dune reference: "The spice must flow. The tokens must flow." Only security can halt the production line.
- If an executive objects, that is a veto, which puts the onus on the objector: "You don't get to relax."
- His rule for approvals: "Send me the email, and when I get time to review it, your product goes out." Vercel has "very, very few and very carefully designed choke points."
- He and the CTO obsessively study throughput, for example by asking agents to study the changelog rate (how frequently product improvements are communicated to customers).
- He resolves the speed-vs-taste tension by raising the floor: hiring, culture, and the platform make it "kind of hard to come into Vercel, be competent... and then ship a POS into the world."
- Example: shadcn built a component system that raised the floor of the internet, and Vercel extended it into its own Geist component system.
- Design engineering is building an agent that reviews work for polish and delight. He says AI and taste are a "false dichotomy": what's tasteless is taking raw model output (purple gradients, uppercase separated text, a green "online" dot). Skills can encode taste and best practices.

chunks.heading: "Everything is code": building the software factory
chunks.text:
- One of his banger tweets: "everything is code." A slide deck, a document and an Excel spreadsheet are code (tool calls plus a little Python). The data from Vercel's AI Gateway shows most token volume is from coding agents. "Coding is a misnomer."
- The new engineering skill is a meta-skill: "I work on the output" shifts to "I work on the machine that produces the output." He sees the acceleration of delivery correlated with the acceleration of revenue.
- Example: the AI SDK repo is being turned into a public software factory. Issues and model changes get typified and handled automatically, so keeping up with new model capabilities is largely automated.
- He expects the rise of the "product engineer" (Lee Robinson's post): someone who covers product management, P&L, customers, retention and expansion, plus engineering.
- Past waves of gatekeeping repeated: JavaScript as a "toy language," data center operators dismissing AWS. His takeaway: "the fork in the road" is either an identity crisis or a leap to the next platform. His family mindset is "if it's new, we're into it," as with mining Bitcoin early and seeing Copilot-style autocomplete as the second coming.
- Skills: Vercel launched skills.sh, an open repository of skills. He open-sourced Vercel's Next.js knowhow so any customer's AI-written code can be as good as his. His conviction is that Vercel's value is the whole platform and the trust earned by giving things away. He is also converting his own communication craft into internal skills.

chunks.heading: V and Eve: one internal agent for the whole company
chunks.text:
- Many companies gave everyone a Claude subscription, and usage diverged widely: some people use prompt libraries and skills, others "clock in, clock out." Vercel's fix is an internal agent in a self-improvement loop, called V.
- Principle: like the iPhone, agents need "one front door." Internally it was the "omni agent project." Employees ask V when they want a job automated or have a question about the business or a customer. Under the hood are agents, applications, skills and a team that maintains it.
- Vercel open-sourced the Eve framework for building agents like V.
- Examples: the COO built about a dozen go-to-market agents (lead routing, sales skills) and rethought go-to-market agent-first. The data team built a data agent, with a security model so policy on who can access what is in the agent's brain. Their SLA is now measured as time to first token instead of a ticket queue. V once suggested a tweet about reaching two billion deployments by combining the data agent and its own hypotheses.
- Executives are "agent builders." Guillermo says a company's foundation increasingly starts with the agent that helps run the business, even before a website or incorporation. V's personality is even being tuned (an intern improved it because it didn't "speak like a Vercelian").
- Collaboration pattern: "It's always going to be you, me and the agent." He wants agents in DM threads (with consent) so people see how capable they are. If he DMs a person, "it probably meant that my agent couldn't figure it out."
- His personal workflow: CLI-first, firing asynchronous research tasks at the lowest-level substrate he can get, and he keeps a research folder. Example: he asks an agent how easy it is to sign up for the AI Gateway and get an API token, which used to require a product review meeting.

chunks.heading: Agent-readiness, token economics and model benchmarking
chunks.text:
- He now judges vendors on agent interoperability. He approved spend on a sales and marketing platform that plugs into V, and has vendors on the "chopping block" because their MCP took thousands of tool calls and failed often.
- Infrastructure must absorb agentic load: Vercel's own load doubled in a couple of months, and agents can 100x load week to week. He cited a GitHub outage as an example of infrastructure not holding up. A legacy internal platform that can't absorb agent-driven deploys gets replaced ("I gave you a Ferrari... I just went into a two-week queue").
- Cloud services for the agent age: "a CDN for tokens" (AI Gateway), sandboxes, and MCP 2.0 backends deployable on Vercel. Agents increasingly choose their own tools. He quotes Notion's founder: designers should now design CLIs and APIs.
- Vercel built DeepSec, a security-review tool that tells models to be paranoid about auth, security and privacy. He found a model that was great at finding vulnerabilities cost thousands of dollars on their codebases, while Kimi was cheaper (about seven times) though less capable. Vercel builds benchmarks (like a DeepSec bench) because model cost and quality shift constantly, including new open-weight releases.
- Vision: ask V for a security review and it automatically calls DeepSec and decides how much to invest. "Tokens are going to become a huge percentage of your operating budget" and will inform P&L by business area.
- Why v0: he thinks about time to "aha." v0 packages Vercel's skills so a prompt yields a Next.js project at Vercel's quality bar, making it faster to try and sell Vercel. Vercel's soul remains the platform: whether you use Claude Code or v0, can you deploy software and agents?

chunks.heading: Platforms, moats and the future of software
chunks.text:
- He doesn't buy a "complete SaaS apocalypse." Bespoke software that doesn't fit a platform may not survive, but platforms will do extraordinarily well.
- Example: a large marketing agency moved from buying 10 to 20 point products to building its own agents and internal tools on Vercel (even competing with an Adobe product for its own needs). That adds to its IP and consolidates procurement to one platform.
- Infrastructure is hard to "vibe code": it needs operational rigor, security and global distribution, so infrastructure and platforms are strong moats.
- He expects the bar for a venture investment to recalibrate, and a reinvigoration of small businesses and solopreneurs (he hears of single-person companies doing tens of millions in revenue).
- Standing out as a builder: building software is baseline now. Differentiate with storytelling, landing page and call-to-action skill, and getting customers. He invited indie maker Marc Lou to a Friday fireside chat to explain how he designs landing pages and correlates visitors with revenue. His regret about Socket.IO: Microsoft embedded it in Microsoft 365 and he didn't tell that story. "Open source is blurring the lines with businesses and startups," so name, logo and website now matter.
- Optimistic view of society: the web becomes more "whimsical" and immersive (e.g., someone vibe-coded a 3D examination of the human body), artists and handmade small businesses come back, and partnerships like Shopify's backend let people launch shops by prompt.
- What stays human: capital allocation, values and taste, empathy and connection. "I refuse to have an AI as a friend." He writes his own tweets (AI only reviews them): "farm-to-table next token from me, not from a machine."
- CEOs should build with agents themselves (he praised Gary Tan for going back to the arena), and should get their top leaders to SF to see what agents can do.

chunks.heading: Leadership and operating principles
chunks.text:
- Early-stage founders do everything and aren't world-class at all of it. In the AI era, leaders must become more full-stack, because bandwidth is amplified; staying in your lane ("the CSS expert") gets you left behind.
- Quote he cites from Elon: the product is the factory that produces the cars at scale. Guillermo applies that to software and to his personal "factory" (his psychology, energy and routines).
- Scaling a manager: he cites Jensen Huang's large-group meetings over one-on-ones. Values and leading by example scale more than one-on-ones. He does customer support rotations ("it's become a meme"), stays in the weeds, and invoked the value of iterative greatness.
- Focus lesson: Vercel succeeded with simplicity (a single-command deploy). When he got distracted and "threw things at the wall," life "gave me the A/B test."
- Mistakes: he hates making them, but most are two-way doors; "breathe, this too shall pass."
- Energy: he works out every morning; the gym "expands your energy capacity" ("you have to spend energy to increase your energy budget"). He vibe-coded an app to count his keystrokes per day. He frames low periods as observations, not "burnout."
- Quick-fire: overrated startup advice is "ambition" (many startups ship slop because they're too ambitious; moderate it); overhyped is voice control of computers; his advice for aspiring builders is discipline and hours ("10,000 hours, 996, that's rookie numbers").
- Tooling goal: deployments in single-digit seconds at any app size (he recalls the magic of FTP); fast feedback loops matter for agents. A new Next.js release cut build time sometimes by 50%.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Guillermo Rauch explains how teaching and open source took him from Argentina to Vercel, why iteration velocity is the one thing he optimizes for, and why small, simple products that evolve beat complete ones. He then shares free AI startup ideas built as opinionated vertical platforms that combine software 1.0 and 2.0.

chunks.heading: Teaching beats credentials: how Guillermo bootstrapped his career
chunks.text:
- Guillermo started coding seriously around age 10, building websites and doing paid freelance work online. His first check came at age 11.
- A stranger on a forum pointed him to a freelancing marketplace, because he already helped people with Linux and PHP tutorials. He had "figured out a business model" for himself early.
- His advice to young people on bootstrapping a career: "start by teaching anything." Write tutorials, help people in forums, build a reputation.
- At 15-16 he contributed to MooTools, a JavaScript library that Facebook used as inspiration for its JavaScript infrastructure. He got a Facebook job offer around 16-17, but it fell through when they learned his location and age.
- The same project kept opening doors. Other startups hired from the contributor list, and at about 18 a Swiss startup offered him a job. That is when he left high school.
- Vercel does the same thing today: it looks at who contributes to Next.js and recruits them.
- He gives caveated advice on dropping out. His free public high school in Argentina gave him a strong foundation (college-level science and math). By the time he left, evidence of his skills was already substantial, so it was "a leap of faith" backed by results.
- Open source and the web were "my ticket to success."

chunks.heading: Finding asymmetries: why he bet on JavaScript
chunks.text:
- Guillermo's rule: "you always arrive to success by finding asymmetries or finding alpha or finding unfair advantages."
- JavaScript's unfair advantage: it is the only language every browser on every device can run. It beat Flash, Java applets and others.
- Early on JavaScript was seen as a toy. The criticisms (can't be fast, typed, scale, have modules) were true of the language as it then existed, but not of what it could become.
- His edge was taking it seriously and adding what was missing. With MooTools he faked classes using a function called `Class`, which stood out to Facebook and Bay Area teams.
- He frames technologies and startups through evolution rather than intelligent design (via Brendan Eich). JavaScript started tiny, inline in markup, and grew more sophisticated.
- Early products look rough. He recommends looking at the Wayback Machine versions of early Airbnb and Uber sites. It shows founders are probably overthinking their launch, how far iteration must go, and how narrow the initial wedge was (Airbnb: design conference, hotels booked, sleep on a designer's couch).
- Things that look like toys, start narrow, or seem limited on many dimensions but are great at one thing "can't be underestimated."

chunks.heading: Minimum surface and forcing functions
chunks.text:
- JavaScript was conceived in about 10 days under a deadline. Guillermo's takeaway: ask what the minimum surface is that you can ship on top of which evolution can bootstrap, rather than aiming for completeness in version one.
- Brilliant builders delete and delete. Alternatively, a deadline forces the reduction, as in YC's ship-in-3-months.
- The human instinct is to add more: a bigger homepage, more images, more gradients. Early successful products focused on content and essentials.
- DoorDash is his example: it started as one HTML page and six PDFs of restaurant menus. "Get the idea out into the world as a URL and see if it sticks."

chunks.heading: Iteration velocity: the founding thesis of Vercel
chunks.text:
- "The pattern throughout my career has been iteration velocity is the most important thing to optimize for."
- At his previous startup (sold to WordPress/Automattic), where he was CTO, he built the mechanism for engineers to ship fast before starting any project. His obsession: how quickly can you go from idea to shareable artifact, idea to URL.
- At WordPress he saw a company good at deploying one app but stuck when someone had a new idea and needed IT to set up a server. Vercel began as reducing that friction from idea to live to seconds, measured down to the millisecond.
- He uses a Formula 1 pit-crew metaphor: the business wins by shaving seconds off the stop between idea and deployed product.
- The same principle explains Vercel's traction with large companies (investment banks) and with YC startups racing to demo day.
- Vercel narrowed its scope heavily. It began as "deploy anything" (Java, Haskell, PHP), then simplified to betting on modern web frameworks like Next.js and JavaScript as a unified front-end and back-end language. "We didn't pivot in the sense of going into a different space but we simplified the offering way way way significantly."

chunks.heading: Open source as a business engine (Next.js)
chunks.text:
- Next.js came from his own pain: starting a React project (for zite.co) required assembling everything from scratch, like shopping at Home Depot for wheels, chassis and engine.
- Open-sourcing Next.js benefits Vercel because it serves the core mission: cut the time from hypothesis to production-grade deployment from weeks of setup to seconds.
- Next.js powers sites like Midjourney. Vercel customers include Ramp, Supreme, Brex and drink AG.
- Performance is a selling point. He cites a public consumer electronics retailer selling billions per year that improved conversion by 30% in some markets and up to 90% in others because its site got faster.

chunks.heading: Building AI products: v0 and "software 1.0 + 2.0"
chunks.text:
- v0 is "chat for creating web applications": instead of text, it returns a fully working web app. Its edge is the last decade of Next.js and production infrastructure behind it (partners like Supabase and Neon for databases).
- He uses Karpathy's framework. Software 1.0 is deterministic code. Software 2.0 is trained models with emergent, unpredictable capabilities. Even model makers don't know what a new model can do, and builders spend time "discovering the latent space."
- His thesis: successful AI products of the future combine both. v0 still writes Next.js, has friendly UI, templates, one-click deploy and Vercel infrastructure.
- Entrepreneurs don't need to train foundation models. They "put the pieces together into opinionated workflows."
- "Unbundling ChatGPT": look for clusters of queries people already send to ChatGPT that can become whole platforms. NDA drafts led to AI legal tools. Web UI output led to v0.
- Vercel's goal is to be "the platform of platforms," the place where "the next Shopify" gets born. He sees v0 as one "video game" built on Vercel as the "game engine," with many others to come (v0 for video games, lawyers, doctors). Vercel open sourced much of v0 so entrepreneurs can build vertical versions.
- Example: the general counsel uses GC.AI, described as v0 for lawyers, built on Vercel.
- He says he no longer writes code after "a couple decades" as an engineer; he only prompts.
- Viral demo: a Doom CAPTCHA built over a holiday break with v0. It looks like Google CAPTCHA but requires killing three enemies in Doom, using a WebAssembly build of the open-sourced game. It earned several news articles from a few hours of prompting.

chunks.heading: Free AI startup ideas he shared
chunks.text:
- **AI form builder (Typeform-style):** an AI-first form creator that writes the questions, summarizes results, and makes the answering experience conversational or generative UI. Rule of thumb: "if drag and drop is involved as a primary interaction mechanism it's probably ripe for disruption."
- **Onboarding rule:** give one thing to do, remove distractions and links that pull people out of the flow (e.g., don't make the logo clickable or add footer links in a task flow).
- **AI camera:** treat the shutter click as input to a prompt, not output. Combine models into a pipeline that fixes blinks, lighting and backdrops, offers several versions, and removes unwanted people or objects.
- **Absurdly smart autocomplete:** better context makes LLMs better. Feed in the clipboard, recent apps and the sequence of what you are doing, because work is sequential. The Mac spell checker not knowing a word you saw 10 seconds ago is the example.
- **Granular v0s:** vertical platforms (video games, e-commerce, legal) that start with intelligence, for example a store that imports product photos or an existing store's catalog in one click.
- Prediction on cameras: windows for new consumer apps reopen about every 8-10 years as social norms and tech shift.

chunks.heading: Silicon Valley serendipity and Bitcoin
chunks.text:
- He loves walking up to people with something to show, not a networking pitch. In 2012 Brian Armstrong approached him at a party, showed him an early Coinbase app, and promised a Bitcoin for installing it (worth $1,081 in the email and over $100,000 in recent value).
- After selling his first company, he put money into Bitcoin, partly viewing it as an angel investment, inspired by a JavaScript community peer who did the same.
- His Argentina experience (a rapid string of presidents around 2000-2001 and bank deposits forcibly converted to pesos despite on-air promises that "if you deposited dollars, you will receive dollars") made him a Bitcoin believer: a globally distributed, immutable database you do not have to trust anyone to hold.
- He prefers proof-of-work systems because they avoid uncertainty about which chain is canonical.
- His allocation: "I put my entire net worth into Vercel," first betting on himself, but he wants both productive assets and Bitcoin (the Buffett gold-cube versus farmland framing). He would feel "really worried" without Bitcoin as a foundation.
- He is intrigued by an "energy dollar" idea given that energy is turning into intelligence via GPU compute.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Guillermo Rauch explains how Vercel paired open-source Next.js with a cloud business, why he narrowed to a niche instead of pleasing everyone, and how he decides when to expand. He also covers pricing for the AI era, treating the LLM as a customer, and agentic commerce.

chunks.heading: Start with a niche and earn the right to expand
chunks.text:
- Guillermo's early mistake was trying to make everyone happy. Vercel's infrastructure was so generic that he was "appealing to everybody" (Java, Next, and more), which stretched the company thin.
- His principle: ambition for a venture-backed business should be "pretty much unbounded", but it has to be met with realism. Pure ambition leaves you "jack of all trades, master of none".
- He contrasts "a million mediocre customers" with "a thousand customers that really love you".
- Vercel first dominated a niche: the front end, meaning hosting the front end of websites and web apps, then CDN and security services.
- He says the "niche" has produced $250 million of revenue (earlier in the talk, $200 million ARR and a doubling of users year over year). Things that look like niches often turn out to be very large markets.
- Back end, agents and the AI cloud came later than he expected. "You have to earn the privilege to expand."

chunks.heading: Rules for when to expand into the next chapter
chunks.text:
- Once a business reaches product-market fit, he says you can't get too satisfied. Customers and the world expect more, and you have the people and funding to expand into adjacencies.
- Brand permission: if Vercel launched a washer and dryer, people would find it strange. They would expect an AI coding tool. The brand has to give you permission.
- Adjacency to core competence: his example is that a payments company can do billing or fraud next.
- For Vercel's AI cloud, the same demand carries over. Developers want simple frameworks, tools and solutions for building agents.
- He treats platform shifts as the moment to start. The shift 10 years ago was the cloud; the current one is AI. Old technology doesn't disappear. Pages, URLs and links stay relevant, much like AM and FM radio.

chunks.heading: Pairing an open source framework with a cloud business
chunks.text:
- At the start, Guillermo wanted to remove all friction from "idea to global cloud application". He needed two halves: tooling (framework, runtime, compilers) and cloud infrastructure.
- He saw an asymmetry in the market. AWS and Google Cloud gave you primitives such as VMs, clusters and networking and left the application framework to you, "draw the rest of the owl".
- Next.js was built for the sophistication, performance and flexibility of the internet's giants. Vercel hosts and scales it with universal performance, so no one needs to be an infrastructure expert.
- The goal is to be born on Vercel and never graduate, "much like Stripe", because scale is effectively infinite.
- Open source is the company's "cover letter to the world". Starting with Next.js, or another open source framework Vercel contributes to, leads people to the business.
- His own open source contributions (such as MooTools) served as his résumé and let him reach a worldwide audience from Argentina.
- The AI SDK follows the same pattern as Next.js, a framework for the agent era. He says it may surpass Next.js in downloads. The conversation cites about 4.3 million downloads a week.

chunks.heading: Going from developers to everyone with v0 and Stripe
chunks.text:
- Vercel's v0 is a deliberate "self-disruption". JavaScript let Vercel enable tens of millions of people to create. Natural language, where "English is becoming the next hot programming language", could reach far more.
- His proxy for the market is Slack and Teams, with roughly half a billion combined monthly active users who talk about building software or a business. He wants to turn those words into software, taking the creator pool "from like 20 million to 500 million".
- Vercel added a Stripe integration so anyone who prompts v0 or deploys to Vercel gets a Stripe sandbox provisioned without setting up the environment.
- It quickly became the third most popular integration on the platform. His reasoning: when people build something, they want to monetize it, and selling is the best way to get market feedback.
- Surprising users: people building side-project startups they previously found too hard to build, 12 to 13 year olds selling products online, and enterprise staff who lack resources to execute. One company went "from v0 to patent filed" by prototyping and talking to customers.
- He thinks enterprises could innovate from within, rather than only by acquiring startups.
- He doesn't think the tool replaces engineers. Many people start in v0 and grow into proficient engineers, moving to Git and other tools. He personally sends prototypes from v0 to his team rather than describing ideas in Slack.
- Non-English use is strong. People build in Japanese, Spanish and Arabic, and he rates Spanish as "amazing".

chunks.heading: Designing for the LLM as a customer
chunks.text:
- Internally, Vercel now treats "the LLM as our customer". Next.js used to be designed only for people; the first version looked like a templating language (like MySpace codes, or Shopify Liquid) to make React relatable.
- His design rule is progressive disclosure of complexity. Meet each customer at their level and reveal sophistication only as needed. The hard part is keeping the simplicity of the early days at scale; Stripe supporting Shopify has far more advanced needs than a one-person shop.
- Vercel now hosts two of the top 20 websites by traffic, so the complexity must be exposed carefully, now to agents as well as people.
- Example: agents boot up and kill many dev servers, which humans don't do. Vercel added the process ID to a Next.js error message so the agent knows which process to kill to free the port. A tiny change that is marginal for humans makes "a gigantic difference for agents".
- He says to think of yourself as a junior engineering manager managing a fleet of agents, not a junior engineer.
- Context is king: "the context we put into the agent determines the quality of the outcome". The error-message tweak is context engineering.

chunks.heading: Pricing and billing for the AI era
chunks.text:
- Early platform decisions can be regrettable. Examples are how you structure users, teams, organizations, workspaces and roles, and pricing models. You can wake up five years later wishing you had done it differently.
- His rules of thumb:
  - Optimize for high iteration velocity in pricing, packaging and billing, because they will change constantly.
  - Optimize for transparency. Vercel shows the exact cost per request, data transfer unit or AI token, with real-time accounting.
  - He frames cloud as power and Vercel as "a utility". Customers draw capacity on demand, so prediction markets like Polymarket and Kalshi can scale on election day without calling Vercel.
- Usage varies widely. Some engineers run long agent sessions, others run parallel ones, and some on frontier domains get little return from AI today. This calls for fluid accounting and billing.
- He runs a hybrid model: on-demand for compute, builds and tokens, plus traditional per-seat or per-project pricing for collaboration (as with GitHub or Figma).
- Warning on pure on-demand: you can face a cold start problem with 100,000 customers paying around 3 cents a month while carrying fixed platform costs.
- He advocates extreme experimentation because "no one really knows the answer", and recommends against building billing infrastructure yourself.

chunks.heading: Interfaces and protocols for agents and commerce
chunks.text:
- If English is the programming language, you must be where conversations already happen (WhatsApp, Slack, ChatGPT, Cursor). He is paying close attention to MCP, since many enterprises (Vercel, Stripe, Shopify) have internal chatbots and your product may have no pixel interface at all.
- On agentic commerce, he thinks it is overrated for repeat purchases, using his habit of buying the same black shirts. He sees real potential for personalization when an LLM has good context about preferences and purchase history.
- His mental model for future pages: an LLM with context produces the page, and its tool calls orchestrate UI components. Businesses need both a protocol to integrate into big chat platforms and their own interface.
- He describes three interfaces: a human in a personalized storefront, an agentic browser ("get me my black sweater"), and agent-to-agent.
- Demo with Stripe: a coding agent told to deploy picks Vercel, procures an account and pays for it, delivering a live URL while the purchase is an implementation detail. He says oversight, persistent payment methods and fraud prevention remain necessary.
- He thinks B2B procurement by agents is under-discussed compared with B2C.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Vercel's CEO explains why code generation is nearly solved but review and shipping are the new bottleneck. He argues for constrained vertical agents, measuring business outcomes instead of code, and blending first-principles vision with close customer listening.

chunks.heading: Why Guillermo built Vercel: make the first deploy feel like a new laptop
chunks.text:
- At his earlier startup (sold to Automattic, parent of WordPress.com), he was CTO and focused on how to help his team ship the right things with the best tools.
- His most impactful move was investing heavily in continuous integration and deployment. You write a small feature, push to git, and get an instant result.
- He built a real-time system that returned a link with a commit ID, so a team could edit "the internet" almost in real time. Teammates later named iteration speed and deploy speed as the thing that mattered most.
- His analogy: a new Apple laptop feels great because Apple solved the bootstrapping problem and everything works out of the box. He wanted that same feeling for developer tooling.
- He saw that WordPress.com was excellent at hosting its own site but had no zero-to-one experience for a developer with a new idea. Cloud was powerful and scalable but felt like the opposite of a new computer, with complex setup and instance concepts.
- His first-principles benchmark was PHP in the 90s: edit a file in a folder and it is live. He describes it as a Dropbox that is also a live deployment, and Vercel chased that experience.

chunks.heading: Frontend focus and business outcomes
chunks.text:
- Vercel put heavy emphasis early on the frontend. Backend code mattered, but standout web experiences depended more on the frontend. He points to ChatGPT, which streams, thinks and splits into a live document in front of your eyes, as something that needs strong frontend frameworks.
- Next.js was the competitive advantage. A brand-new language like PHP would have been a big ask, because any new tool forces people to learn something and possibly migrate. He asks what a migrating enterprise gets in return.
- Vercel's answer is concrete business outcomes: faster, more dynamic apps, faster iteration, and the ability to build AI products. He cited stats on a large retail chain that recently moved to the platform.
- Great developer experience without business results is an incomplete equation. Early cloud had a bad financial equation: companies paid for their own data centers and then also paid a cloud bill, with no visible payoff.
- He has always cared about visual design. If there is nothing to see or touch at the end of the path, a software project feels unjustified to him. Vercel works backward from the site URL you deploy, and you feel an improvement even without complex performance tests. Then it teaches you the technology behind it.
- His line: cloud used to be about implementation details and primitives; Vercel made it about products and experience.

chunks.heading: Enterprise rigidity and the AI infrastructure problem
chunks.text:
- He found that as companies grow they get more rigid, locked into legacy infrastructure choices. Some deploy once a quarter, and some freeze code for weeks or months around Black Friday.
- He says AI makes this ten times more important. New models appear daily, and two new open-source models shipped the week before. A company locked into its deployment and infrastructure choices cannot keep up.

chunks.heading: Defining "shipping" and the review bottleneck
chunks.text:
- At Vercel, shipping means more than writing code. It means a tangible business result along the whole conversion path (conversions, signups, new information, impressions), working backward from pixels on someone's screen. He says the higher you set the bar for what counts as shipped, the better.
- He sees a new bottleneck: code generation is "almost solved," with companies reporting 50%, 80% or 90% of their code comes from AI, but the bottleneck moved to reviewing that code.
- His framework has two ends of a spectrum:
  - Vibe coding for a wide audience, where v0 operates ("everyone can cook").
  - An engineer on a 20-year-old codebase, which he calls AI-assisted or agentic engineering.
- He expects code to be fully solved because models will keep improving as they learn from accepted and rejected code, a self-fulfilling prophecy. But for mature projects it is unclear a human can fully trust the output.
- Example he shared: an agent produced a PR that did what the engineer wanted, but deleted one critical line. In a sensitive production codebase, one line (an infrastructure file deleting a critical resource, or auth code) can be the difference between the internet going down or not.
- His response: Vercel is investing heavily in giving higher confidence that a change is good, safe and follows best practices. He expects agents to review code too, with a human still in the loop.
