chunks.heading: Why constrained, vertically integrated agents can beat humans
chunks.text:
- He says v0 is more opinionated because it serves everyone, not only developers. v0 outputs Next.js, Vercel builds Next.js, and it integrates with a specific set of database partners, so Vercel can closely control the known quantities.
- With a restricted approach the model can embed every security best practice and refuse to do something security-wise foolish, going beyond what a human does.
- The harder general case needs a model to know the company's full history, code semantics, runtime behavior (logs, metrics, such as a baseline of 1,000 requests per second that makes a hot-path algorithm risky), and every language, cloud and deployment tool.
- His self-driving analogy: Waymo is restricted (not on highways, not in New York), but has far fewer accidents than humans. He wants tools like v0 to restrict what they can do realistically so that quality is near guaranteed, rather than being "a machine for producing slop."
- The flexibility scale: Claude Code or Cursor can work on any codebase, while v0 is more specialized and opens programming to everyone.
- He floated an idea: a convention where agents announce to tools that they are agents, not humans, so tools can adapt their interface (a human gets the hammer for their motor skills, an agent could hold 20 hammers). He says this opens a whole set of languages, runtimes and frameworks designed for agent engineering.

chunks.heading: Perceived vs. real productivity from AI tools
chunks.text:
- He is not surprised by the study showing developers felt 20% faster but were 20% slower. He talked to a CTO of one of the largest engineering forces in the world, who said they spent a long time measuring perceived vs. realized gains from AI tools and the gap was large: people thought it was the best thing since sliced bread, but measured output was much smaller.
- His explanation: a multi-step process where some steps become very fast while others are slower, and people focus on the parts where they started flying.
- Counterpoint he offers: engineering is emotionally brutal. He describes the pager, the weight of knowing one deleted line took down a famous .com, and day-long loops of error after error. Agents now absorb that mess, so the shift to agents makes developers feel in control.
- His internal line: "the agent is the new model." An agent is "an LLM on steroids" focused on outcomes. Early LLMs responded to prompts (write a poem, translate this); now the ask is "get me an outcome."
- Vercel added a sound to v0 when generation completes. People said it feels like winning the jackpot, since it only plays after the agent gets through all the errors a human would have suffered. He says psychological and emotional effects should be factored into productivity studies.
- He expects both v0's platform API and Claude Code's SDK to let companies embed agents. For example, a company like Squarespace could use the v0 platform API to build its own site-building agent.

chunks.heading: Personal software, internal tools, and where vibe coding fits
chunks.text:
- Vercel's design team has built small tools to process and ship assets, work that used to take days or weeks.
- Vercel now uses traditional BI tools much less. Static dashboards pile up unmaintained lists nobody opens, while people want generative UI: ask a question and get the ideal visualization at that moment. He says he would not claim vibe coding can replicate Microsoft Power BI for 10 million enterprise customers, but the platform can lose by people simply no longer needing it. Each customer builds their own small tool, with better visualizations, and can add features the same day.
- Story he shared: a CTO at a company started vibe coding on his personal account during a customer call. The customer threatened to cancel unless a feature existed. In a 30-minute conversation the CTO built a version, and the customer said "this is exactly what I want." The CTO then told the field org he wanted everyone to build this way, and wanted their data available to the platform. It was announced for Q4.
- Caveat: building it in 30 minutes is not the same as integrating it into a huge production system with millions of customers. That is why he argues the world will split into more and more specialized tools and agents for each kind of problem.

chunks.heading: Advice for kids, taste, and the human skill that remains
chunks.text:
- For a 10 to 16 year old, his advice is to start with a product idea rather than "learn to code." Starting with v0 builds the muscle of asking what you actually want and what you picture in your head.
- He defines taste as the ability to refine a vague idea until you can visualize its end state, "predicting the next step" rather than "predicting the next token." He admits it's a debatable psychological idea, since people differ in how much they can visualize.
- Story: he built a football game with his six-year-old son. The idea was entirely the son's, but it was hard to get him to ask for next steps or improvements. They ended with a dribbling game that scores points and gets harder, and the polish came from Guillermo. His lesson: you must build the muscle of understanding there is an audience, what the technology can do, and how to combine these into prompts for what you want to see in the world.
- Since code generation is "solved" (his parenthetical, controversial claim), what is left is ideas and capital allocation. Tokens cost money, so the better idea wins the tokens behind it. He says storytelling is the human skill, and your pitch persuades the world to allocate tokens to your idea.
- On whether anyone needs to understand low-level code: he says we already live in a world where most people don't know how a garbage collector works, and nobody fully knows how LLMs reach answers, so we will need frameworks, guardrails and interpretability. He thinks it ends up being about the investment relationship: what you're willing to pay for a level of performance and outcome.
- He wants people to avoid a "Wall-E" future. He recommends making sure your relationship with any tool challenges you, teaches you and leaves you with expanded capabilities.

chunks.heading: Combining product vision with customer listening, and building the culture
chunks.text:
- He says the best product builders for enterprises are extreme: they listen to concrete pain points and build together with customers, but they also hold a vision of the future, which he calls "working from science fiction backwards." Without the vision you miss the next platform shift and what the next generation of builders is excited about.
- He argues agents can do user research, so the agent can act like a product manager: search keywords, find 10 complaints, prioritize them, and check what others say. He expects a world of many specialized agents collaborating, not one agent governing all.
- He wants the next internet to move from HTTP to MCP, with specialized agents collaborating. He opposes a single platform gatekeeper deciding what is allowed (pointing to the story of Apple wanting to remove X from the App Store). Companies could expose tools and data as an MCP interface for agents, in addition to a pixel interface for humans.
- On culture: he recommends "reverse engineering your success." You can succeed without understanding why, or even despite doing A, B and C. He cites a quote that it is harder to predict the past than the future.
- Vercel's culture grew out of open source: an open contribution culture and high transparency. Internal Slack is mostly information, with few DMs, so it works like an internal Twitter. He works behind the scenes coaching engineers to show their own work (what they learned from X, how to make a post shorter, which example to use), so they own the storytelling and learn how to talk to customers and community. He notes privacy and compliance remain top priorities.
- He still reads user issues, error messages and X posts. Example: an escalated outage report from a startup via investors turned out to be another provider returning a 502, visible in the error message. His takeaway: errors should be in natural language and agents can help attribute fault, and Vercel moves "from problems to solutions" (an agent for metric anomalies that sends a PR or a diagnosis rather than raw data). His stance is that every customer problem is his problem.

chunks.heading: Personal discipline and facing hard feedback
chunks.text:
- Coding taught him focus and discipline, including how to take negative feedback from the compiler and push through. He recalls coding for about seven hours straight as a kid while his father marveled at his focus.
- He exercises for the mental benefits, calling hard workouts an "active meditation." He boxed for years, going to a gym from 6 to 7:30 a.m. in Dogpatch, and likes unfashionable training such as bodyweight exercises. His coach would end a session by sending them to run around the Giants stadium.
- Link to product: presence gives clarity, and better taste comes from being responsive to real reactions. The best thing to do for your product is read all the negative feedback, and he asks whether you can face it or flee. He says many people want to help you build the right thing, so "don't get in your own way."

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Rauch explains how Vercel's iteration-velocity philosophy and front-end cloud led to v0, and why every product will gain AI. He covers practical AI-skill building, when to build your own AI product versus a GPT, and why open source and startups win the Software 2.0 wave.

chunks.heading: Building products with AI: ghost text, v0, and why every product becomes an AI product
chunks.text:
- Guillermo caught the AI bug from GitHub Copilot's "ghost text" (a suggestion shown next to what you typed, which you accept or ignore). His framework at the time: "we are going to need ghost text for every product in the world." Coding was only step one, and he argues that makes the insight stronger because programming is a hard task.
- He now uses AI to proofread tweets and rephrase text. When Copilot came out he told Notion's CEO (he is a small investor) they needed to bring ghost text to Notion. It ended up as a slash command and context menu instead.
- Vercel's thesis is that the speed at which a user interface is delivered is king, so the same completion idea should apply to UIs. v0 generates the first version of an interface from intent, offers three or four options, then loops with the user on refinements.
- v0 targets production-grade code. Vercel's customers operate at large scale (he says Vercel is overkill for "your uncle's restaurant website"), so generated UI must be good enough to ship. At the time of the interview, hundreds of thousands of generations had been made for a small group admitted from the waitlist.
- He frames v0's value as fixing "the empty canvas." Engineers still start from a blank text file and he predicts "we're going to look back on this and we're going to be like those were the dark ages of development."

chunks.heading: v0 as an accelerant: his own website test
chunks.text:
- Guillermo rebuilt his personal site (rauchg.com), which he hand-crafted pixel by pixel, using only natural-language prompts. Example prompts: gray background, center it, blog post list top right, an "about" link, a Twitter icon.
- The visual result was satisfying. What shocked him was the code: "better code than what I wrote." It was objectively more accessible. The AI generated a "Twitter" label shown only to screen readers, a detail he had missed in 20 years of front-end work.
- His reasons: AI has "infinite memory," "infinite patience" (he attributes this to Marc Andreessen), and access to ever-growing data, so it is hard to compete with on details.
- For v0 specifically, Vercel steers output with fine-tuning, retrieval and its own knowledge of best practices: accessible interfaces that work on mobile and desktop.
- He sees v0 as helping experienced engineers from other domains (say, back end) who know systems well but not the front-end best practices, plus anyone else who wants to build.

chunks.heading: Skills for working with AI
chunks.text:
- Guillermo says people must build the skill of working with AI: prompting, knowing what it can do and where it struggles.
- Example: someone replicated Angry Birds entirely with AI. Guillermo DM'd the author to check how much was AI-written (all of it). The author said the AI could not reason about the passage of time, which games need for state evolution and collision detection.
- He expects people to use different AIs for different skills, because each domain needs different handling of error correction, hallucination and freshness. His own picks:
  - Perplexity for very recent or real-time information and trends.
  - Metaphor for crawling the web with ChatGPT-like prompts, useful when you don't know the keyword (the "what was that song" problem).
  - Phind for searching developer documentation across many sources, useful for integrations when he needs confidence the AI saw recent docs.
  - ChatGPT for coding.
- Prompting tips:
  - Paste the entire error message from the compiler or tool. Giving the AI lots of context is counterintuitive for people used to two- or three-word Google searches, but more context gives better output.
  - Phrase things as a question. Ask "what is 2+2?" and push back with "no, it's 5," and the model caves. Understanding next-token prediction helps you reduce overconfidence and hallucination.
  - Upload context rather than starting from scratch each time. He sees this as why OpenAI went with GPTs and system prompts. Fresh starts are less helpful and more expensive, since powerful models are needed to reason with little context.
  - He repeats Satya Nadella's line about large models: using GPT-4 is like driving a Ferrari, and you should ask whether you'd cross the street with one.

chunks.heading: GPTs vs your own product: a strategic and technical framework
chunks.text:
- Business question: do you want to keep the direct connection to your customer, or be "a product in somebody else's shelf"? The analogy is Vercel's e-commerce customers (Under Armour, Chico's) that could have handed all their inventory to Amazon.
- The answer is often both. His example: a mattress brand selling on amazon.com and also running its own site. Do not sit on the sidelines training people to go to someone else's website instead of yours.
- Technical question: GPTs are constrained like Amazon product pages. You get a bit of bold, italic and code, and everything must fit the host UI, so he expects them to be very limited.
- Products like v0 need visual and UI freedom, and he thinks that need grows over time. He expects many verticalized AI assistants, some inside existing products and some new. Examples he gives: a new Bloomberg terminal, and AI-first healthcare (looking up preeclampsia, where presentation and regulation matter).
- Shopify's in-product copilot for merchants is his example of companies embedding assistants. He is "talking my book": Vercel bets every product becomes an AI product in some capacity. It offers templates and the AI SDK (sdk.vercel.ai) to add AI to existing or new products.
- Companies can build better AIs with RAG, LLMs and fine-tuning, and keep information current.

chunks.heading: Software 2.0, Cloud 2.0 and who wins
chunks.text:
- He cites Andrej Karpathy's "Software 2.0" essay. Software 1.0 is explainable code: algorithms, data structures, languages. Software 2.0 is "more like cooking than engineering": mix data and compute to train neural networks, and the resulting "code" is hard to interpret.
- Parallel to cloud: Cloud 1.0 gave VMs (EC2) and object storage (S3). Cloud 2.0 gives vector databases, LLMs, indexing pipelines and retrieval.
- Advice to technical leaders: ask how much you invest in the 2.0 paradigm versus the 1.0 paradigm. Vercel's pitch: infrastructure is not your business, so offload it and focus on bringing software 2.0 features to market.
- His speculative prediction: because attention, money and VC excitement go to 2.0, 1.0 technologies may ossify. Models are good at JavaScript and Python but poor at obscure languages, which reinforces existing choices. He compares this to JavaScript automating away memory management, and expects writing code to matter less while attention moves elsewhere.
- Who wins: both startups and incumbents.
  - Incumbents will add incremental AI (assistants in dashboards) fast and with lots of money.
  - Startups can build 2.0 products so different in visuals, function and customers that big companies struggle to pivot into them.
- He wants to see "the Uber and Airbnb of Cloud 2.0," companies that couldn't exist without LLMs and diffusion models. He expects AI-first social networks and compares the opportunity to Zuckerberg as a PHP developer assembling off-the-shelf pieces (MySQL, PHP). Today you can use off-the-shelf services and APIs without a machine learning PhD.
- Advice for the fast-moving environment: re-evaluate your assumptions every week, since models, context windows and architectures keep changing.

chunks.heading: Open source always wins
chunks.text:
- His rule: "never underestimate open source." Betting against it is costly and shortsighted. Microsoft once underestimated it and has since changed.
- Next.js example: in the early days (a 3-4 person startup) a CTO of a popular real estate site said Next.js wasn't mature enough and built his own. A couple of years later every major online real estate player was on Next.js.
- Why open source improves faster: CTOs told him the best feature of Next.js was finding problems and solutions on Google. Proprietary tools can't use that ecosystem of knowledge and intelligence.
- Applied to AI: Llama may trail GPT-4 and Code Llama may trail Copilot, but it will get better. Garage chip startups will download Llama first and battle-test against it, since they can't access GPT-4. His phrase: "business development is not done with phone calls and meetings and contracts, it's done by doing a git clone of our repository."
- Caveats he names: regulatory capture is the main adversary of open source.
- Counter-thesis: the model is only the engine, and APIs win over long periods through ease of use (people use Stripe, not MasterCard directly). Open-source model folks must provide utility on top of the model. Vercel is investing in that connective tissue between product and model, including the AI SDK.

chunks.heading: Iteration velocity and the Vercel developer-first model
chunks.text:
- Vercel's front-end cloud makes sites fast and dynamic, built on open source (Next.js, React). He compares Next.js to "the Kubernetes of front end."
- Modular, composable stacks (Stripe, Twilio, OpenAI) replace monolithic vendors like Oracle or SAP. One retailer's chief digital officer told him moving to Vercel was "the last digital transformation" he needed, because decoupling front end from back end lets him swap payment or order-tracking providers later.
- Developer experience is a business strategy: "developers choose the products that feel the best." A top-three world bank migrating to Next.js was driven by its developers, not by Guillermo convincing the CTO. Next.js is free MIT-licensed software, so anyone can adopt it.
- He prefers "iteration velocity" (speed with direction) over iteration speed. Vercel gives data such as Speed Insights, citing a Google-commissioned study that 100 ms faster mobile pages improved conversion by 8%.
- Teams should iterate "fearlessly": feature flags, rolling a change to a small cohort first (like movie pre-screenings), and automatic reverts based on business metrics. He points to ChatGPT plugins, then GPTs, as an example of fast iteration from feedback.
- He ran a tiny version of this at his previous startup, optimizing the deployment pipeline so engineers could discover customer needs faster, which later became Vercel.
- Vercel has over 450 people. It powers the front ends of AI products such as ChatGPT, Pi, Perplexity and You.com.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Rauch argues the next web will be built design-first: start from the front end, rely on off-the-shelf or legacy backends, and ship every iteration as a shareable URL. He ties speed and personalization to conversion, and shows how comments, draft mode and visual editing pull non-engineers into the shipping process.

chunks.heading: Front-end-first development: design and engineering converge on the web
chunks.text:
Guillermo argues the next decade of the web will be defined by products that are designed first. Designers and engineers with the right tools can craft new, personalized experiences. He frames design as "not a luxury, it's a necessity" and a starting point for how software gets built, not a layer applied at the end.

- The web's advantage is that it is open and free, so anyone can contribute.
- The best web products enable a deeper human connection: they remember your preferences, language, currency and past visits, and the UI is regenerated dynamically for you.
- He cites Amazon and Google as examples. They built heavy invisible infrastructure first (AWS, distributed systems, new databases), and that foundation now enables personalized, even generative-AI-driven, front ends.

chunks.heading: Why he treats the front end as the starting point (the "front-end cloud")
chunks.text:
Guillermo says the industry over-indexed on invisible engineering (databases, devops, cloud infra) relative to design. That investment was necessary, but it is now a foundation to build on, not something to rebuild at the start of every project.

- Old order: start from algorithms, databases, cloud infra and devops. New order: "what can we innovate with in Figma, how do we test it with Next.js, how do we deploy it and put it in front of users."
- The "front-end cloud" starts with a framework (Next.js or Svelte), implements design intent, and deploys. You don't begin by provisioning AWS or Google Cloud.
- Inverting priorities gives free choice of backend. Either use off-the-shelf services over the network (Stripe, including Stripe Elements React components with your design layered on top), or connect existing legacy data systems (his example: an airline's decades-old database). Separating front and back end also lets you modernize old systems.
- Vercel converts framework code into serverless and CDN primitives automatically, piggybacking on the infrastructure investment.

chunks.heading: The business case: speed and conversion
chunks.text:
Guillermo uses data to argue that prioritizing the front end pays off commercially.

- The old meme: Amazon found that 100 ms of added latency cost about 1% of sales (a desktop-era finding).
- A study Google commissioned with Deloitte on mobile found that a 100 ms improvement lifted conversion by 8%, across industries such as travel, luxury, fashion and marketing.
- Developer attention is also shifting: interest in monolithic, database-centric approaches is flattening while questions and tools gravitate to the front end.
- Starting front-end-first also supports accessibility, usability and a distinctive brand, versus the gray-background, blue-hyperlink sameness of early Amazon, Google and Craigslist.
- Consumer-facing payoff: a shift from a static to a dynamic web (infinite lists, ML-ranked video, viewport- and device-aware experiences, modals). He says you could "upgrade your infra all day long" without unlocking these.

chunks.heading: Components as the shared language between design and engineering
chunks.text:
Guillermo calls React's component the pivotal point in his career. Before it, engineers talked about functions, methods, algorithms and data structures. After it, "let's create a component" mirrors the component concept in Figma, giving designers and engineers a common vocabulary and abstraction.

- Advice on design systems: conceive the design in Figma, then adopt a baseline headless component library (he names Radix and shadcn/ui) and adapt the design to it, rather than rediscovering accessibility, keyboard support and interaction details.
- He cites a quote from Rasmus Andersson about the engineering hours a Figma context menu took to perfect, and says every project otherwise reinvents UI foundations from scratch.
- Components must also render fast, or you lose the conversion benefits.
- With a rich, well-designed component library plus AI context, engineers can produce something "statistically good" quickly. He compares it to the CSS Zen Garden: fixed structure, many expressions. Designers can then comment, and the improvement cycle runs both ways between the two roles.

chunks.heading: Preview URLs and the Vercel toolbar: collaboration inside the real product
chunks.text:
Guillermo's workflow thesis is to share a URL of the product, not a link to code, so non-engineers can review real work early. He says the URL is the web's "unreasonable advantage" over native apps (TestFlight, 300 MB downloads, files).

- Every git push yields a preview deployment URL (an "infinite number of parallel environments" that load instantly), so anyone can see what colleagues are working on instead of reading diffs and pull requests. "Seeing is believing."
- Real-world testing early: Safari typeface quirks, mobile web, in-app browsers (e.g. opening a link from Twitter), Chrome for iOS and Android, and real production infrastructure for performance (not a screenshot).
- He contrasts this with the caricature of an engineer who "goes into the woods for three months" and returns with a pull request. He prefers velocity (right direction) over raw speed, and says shipping to others' hands informs the next step.
- The toolbar adds comments attached to the actual rendered component node and DOM structure. If the component is changed or removed, the comment can auto-resolve.
- Comments can be filed in one click to Linear, and become part of the CI/CD process: a non-engineer's critical comment can block merging the PR. This is his example of inviting non-engineers into building real software.
- Comments work across branches and across product types, from blogs and marketing pages to dynamic apps. He notes TikTok mobile and ChatGPT are built with Next.js.

chunks.heading: Visual editing and draft mode: editing content in place
chunks.text:
Guillermo describes making the live product editable while respecting where content really lives.

- Draft mode visualizes which parts of a page came from external data systems (headless CMS or APIs), lets you edit inline, and patches the change as a draft into the CMS.
- It is built on an open spec developed with Sanity. He likens it to luggage tags: every piece of text carries an invisible tag of the system that produced it, so the front-end renderer knows its source.
- Why click-through to the CMS is also needed at scale: companies don't know which CMS to log into, and real products run A/B tests (several headline permutations) and translations (e.g. 18 languages), so inline editing alone may not suffice.

chunks.heading: AI and where this is heading
chunks.text:
Guillermo is optimistic about AI collapsing the gap between idea and shipped product, framed as removing obstacles between creativity and the real world.

- He wants AI to suggest transformations starting from the product itself, not only from the code editor. Ideas include visualizing a product's other states (feature flags, experiments) in parallel and suggesting changes back to the team.
- On text-to-product versus text-to-Figma: it may be easier to skip intermediate steps and go from text directly to the real rendered product, because the web holds so much data on headers and implementations. Text-to-Figma and Figma-to-front-end are also exciting.
- He values copilot-style output: not the fully baked solution but a quick path to the next step. His example is draft mode, visualizing an idea and continuing to code it.
- Generative AI must respect the abstractions in a code base, which makes it harder than making something look good.

chunks.heading: How Guillermo prioritizes delight and performance at Vercel
chunks.text:
Asked how he prioritizes delightful moments (e.g. passwordless login), Guillermo says Vercel starts from what the customer needs at that moment and gets them to it fast.

- No spinners; log users in fast so the product remembers them. The Vercel AI SDK docs are personalized and include live components for prompt engineering from the documentation site.
- His aspiration is that websites and web applications merge into one dynamic experience. He treats a blog post, login screen, dashboard and data visualization the same way: render fast, personalize, stay true to the design system, delete everything unnecessary. His example: he received a pitch for a new homepage that was nearly empty, and said "great, let's start from there."
- Interaction speed matters beyond initial load. He cites Linear, where pressing enter applies an optimistic mutation without waiting on the cloud. He prioritizes initial load time, the speed of subsequent interactions, and feedback from as many people as possible.
- Vercel dogfoods its comments product to get feedback, including from prospective customers, on new experiences like login.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Guillermo Rauch demos v0's new git-native workflow (branches, previews, PRs) using skills.sh. He argues vibe coding is easy at zero-to-one but hard at scale, and that production rigor lets non-engineers ship, collapsing prioritization friction.

chunks.heading: v0 and the git workflow: taking vibe coding from prototype to production
chunks.text:
Guillermo's core claim: going from zero to one with vibe coding is easy, and everyone has seen the demos. The hard part is iterating on a project at scale and deploying changes safely. Vercel's answer was to make real engineering practice a first-class part of v0:
- Work on branches, use branch previews, code review, then merge.
- v0 gained a "new branch" button, so the git flow no longer requires a terminal or GitHub Desktop. "It's the stone age" to branch manually.
- Branches follow the engineering convention of contributor/feature (for example "v0/rauchg"). He says the product deliberately embeds the small details of a real engineering workflow, but makes them easy.
- Each branch runs the real project in a VM sandbox: dependencies installed at exact versions, a full VS Code editor, and the live app preview. He credits the Next.js team for mirroring dev and production environments as closely as possible.
- Importing a GitHub repo into v0 lets anyone start a chat from an existing production project.

chunks.heading: Demo: shipping a rating feature to skills.sh from a prompt
chunks.text:
Guillermo built a feature live on skills.sh, an npm-like hub for agent skills that was itself conceived in v0. It had 34,000 skills submitted by the community (he later says 35,000), with about 500 skills added per hour.
- The prompt: add a five-star rating system for skills, put it on the sidebar, and be mindful to rate limit or prevent abuse on the scores. His reasoning: ask "what could go wrong if we accept ratings from the internet," and the answer is abuse.
- v0 read the project, noticed the data lives in Redis (Upstash) via the Vercel marketplace, and reused it rather than inventing a new storage approach. The result matched the site's "terminal core" monospace style.
- He caught a small layout shift on refresh when there was no data and asked v0 to remove it. He says he has "a laser eye for product."
- v0 then opened a PR and wrote the description. The Vercel bot built a preview deployment on the production-grade CDN and hosting infrastructure. Seeing the rating there gave him "pretty good confidence" it was shippable.
- He frames the preview as a second layer of assurance beyond the dev server.

chunks.heading: How skills.sh was actually built at Vercel
chunks.text:
- It started as a moment of inspiration: "wouldn't it be cool if this thing took shape?" The team iterated in Slack, prompting and discussing what it should look like.
- Guillermo's design contribution was making the top of the site look like a terminal, which became "terminal core."
- Four or five v0 prompts, in conversation with the VP of Design, produced the first version. The VP of Design then took it much further, with input from the CTO and product leader.
- It was production grade from day one because it needed to scale and many people would watch it. Page transitions are instant, using Vercel infrastructure primitives.
- Skills were already on the backlog because customers asked why Opus 4.5 "kind of knows the latest Next.js but not really," and how to embed Vercel's best practices.
- Vercel now plans to preload skills for its frameworks and the AI SDK into v0 so the model gets stuck less often.

chunks.heading: Adoption data and the internal data agent
chunks.text:
- Vercel's internal data analyst agent, d0 ("we take the first initial and we add a zero"), reported PRs merged via v0 growing from near zero in early January to 3,200 per day by January 28-29, which he calls about a 100x increase.
- He says it was still early preview, with people just being let in.
- Why d0 works: it has a computer (a Vercel Sandbox VM). It can do research, write and run Python, query Snowflake, search the web, and fix its own mistakes over a four-to-five-minute process. He argues what makes agents capable is not perfection but having a computer to solve any problem.
- He expects this to change how Vercel works: tasks triggered from a phone, Slack, or v0.app.

chunks.heading: Letting non-engineers ship: marketing, prioritization and rigor
chunks.text:
- Guillermo now creates a v0 prototype whenever he has an idea for improving the product. Before, he says he was "playing in La La Land." Now a prototype can be handed to engineers as a pull request on a shared substrate.
- Example: every marketer at Vercel wants to change the enterprise page. The old way was either "petition the government" (ask engineers to add a logo) or hope the CMS was wired for the idea. Now they open the page in v0 and prompt any change.
- It would be irresponsible to ship unreviewed, so the git workflow, PR and preview build confidence, and changes can be rolled back.
- For enterprise rigor (feature flags, experiments, measured events) he sees skills added to v0 as the way to make vibe coding scale to that standard. Moving a button is never as low risk as it sounds.
- Collaboration is the point: the git substrate lets engineers, designers and marketers work in one medium. When stuck, there is an escape hatch to clone the repo locally or hand it to someone else, so "a lot less people are going to get stuck."

chunks.heading: Product validation: customer zero and customer one
chunks.text:
- Guillermo's new internal mental model: customer zero is Vercel itself, trusting its own taste and the products it wants to exist. Customer one is a close design partner.
- Design partners include enterprise companies, individuals, community members, and people who message him on X DMs. Claire Vo texts bug reports and needs. He wants that constant pressure test from the outside world.
- Vercel's rule for internal projects: hold them to the same bar as an external launch, so people actually adopt them.
- Principle: "Every day we're basically asking ourselves how can we build an agent that takes over a task that we were previously giving to a person," and the person who did the task usually builds the agent.
- v0's roadmap goal is to be great for creating agents, not just web apps. Example: an OG/Twitter card generator combining traditional rendering with image generation, built because social cards were a team bottleneck.

chunks.heading: Agents, workflows and the roadmap
chunks.text:
- Durable workflows: his AI chess match demo (two models playing in 3D, streaming thinking tokens, built with Three.js, AI Gateway and Vercel Workflow) can run forever. If a provider is down or a function times out, the workflow engine retries. He wants v0 to help build workflows like this, since many agents need that reliability.
- He describes background agents you message (for example over WhatsApp, as with the OpenClaw/Moltbot craze) that use workflows and sandboxes.
- Generative UI: "flash v0," where an agent spontaneously renders UI code without deploying an application, is being researched as another tool for agents.
- Mobile: no timeline promised, but a long-held dream is to make pushing to app stores like pushing to the web, using React Native skills and a React-based deployment platform.
- Debugging tip: when stuck, ask v0 to build debugging tools for itself (he had it visualize the 3D mesh and toggle textures), and ask other models to explain unfamiliar domains, then paste their answers into v0.
- Tooling notes: he generates 20 images in parallel with Nano Banana and picks one before taking it into v0 for higher-fidelity implementation. Vercel built its own playground for it and is dropping text-to-SVG via Recraft models on AI Gateway and a video-generation feature.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Rauch recounts how Vercel went from many open-source bets to focus on Next.js and deployment, then to repeatable use cases like e-commerce. He argues for simplicity, solving your own pain, entering big markets via a wedge, marketing with real customer results, and saying no often.

chunks.heading: Two companies, then the Vercel bet
chunks.text:
- Guillermo describes Vercel as his second serious company. He says he's been an entrepreneur since selling CDs at school around age 10 ("The teachers didn't love it").
- He built a first startup in Silicon Valley, sold it to the company behind WordPress, then spent about 2 years there. He started Vercel in late 2015/2016.
- Reason he left: "I love building stuff. I don't love working for a boss."
- He bet on two waves without knowing the product yet:
  - **The cloud.** WordPress ran its own data centers, and he doubted "the next billion companies" would. The Instagram founders in his first co-working space ran on AWS and became one of S3's biggest customers as photo uploads grew.
  - **Rich client-side front ends.** The PHP monolith put everything in one runtime and one code base, and React was arriving.
- His intuition was that there'd be "something like Ruby on Rails but for this new generation," and that the cloud was powerful but "insanely hard."
- His advice: "noticing these asymmetries about the world is really important for entrepreneurs."

chunks.heading: Gathering feedback and discovering pain
chunks.text:
- Guillermo tests ideas out loud. After he left WordPress he floated a framework idea over dinner in Finland, which he thinks was the first time he said aloud what became Next.js.
- He says he's always been outspoken about what he's building, even though founders fear theft, because people's reactions are useful.
- "Everything is feedback." That includes noticing that someone isn't following your train of thought, or a lack of reaction.
- He does deliberate pain discovery: he tries to pull every negative out of a customer.
  - Customers often don't volunteer what's bad, or are oblivious to what's painful.
  - Opportunities appear "commensurate with your ability to dig."
- Before a hard customer meeting, he tells the responsible engineering manager in advance that the customer will say a lot is broken, so the team expects it.

chunks.heading: Running with high standards: annoyance, impatience, and ideas over opinions
chunks.text:
- He agrees that being annoyed about everything is a useful trait for a CEO, because you stop taking things for granted.
- He borrows Stripe's framing, "short-term pessimism, long-term optimism": tearing apart the company's own sites and apps is his process for extracting greatness over time.
- He pairs impatience with shipping discipline: if something takes 3 months, ask whether an intermediate step can ship in 2 weeks, without shipping junk.
- He balances criticism with celebrating wins and "the joy of our accomplishments," so the company doesn't sit in permanent critique or in "everything is perfect."
- He uses Jony Ive's distinction between opinions and ideas.
  - Opinion: "this app sucks," plus a screenshot.
  - Idea: "this app sucks because X, and here's how to improve it." He calls the concrete idea the superior form of feedback.
- Ideas can come from anyone in the company, and the ones he celebrates most came from customers. He corrects people who credit Vercel with an invention: "No, that was invented by HashiCorp, who was a customer of ours in the early days, or that was invented by TripAdvisor."

chunks.heading: Killing bad ideas, using data, and saying no
chunks.text:
- To test a questionable idea early, he asks the team to build it: ship it as an experiment or a V0 prototype. Seeing it in action, people quickly realize it's bad, as long as the cost isn't too high.
- He uses the voice of the customer and data to contrast the hypothesis with what happened. He has Slack workflows where an agent sends him a weekly download of metrics plus an analysis.
- Data often shows that an idea isn't bad, but that a much greater idea deserves the attention.
- He says Vercel's reputation for shipping fast hides how often he blocks things, says no, or asks for refinement every day.
- On AI: "Just because you can prompt... doesn't mean you should." Even if code is nearly free, you still have to afford to maintain it and market it. He wants a "fair amount of no" in his own head before he verbalizes an idea or greenlights a feature.
- He cites Satya Nadella's "brand permission": a company can have the team and the technology but not the permission, as Google did when it tried to become a social network.

chunks.heading: Vercel's chapters: focus, repeatability, then the organization as the product
chunks.text:
- **Chapter 1: finding focus (roughly $0 to $1M).** The problem was too many ideas, not too few. Among the open-source projects (Next.js, the Hyper terminal, a microservice framework), Next.js was clearly being adopted by enterprises and individuals. On infrastructure, his instinct was to "build infrastructure for everything," and he had to narrow to one kind of deployment, done really well, with focus on the CDN and global distribution. "It was a process of trimming the forest and finding the thing that would stick."
- **Chapter 2: repeatability ($1M to $5M, then 5x again from $5M to $25M).**
  - Next.js distribution let him pick three use cases to dial in. One was e-commerce and storefronts, "anything that has a commercial transaction."
  - E-commerce gave him an ROI calculation for business buyers: Next.js cost, Vercel cost, conversion-rate improvement, development cost, total cost of ownership, profit, and higher top-line retail sales. CIOs and CTOs had asked him to spell out why making developers' lives better pays off.
  - His marketing was built on what he heard from customers: "This is the easiest way to do marketing in the world."
  - Startups stayed a strong segment, and Vercel became synonymous with getting an idea to market fast for crypto, then AI and agents.
- **Chapter 3: scaling beyond comfort.** Vercel was a product-led growth machine where people recommend and invite friends, with everything growing bottoms-up. He then layered on top-down enterprise sales, which pushes into less comfortable territory and adds product requirements founders wouldn't otherwise hear, so the company isn't trapped in a local maximum.
- **Next:** turning Vercel into an "innovation machine" by making the organization itself the product, like Next.js.
  - Escape hatches, a shared set of values, known operational best practices and rituals, and clarity on what's rewarded and punished.
  - He doesn't want every decision to run through the CEO.
  - This is what let Vercel become multi-product (front ends, back ends, agents, AI Gateway, V0) while keeping a high quality bar.

chunks.heading: Building for your own pain and betting on simplicity in a "crowded" market
chunks.text:
- The projects that worked best were solving the team's own pain, proven before they went to market. He built Next.js for himself: after leaving WordPress he planned to use React for everything, but even one page "almost took a PhD." Only later did he notice that other people had the same problem.
- He says he tries not to think about competitors: "I would have never shipped anything if I was motivated by competitors." There were probably 20 React frameworks before one got minimalism, zero configuration, server-side rendering and the rest right.
- Skeptical VCs argued each piece was already solved: CDNs, CircleCI for CI, Heroku for hosting. His answer was ease: "I kept dreaming of that simplicity that I could give to the world."
- Analogy: as a kid in Argentina he built a PC from parts; Apple later offered a MacBook. "So much of the world is won by the people that bring simplicity and ease of use."
- On markets: "you really have to play in enormous markets." Next.js became a wedge into what is now the entirety of the cloud for Vercel.
- On consensus: "what you do cannot fully be consensus." If everyone is already talking about the idea, it may already exist by the time you build it.
- On hype categories like AI, he says to talk about the customer. He asks founders who lose him to restart "from the point of view of a customer." He notes that many pitches get excited about the category (AI for books, AI for drinks) without depth.

chunks.heading: Multi-product growth: strong core, adjacencies, and customer-pulled products
chunks.text:
- He rejects the idea that a second product is hard for a big company: distribution and hiring advantages make it easier than zero-to-one, and believing it's hard is what makes it hard. Zero to one is "the hardest thing in the world."
- Risks he names for a second product:
  - Promoting it can damage the first product, for example by spamming it with ads for the new one (he cites Meta as a company people accuse of this).
  - It can end up a mediocre success, which is unacceptable once you have distribution: a product that took years to reach its first million ARR "should get it in a day."
- His answer is to build "a very strong core" and then "really smart adjacencies" to it. His metaphor is iPhone and AirPods: AirPods sell tens of billions a year but would never have succeeded "if the iPhone wasn't this good." So "your job is to create the iPhone."
- He warns early-stage founders not to jump to the second thing too quickly.
- The best expansion comes from customers: with a core in the critical path, customers pull features out of you. He gives the example of HashiCorp, which had outgrown static sites but wanted every click to stay instantaneous, and came to him with that conundrum. If he could solve it they would drop their existing provider and use more of Vercel, so he calls it true design partnership, and the customer supplied both the product and the marketing story.
- He dislikes logo banners without substance ("none of these logos use this company"). His test for founders is: "tell me about one happy customer. Just one."

chunks.heading: Staying sane: ignore the noise, find product-market fit, and manage your own psychology
chunks.text:
- He tries to turn off the narrative noise ("company X will destroy company Y"), noting that Steve Jobs did not read the Wall Street Journal to outsource his opinions. He calls X a double-edged sword: a source of fog and anxiety, and also the best marketing channel in human history.
- He says he remains "insanely optimistic": "if I create something great, the rest of the world sorts itself out." He repeats his previous company co-founder's line, "product market fit solves all kinds of problems," while noting he isn't advocating selling dollars for a penny.
- His allocation of attention: "product product product, customer customer customer, code code code. Not media media media."
- On Silicon Valley's competitive pressure, he sees it as like athletics: you put in hours and optimize your company, agents and life. Stress is ambient, and he says the founder has to be their own coach.
- "Being a founder can be so lonely." He describes managing your own psychology (Ben Horowitz's phrase) as something to master: deciding when to unplug, go for a run, or invest in your social life. He found this hard coming from another country alone.
- On raising money, he says it is celebrated but is like going from 10 to 14 on a treadmill: stress goes up afterward.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Guillermo Rauch reviews Vercel's App Router bets, arguing that composition and co-location win while global, implicit caching failed. He announces Turbopack as default in Next.js 16, an open benchmark for AI agents on Next.js, and a deployment adapters API. Cache components were presented by Sam and Jimmy.

chunks.heading: Next.js 16: Turbopack, defaults and what the app router bets taught him
chunks.text:
- **Adoption:** Next.js went from about 7 million downloads per week a year earlier to 13 million per week ("nearly double the adoption in just one year").
- **Turbopack is the default in Next.js 16.** Guillermo says it already drove more than half of all Next.js 15 dev sessions, with over half a million developers using it weekly.
- **Test suite:** reaching default meant passing the existing suite of 8,266 tests, then proving it on Vercel's own internal sites for production builds.
- **Webpack stays:** "We are shipping both." He cites backwards compatibility.
- **Benchmarks vs Webpack:** up to 7x faster production builds, up to 3.2x faster initial dev load, up to 70x faster HMR updates.
- **File system caching for dev** is in beta. It extends Turbopack's in-memory task tracking across full server restarts. A production-build version is already being worked on.
- **Why speed matters for agents:** when he first saw single-digit-millisecond fast refresh, the doubt was that a human can't tell under 100ms. His answer: "for an agent loop, every millisecond counts."

chunks.heading: Bets that paid off vs the one that didn't
chunks.text:
Guillermo reviewed the app router "portfolio": server components, server actions, file system routing, Turbopack and caching.

- **Server components:** a novel, unproven architecture when adopted. Now Vite, React Router, Redwood SDK, Waku and Parcel have adopted it, TanStack Start is integrating it, and Svelte is moving more rendering to the server. "The server is so back."
- **Server actions:** with RSCs they give Next.js first-class APIs for both data reads and writes, which the pages router never had.
- **Routing:** layouts persist across navigations, avoiding unnecessary renders and keeping ephemeral state. Parallel and intercepting routes support advanced patterns, and file system conventions keep each screen's UI, data and logic together.
- **What didn't pay off:** caching. Trying to marry static rendering with nested layouts produced "confusing APIs and unpredictable behavior." He says `fetch` cache no-store and `export const dynamic = force-static` "give me a little bit of PTSD", because they created implicit coupling and "spooky action at a distance."

chunks.heading: Design principle: composition and co-location
chunks.text:
- The winning features share two traits: composition and co-location, which let developers "reason locally." Server components let any component fetch data, where `getServerSideProps` was restricted to the page module.
- Caching failed because it spans CDNs, Redis, `cache-control`, TTL and `vary`, so it always felt separate from React rather than "another Lego brick."
- RSCs pulled server-side rendering and API routes into the component boundary. `use cache` pulls caching in too.
- "Composition wins over separation of technology every single time."

chunks.heading: Designing for LLMs and agents
chunks.text:
- Models are now a design constraint: "An LLM's context window is even shorter than a human's attention span. So, if we make an API that's confusing for anyone in this room, the LLMs stand no chance."
- Rule of thumb: "The easier we make the developer experience for humans, the better we make it for agents."
- Composition and co-location also suit LLMs. His examples are React with Tailwind, shadcn, and Next pages with server and client logic in one file.
- Writing code has moved from by hand, to suggestions, to models, to agents that "author, test, execute, and ship entire features."
- **Next.js evals:** Vercel is open-sourcing a public benchmark of how well coding agents build with Next.js. His pitch: "The better AI gets at Next.js, the better everyone's developer experience will become." He invites AI companies to collaborate, partly to stop models using old APIs ("You're absolutely right" followed by outdated code).

chunks.heading: Cache components and partial pre-rendering
chunks.text:
Presented by Sam (Next.js team) as the answer to Guillermo's caching problem; Guillermo introduces the direction but the feature detail is the team's.

- Cache components (`use cache`) make partial pre-rendering the single rendering mode, with explicit caching at the component level. Guillermo frames it as bringing caching into the component boundary.
- The goal is to keep the server-first model while restoring instant client navigations.
- It is opt-in in Next.js 16, with guides and migration paths promised.

chunks.heading: Open platform: Build Deployment Adapters API
chunks.text:
Presented by Jimmy (Next.js and Turbopack lead). Guillermo's framing is the Vercel-side strategy.

- Vercel acknowledges the lock-in perception: "a lot of people claimed it was by design", though lock-in was never intended.
- The Build Deployment Adapters API is a versioned, documented contract between Next.js and the host platform. It is in alpha.
- Vercel uses the same API for its own adapter, "with the same rules we're imposing to our partners."
- The same test suite used to validate Next.js on Vercel is shared so users can verify any platform.
- A working group formed earlier in the year with AWS, Cloudflare, Firebase, Netlify and OpenNext shaped the RFC.
- Cache components also let Vercel serve the static shell from the CDN and stream dynamic content from the origin, "composing it over space." Everything works the same on a $5 Hetzner VPS.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Vercel's CEO explains why foundation models are "Cloud 2.0" backends, why integration and product design matter more than training models, and why dogfooding drives better products. He also covers abuse of AI endpoints, SEO for retrieval engines, the swing back to copy-paste, and taste-driven AI-assisted UI building.

chunks.heading: Why Vercel's AI strategy is integration, not model training
chunks.text:
Guillermo describes Vercel as a web infrastructure company that provides the frameworks, tools, infrastructure and workflows for deploying dynamic websites. It powers ChatGPT's front end (via Next.js, the open source framework) and customer sites like underarmour.com and Nintendo.

His AI thesis is that foundation models are "Cloud 2.0": the new backends. Just as great SaaS companies were built on AWS and Snowflake, he expects many AI-native companies to be built on top of models.

- He argues you do not need to train or fine-tune a model to build a useful product.
- He advises teams against "random acts of AI" (checking a box) and pushes for genuinely useful products.
- He believes much of the value accrues in the last mile of integration.
- Vercel's AI SDK is meant to be the easiest way to build an AI app without reinventing the backend. It connects to OpenAI, Hugging Face and Replicate, and he said text models were supported with voice, audio and image generation planned.

chunks.heading: Build AI-native products instead of bolting AI onto existing ones
chunks.text:
Guillermo contrasts "adding AI to an existing product" (his example: adding AI to a word processor) with starting from the problem and asking what solving it looks like when AI is an input to the design.

- His example is Jenni.ai, which he says went from $1M to $1.5M ARR over two months with a specialized product that helps researchers write papers.
- He says many productivity tools he uses daily could be rethought from the ground up.
- Vercel's template marketplace includes viral apps like Room GPT, which redesigns a room using an image generation model hosted on Replicate, packaged with a turnkey subscription, login and signup, and deployable in seconds.
- He pitches this as a way to put AI into as many developers' hands as possible.

chunks.heading: Dogfooding: being customer zero
chunks.text:
Guillermo says Vercel builds the best products by being customer zero of its own.

- All of vercel.com is built on the Vercel platform, which pushes the team to improve Next.js, infrastructure and build speed, especially as engineering headcount grew.
- He applies the same approach to AI: Vercel dogfoods its own AI SDK to automate front-end work such as forms, UIs and layouts.
- His reasoning is that good UI is statistical in nature. Users expect it to be familiar, so it is a good target for automation.

chunks.heading: Infrastructure for streaming AI responses
chunks.text:
Guillermo explains that AI apps change performance expectations on the web.

- Traditional e-commerce backends are optimized to respond in about 100 milliseconds, while AI responses can take 15-20 seconds to fully form.
- Vercel's Edge Functions run compute as close as possible to the user and support long sessions of dynamic streamed responses.
- The AI SDK demonstrates the difference between a blocking backend and a streaming one, and he says streaming makes AI apps feel good to the user.

chunks.heading: AI security, abuse and cost control
chunks.text:
Guillermo says security is a key Vercel investment area for AI.

- OpenAI is the most popular backend his aggregated, anonymized telemetry shows Vercel server functions talking to.
- When GPT-3 launched, many demos were published and abuse followed: people ran bots and proxies to get free tokens, which he calls "scraper 2.0" ("free GPT-4").
- Many products integrated AI so generically that they opened up their tokens, even with authentication in front, including to countries or companies where AI use is banned. He says this is still a huge problem.
- Vercel's response is tooling for rate limiting, bot detection and integrated caching of cacheable OpenAI responses to reduce cost.
- He expects an AI-vs-counter-AI dynamic: better AI to block bad bots while still letting authenticated good bots, such as user agents, through. He notes many AI companies are very strict about blocking bots.

chunks.heading: Observability and frameworks for AI are still immature
chunks.text:
Guillermo sees a gap in monitoring, testing and feedback tooling for AI.

- He credits Datadog and Zapier for onboarding that enumerates integrations and won't let you move on until you send a data point or choose your tools. He says this has not fully landed for AI, where the topology and frameworks (AI SDK, LangChain) differ.
- He says observability is mandatory from the first version of an AI app (V0.1), because the feedback loop is critical, whereas early startups in Cloud 1.0 might be lenient about it.
- His "hot take" is that today's opinionated AI frameworks (agents, indexing, retrieval, the last mile, not training tools like PyTorch) will have to evolve a lot, and a second generation will come out of running AI at production scale.

chunks.heading: SEO, content and the dynamic web
chunks.text:
Guillermo describes how AI shifts SEO and web architecture.

- Intermediaries to content are no longer only Google. Retrieval engines like Perplexity work in real time, and customers keep asking whether the rules of SEO still apply.
- He wants AI models to have the latest Next.js docs (ChatGPT gives the 2020 solution) and says he'd happily provide docs in whatever format. Other companies will have different content-negotiation needs.
- He expects APIs to become duplex streams of content plus citations, partly because logging sources may become a legal requirement and for UI features like hover-to-see-source.
- On crawling: Google's open Chrome User Experience Report (CrUX) shows a power law, with the top 1,000 sites making up about 50% of page views (more skewed on mobile). He suggests covering the top ~10,000 sites, delegating broad coverage to model pre-training, and adding your own up-to-date indexing of domain-relevant sources. He cites Phind as an example of a focused developer search.
- Architecture is moving from static to dynamic: static generation, which rebuilds the whole site on every content change, can take an hour to go live at scale in 2023. He notes headless CMS vendors and tools like Notion adding AI, which increases the rate of content change and personalization ("a web that's just for you").

chunks.heading: Front-end tooling, copy-paste and taste
chunks.text:
Guillermo argues the front-end ecosystem is more stable than its reputation.

- Despite the meme that front-end engineers change tools every week, the Chrome report shows React, Svelte and Vue clearly staying at scale, with React dominating. He expects innovation to shift to AI tools that generate the code.
- UI generation should resemble Midjourney: every prompt gives a statistically pleasant start. He sees this avoiding both hand-crafting every pixel and the same-looking startup template (the purple gradient hero).
- He expects the product engineer role to become about taste, like Rick Rubin ("artists hire me because of my taste"): "I like this, I don't like this, re-prompt," with the option to dive into code.
- He says AI makes copy and paste more ergonomic, questioning whether you need a package. He quotes "copy and paste is always better than a bad abstraction" and points to shadcn/ui, whose author told people to copy and paste from the browser.
- Owning the code means you can audit and secure it, avoiding dependency liabilities. He ties this to monorepos (Vercel built Turborepo), which the largest software companies use without global package managers, and sees a swing back to vendoring with AI doing code scanning.
- On languages, he notes GPT-4 is strong in JavaScript and Python because of available data. Token efficiency already favors terser syntax (e.g., redundant closing tags in HTML), and he thinks AI could operate in a purer logic layer mapped back to code.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Vercel's founder explains how betting on open source, composable "blocks" and developer experience made Vercel the default deploy target for coding agents. He covers agentic infrastructure (sandboxes, AI gateway), why software is becoming free and tailored, and why consumption pricing with no rate limits wins.

chunks.heading: Why Vercel went agent-first: the market shift
chunks.text:
- Guillermo started Vercel on a developer-experience obsession. Deploying his own startup's site on AWS, Google Cloud and Azure "took me weeks", and he decided it "can't be this hard" to deploy a site built on React and Kubernetes.
- He targeted JavaScript developers first, a pool he sized at roughly 20 million. Anyone who could build a front end got the superpower to deploy something fast everywhere and able to scale to the whole planet.
- AI coding agents then expanded who can create software. He frames the history of technology as the story of expanding access, and says AI is the biggest expansion of software creation's addressable market ever.
- Vercel's growth accelerated sharply from October 2025, especially with Opus 4.5. He says the platform "3x'ed in a few short months" and daily deployments doubled since January.
- Support on Vercel has a similar example: an agent now answers 93% of user inquiries, which improved customer experience and let Vercel give free support to far more people.

chunks.heading: Agentic infrastructure: three sides of the triangle
chunks.text:
- Guillermo's term is "agentic infrastructure", and it has three legs:
  - Infrastructure for coding agents. Claude Code, Codex and v0 need somewhere to deploy.
  - Infrastructure for building your own agents. He expects the software of the future to be agents.
  - A self-driving cloud, where the platform configures and optimizes itself.
- Self-driving cloud: the agent comes back and says "I just optimized all your software. I made it twice as fast. Here's the PR," or has already shipped it and measured improved conversion. The goal is to end pager-duty pain.
- He calls Vercel "the AWS of AI or agents": a full-stack cloud from developer tools down to infrastructure.
- He thinks Amazon might name AWS "Amazon Agent Services" if it started today, because the thing people ship is now an agent.

chunks.heading: The cloud is changing: from pages to agents, from pixels to tokens
chunks.text:
- Old web assumption: instant request-response. Amazon found that every 100 ms of slowdown cost 1% of conversion.
- Agents break that. Runs went from seconds to minutes to hours, and some now work for an entire day before returning a report or building software.
- Vercel hosts platforms that create whole companies for people and deploy agents to maintain, advertise and grow them.
- EC2 was designed for human-written code, so compute demand was bounded by the number of programmers. Agent-written, agent-repaired and agent-secured code lifts that bound.
- Vercel used to stream pixels; now it streams intelligence as tokens. He says this changes pricing and business models: seat-based pricing gives way to token-based pricing that measures intelligence.
- He is still "super bullish" on human-centric experiences and predicts a return of a more whimsical web, citing Microsoft Encarta as the model. He expects immersive experiences from video and 3D generation, including just-in-time 3D rendering on Vercel.

chunks.heading: Products built by reusing the same engine
chunks.text:
- **AI Gateway:** described as a CDN for tokens. It adds observability, failover, security, acceleration and caching for tokens from Anthropic, Gemini and others, plus load balancing.
  - His example: if a user says "thanks", a smart gateway could route to a small model to reply "you're welcome" instead of firing up huge GPU capacity.
  - Also a semantic cache. Vercel open-sourced the recipe so others can build a competing gateway.
- **Sandbox:** the EC2-equivalent for agents. Models get better results given a computer, and are post-trained in Docker containers. His analogy: the first thing a company does with a new hire is hand over a laptop.
  - Sandbox reuses the virtualization primitive behind every Vercel deployment.
  - Because agents can fall for phishing and exfiltrate data, Vercel is building security products to protect sandboxes.
- **Dogfooding principle:** Vercel builds new products on its own platform. AI Gateway is built on Fluid Compute and the global network, so he "reused 95% of the rocket engine" from the CDN of pages.
- **Why Vercel built the whole stack:** "You have to do the whole thing for the thing that matters." He says agents are "probably the last class of software" and Vercel can't skip the fastest-growing economy.
- Almost nothing broke under the surge, because Sandbox and deployments share the same compute expertise.

chunks.heading: How Vercel became the default for coding agents
chunks.text:
- Agents arrive with a world model. Models learned from years of public content about Next.js, React and Vercel's open source tools.
- A report he cited gives Vercel's shadcn UI library 90.1% share in coding-agent output, and Vercel near-total share on deployment.
- His answer on how it happened: "All of the above" (content, API quality, composability), and he neither confirms nor denies deals.
- **Design for local reasoning:** he bet on Tailwind despite finding its long lines ugly, because components can be reasoned about and moved in isolation. This suits context windows (about 1 million tokens today) that can't hold all of humanity's code. Next.js and React have the same property.
- **Composability** is the prerequisite for agentic scalability.
- **Block economy** (Mitchell Hashimoto's phrase, who recently joined Vercel's board): to get Claude Code, Codex or Grok CLI to choose your technology, build blocks that fit "agentic ergonomics". Open infrastructure gives agents a target, like LEGO bricks.
- Domains were an early bet. Codex users want to name their creations, so many find Vercel first through domain purchase. He wants Vercel to be "the front door to any emerging idea on the planet."

chunks.heading: Software, SaaS and what survives
chunks.text:
- He doesn't call it the death of software: "software has never moved faster and been more alive."
- Examples:
  - A startup CEO replaced the company's parking-lot management software with a v0 prototype.
  - Vercel rebuilt its own Salesforce front end with a team of two, for sales reps' account, opportunity and business-intelligence views, while keeping Salesforce as the system of record.
  - Sales engineers use v0 to arrive at customer calls with working custom software instead of a slide deck.
- Software is now close to free and often throwaway, but this raises engagement. He cites Tobi Lütke's "reflexivity of AI" and his own essay, "It's Hard to Forego Efficiency."
- Hard infrastructure engineering remains hard. Sometimes Vercel convenes three agents plus smart humans to review a single line of code.
- SaaS companies that expose agentic interfaces (MCP, CLIs, APIs) will fit this world. System-of-record and access-control layers get reused.
- Customers' agents now find Vercel on their own. He asks customers for their agent transcripts to turn into evals. He expects agent-to-agent bug reports and feature requests.

chunks.heading: Where value accrues and who loses
chunks.text:
- He expects the most value in useful services that agents need to do real work: sandboxes, deployment platforms, domains. He says whether this is a bubble depends on delivering useful services.
- Security and governance (guardrails, securing the broader internet) are big opportunities, and Vercel keeps hiring engineers because "there's just so much more to build."
- **Short:** static data and content businesses (Stack Overflow as the example), and drag-and-drop builders ("coding with training wheels", which he found patronizing). Also companies that don't open up, the "e-brochure" model where you talk to enterprise sales for months.
- **Long:** anyone "moving at the speed of tokens". Agents want raw signal: consumption-based pricing, instant sign-up, no sales call.
- **No more rate limits:** he told his company to drop arbitrary rate limits (e.g. a made-up 100 deploys per minute), keeping them only for abuse prevention and KYC, since pay-for-what-you-use should not cap demand. A YC company that didn't exist three months earlier was generating so many deployments it surprised the team.

chunks.heading: Open source and personal background
chunks.text:
- Open source came from being a teenager in Argentina wanting free tools. Vercel built a large business on top of open source, which he calls contrarian.
- His advice on schooling: dropping out of high school made his visa harder (he wrote *Smashing Node.js* to qualify for an O-1), so he suggests not dropping out of your degree, with caveats.
- If not building Vercel, he'd work on space tech (Mars, a multi-planetary species) and energy (fission, fusion, geothermal), viewing intelligence as energy in, intelligence out.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Rauch explains Vercel's shift from human developer experience to agent experience, with agents now making 60% of deployments. He covers publishing agent-readable content and protocols, why custom software beats SaaS, open-source distribution, non-gameable retention metrics, and what he hires for.

chunks.heading: Agents are now the main deployers, so Vercel is built for them
chunks.text:
- Guillermo says Vercel took about 10 years to reach 1 billion deployments, then added another 1.5 billion in roughly the next 10 months.
- Coding agents made 3% of deployments at the start of the year. Now they make 60%.
- His founding idea was to make deployment easy, because deploying a fast, secure, scalable app once required "a PhD in cloud computing."
- Agents write good code but have nowhere to put it. He calls code a liability: it can hold vulnerabilities, delete things or leak customer data, so it needs a responsible place to run.
- Vercel became that place. He says most of what goes viral on X is a Vercel app, often visible from the default vercel.app domain.
- Open source helped. After 11 years of making everything open, models trained on that material know Vercel well, so agents default to it.

chunks.heading: Building the internet for agents
chunks.text:
- The old internet is HTML pages for humans. The agent internet runs on protocols: MCP for exposing tools, plus new agent-payment and agentic-commerce protocols.
- When an agent visits vercel.com, he wants it to get direct information, not the gradient triangle and polished UI.
- Companies should give agents context and also expose their tools, products and services. Vercel works with Stripe and Shopify so agents can transact.
- Agents already buy from the Vercel marketplace: one of the most popular tools in Vercel's toolkit lets an agent purchase a product for an employee with no human step.
- He criticizes a web built to block bots. Vercel's stance is to help every company re-tool for agents.
- What matters is bot intelligence: knowing which agents (ChatGPT, Claude, Grok, coding agents, crawlers) visit and whether they get a good experience.
- Content tactic: publish transcripts alongside podcast episodes. Models have training cutoffs and agents rely on web search, so published text is what they can find.
- Inside Vercel, agents sit on top of Salesforce and similar tools. He asks the Slack agent for a briefing on an account before a meeting and never opens Salesforce.
- Interfaces become dynamic and contextual. A junior sales rep and the finance team would see different depth from the same data.

chunks.heading: Custom software over bundles of SaaS
chunks.text:
- He is "yes-code," the opposite of the no-code wave. Coding agents make code free, so he argues the winning combination is to "buy or sell as a platform" and never need to buy software again.
- Teams can build the exact podcast scheduler, note-taker or agent they need. He says enterprises get the biggest return from tools built for their own domain.
- Systems of record (customer records, contact info, meeting notes, support tickets) stay as critical data infrastructure.
- Software that was mostly a UI over that data is what changes.

chunks.heading: Open models, model choice and the frontier labs
chunks.text:
- Vercel runs one of the largest token-distribution networks through its AI Gateway. It serves open and closed models and republishes anonymized usage data under a Creative Commons license.
- At the start of the year most traffic went to proprietary models (OpenAI, Gemini, others). Now, he says, 80% of tokens on the network are open models.
- The cause: Chinese labs shipped open models that compete with the frontier on coding. He used Kimi the day before and liked it.
- His reasoning is that most work doesn't need "Albert Einstein." Support replies, proofreading and data labeling are fine on open models.
- Pattern he describes: use a frontier model for planning, then open models to execute the plan.
- He wants model choice to be modular like an engine. Swapping a provider should take one line of code, and auto-selection by task is where the field is heading.
- Enterprises like this because it avoids lock-in, gives them leverage and forces labs to compete on price and quality. A leading model may hold the lead for only two weeks.
- His view of frontier-lab risk is that loyalty and retention are hard to measure. Parts of AI feel like crypto, where money "comes easily and goes easily."
- He names free promotions, inflated token volumes and fake zero-data-retention claims as things to question. Vercel's gateway contractually guarantees zero data retention with its providers.
- His stated goal is to push token prices toward zero.

chunks.heading: Security, sandboxes and verifiable code
chunks.text:
- Agents will do whatever it takes to finish a task, and prompt injection (malicious instructions hidden in a YouTube comment, say) can redirect them using your tokens and tools. He says most people haven't mastered agent security.
- He cites the OpenAI/Hugging Face breach story as his example: an agent escaped a sandbox. He prefers FreeBSD's old word "jail" to "sandbox," because once out of a sandbox the agent is everywhere.
- Vercel runs a $1M sandbox challenge, inviting the world to break its sandbox. One participant with an army of agents made progress, and Vercel is sharing the findings with industry peers.
- He opposes banning open models over cyber risk. Their intelligence is what makes them useful for defense too, and he expects a near-term war between good tokens and bad tokens.
- Vercel is not tied to one lab for security work. Enterprises can pick whichever model is best at cybersecurity.
- For enterprises he built an "intranet for the agent era": a private platform to deploy internal software without it leaking to the public internet.
- He launched a proof system over a weekend so AI doesn't ship bad code or leak data. He expects code to move toward mathematical verifiability, and likes Rust because its compiler tells you you're wrong, a burden agents now carry instead of humans.
- Compute vision: "serverless" evolves into "fluid compute" that scales up with traffic and shrinks to nothing, serving sandboxes, jobs, websites and agents.

chunks.heading: Humans still need to understand the code
chunks.text:
- His tweet "refuse not to understand" rejects the idea of prompting an agent and shipping without looking. He asks the AI to explain what it did, and he still reads code.
- His analogy is an engineering manager who unblocks work and sometimes writes code, tests or benchmarks. The best ones he has worked with love code.
- He doesn't want to be the person demanding that everyone understand every line. Beginners should be able to ship, as he never could at their age.
- For truly critical systems (infrastructure, security, national security) he thinks human engineers are still needed, including those who go deep with AI.
- A migration example: Vercel moved Mercedes' F1 site to its platform using an agent in about five minutes on the first pass, work that used to take months with consultants. Migration fear used to block cloud adoption.

chunks.heading: Hiring, running the company and personal operating principles
chunks.text:
- Hiring: he looks for people who can build teams of agents ("agentic engineering," "software factories"). A demo or side project is no longer proof, since projects are easy.
- He also wants strong human communication. He doesn't want to read machine-written tweets.
- He expects much higher technical depth from sales engineers and account execs, because agents let them handle questions that used to need engineering. Borrowing a former Splunk CEO's line: the two most important people are the ones closest to the code and closest to the customer.
- Company values: "continuous improvement toward excellence" and "dig into the details."
