- He treats the company as a product and invests in the infrastructure that produces future innovation. The core of it is values and mission.
- Public communication: his advice to founders is "be yourself," share your story and don't overthink it. He uses no hidden ghostwriters.
- Decisions: use data, but in a fast-moving AI market pair it with anecdotes and intuition, because a quarterly analyst spreadsheet is too slow.
- Founder metric advice: focus on metrics that can't be gamed. Ads and viral marketing can be gamed. Lifetime customers can't.
- Pace: what Vercel sells is speed of iteration, not raw speed, which can mean spinning in circles. He says peers are working roughly 7am to 7pm, seven days a week, and mostly enjoying it.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Guillermo Rauch argues the cloud, interfaces and who can build software are all changing as the web moves from pages to agents. Coding is one skill among many; the durable meta skill is shipping end to end with taste. AI should serve quality, not only productivity.

chunks.heading: The shift from pages to agents
chunks.text:
Guillermo frames AI as "perhaps the most important transformation we'll see in our careers": the move "from pages to agents," or "from pixels to agents," or "from foreground to the background."

- Vercel started in 2015 to give everyone the internal infrastructure that Amazon, Google and Facebook used to build and ship fast. He cites Next.js at 13 million downloads per week and a platform serving over a trillion requests per month for over 10 million customers.
- He says the same wall-hitting situation is now repeating with AI, and that "even the giants haven't figured it out yet."
- His stance is that developer jobs are not going away, but surviving requires changing how developers think and create.

chunks.heading: The cloud is being rebuilt for agents
chunks.text:
Guillermo argues the infrastructure built for pages does not fit agents.

- The old cloud: static assets on a CDN, optimized for page load time. Google rewarded fast pages with higher rankings, which created a flywheel of more business, conversion and organic traffic.
- The new need: a "CDN for tokens."
- Compute shifts from fast one-shot request/response to long periods of "thinking time" and background multi-step workflows.
- Search rankings give way to embedding intelligence everywhere, with agents "meeting customers where they are."

chunks.heading: Interfaces become generative, and the move from code-first to code-last
chunks.text:
- Before, interfaces were deterministic: you designed a dashboard and "every pixel was specified." Now they are generative and adaptive, created on demand, with context, personalized to the user.
- Example: Snowflake announced an integration with v0, Vercel's generative UI agent, which creates data visualizations on the fly.
- His position: "Front ends aren't disappearing. We're just generating them on demand," and user experience matters more than ever. What changes is how it is created.
- He describes the decades-long trend away from the code itself and toward the end goal (great products and experiences) as a move from a code-first to a code-last world.

chunks.heading: Everyone can build, so the barrier is clarity of intent
chunks.text:
- Software used to be limited to people who learned syntax, command lines, data structures, IDEs and complex infrastructure.
- Now "the barrier isn't technical knowledge. It's clarity of intent." Prompting and understanding how AI works is "the new literacy."
- He used to see JavaScript as a great democratizer: framework-defined infrastructure let millions of JavaScript developers become cloud engineers by pushing code and getting globally optimized infrastructure. AI is a superset, "because we can all yap. We can all talk. We can all prompt."
- Distribution tactic: put agents inside Slack, Zoom, Teams and Snowflake and treat platforms as primary prompting surfaces. This reduces friction and could take the field "from tens of millions of developers to a billion developers."
- Anecdote: a company founded in the cloud's early days has one rule, "they don't do code." Internal communication is just conversation about what to build, with no GitHub or infrastructure talk.

chunks.heading: Meta skills for developers: don't get attached to individual skills
chunks.text:
- "Don't get too attached to your individual skills." Doing math in your head is a great asset, but a machine now does it better. He sees coding as one of those individual skills.
- The meta skills that matter are the ones machines can't easily replicate: what problems are worth solving, what experiences could be better, faster or more delightful, and what is about to become possible.
- Developers should uplevel by becoming more full stack (front end, back end, middleware, data). Data engineers can build interfaces; front-end developers can orchestrate complex back ends.
- The opportunity is to become an orchestrator of a variety of agents, without going as deep into each line of code.

chunks.heading: Shipping is the meta skill
chunks.text:
- "Shipping is a distinct skill from coding. Shipping is the meta skill."
- Shipping means building end to end: messaging, designing, coding, QAing, teaching, marketing, selling, pivoting, iterating. Coding used to dominate because coding ability was scarce.
- "Shipping is about storytelling," including in data, and it starts with communicating your intent clearly.
- Shipping also requires taste: experience, craft, attention to detail. He treats taste as a developable skill, not an innate gift. His exercise: quantify how much time you spend watching people use your products, or other products.
- "In a world where AI can generate infinite variations, the ability to discern quality will be a gold standard skill."

chunks.heading: Move fast and raise quality
chunks.text:
- His counterposition: everyone talks about AI for productivity, but AI must also serve quality.
- He cites former Snowflake CEO Frank Slootman's line that when velocity increases, excuses get made about quality ("We can't possibly move this fast and maintain quality"). Guillermo's response: "Move fast and raise quality."
- Advice to customers asking what to build: care about both productivity and quality. "Productivity without quality is just noise. And quality without productivity means you're probably getting left behind."
- Just because code generates faster does not mean standards should drop: "we should raise them."

chunks.heading: Which agents to ship, and keeping the AI cloud open
chunks.text:
Agents Vercel has recently shipped:
- Support agents that resolve common customer questions instantly.
- Abuse agents that analyze threats and recommend actions.
- Content agents that turn conversations into structured drafts.
- A data analyst agent (announced with Snowflake) that turns natural language into SQL and visualizations.

How agents raise quality:
- They concentrate judgment, reserving human time for decisions that shape the product and business.
- The bar rises over time because the system learns from what the team accepts, edits or rejects.

Openness:
- He believes every organization and individual should be able to create and deploy their own agents, like owning a domain name and deploying to it.
- He criticizes the first AI wave as dominated by closed models, proprietary SDKs and centralized interfaces, and calls for an open AI cloud with access to models, platforms and infrastructure.
- Closing thesis: the future of developer experience "isn't about coding less necessarily. It's about shipping more": more ambitious products, more innovative solutions, more value for users.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Guillermo Rauch argues that JavaScript on the web should be judged purely by user experience, especially how fast users get the data they want. He gives seven principles: pre-render pages, act instantly on input, push data and code updates, control data exchange, respect history, and predict behavior. This dissolves the website vs web app divide.

chunks.heading: Pre-rendering is a performance requirement, not an SEO feature
chunks.text:
Guillermo argues that "pre-rendered pages are not optional" and that the usual choice between pre-rendered/server-rendered apps and single-page apps (SPAs) is a false dichotomy. Giving up either one costs user experience.

- Latency, not bandwidth, is the bottleneck. Bandwidth keeps improving, but the speed of light sets a floor. He cites a theoretical minimum of about 50ms between the US coasts (Stuart Cheshire's Stanford-to-Boston round trip is 43.2ms at light speed in fibre, about 85ms in practice). So the number of round trips to show data is what matters.
- A typical SPA returns an empty body plus `<script>` tags. That means one trip for the script and another for the data, when the server already knew from the URL what the page would show (for example, the orders for `/orders`).
- Caching the bundle doesn't remove the cost: parsing and evaluating scripts can take hundreds of milliseconds on mobile, and users usually see a blank page with no feedback meanwhile.
- TCP slow start and SSL handshakes add round trips. Reaching 64 KB of throughput takes about four round trips, so the first roughly 14kb of the response matter most.
- Pre-rendering is application-specific. Options he lists: render the page "shell" immediately and fetch sections in parallel; pre-render only the content above the fold; leave non-essential parts for the client. He also suggests loading "structural CSS" (blocking) separately from "skin/theme CSS" (async), and prioritizing scripts by URL (sorting scripts matter for `/orders`, not for settings).
- He expects HTTP/2 server push to eventually allow cacheable client code in a single hop. His example of a SPA with no extra round trips is the StackOverflow clone in 4096 bytes (everything inlined, at the cost of cacheability).
- Sharing render code between browser and server, with progressive loading of scripts and styles, erases the website vs. webapp distinction: "A blog and a CRM are fundamentally not that different." Both have URLs, navigation and data to show.

chunks.heading: Act immediately on user input and mask latency
chunks.text:
JavaScript's biggest UX advantage, in his view, is masking network latency to approach zero perceived latency.

- Act optimistically on clicks, buttons and form submits instead of waiting for the server. Example: Gmail archives an email in the UI right away while the request runs asynchronously.
- "Layout adaptation": the first state of a page knows the layout of the next, so it can transition before data arrives. Google Instant Search switches to the results layout as the user types or holds down a key. iPhone `default.png` launch images did the same for CPU latency.
- File input: show uploads (drag and drop, paste, file picker) immediately by rendering thumbnails client-side, as in Cloudup uploads.
- Perceived speed is real value. He cites the Houston airport complaints that dropped after lengthening the walk to baggage claim, without faster baggage handling.
- Spinners and loading indicators "should become a rarity." Where optimism is risky (payment forms, logout), defer the spinner until the user no longer feels the response was immediate.
- Nielsen's limits: 0.1s feels instantaneous (no feedback needed), 1.0s keeps the flow of thought intact, 10s is the limit of attention.
- PJAX and TurboLinks miss this opportunity because the client doesn't know the next page's representation until a full server round trip finishes.

chunks.heading: Make the UI self-updating and reconcile state
chunks.text:
His third principle is reactivity: when data changes on the server, tell clients without being asked. "Your UI should be self-updating."

- Think in terms of concurrent data points rather than users. Even a single user sending a photo from phone to laptop needs live updates. Facebook's newsfeed was fine as a static render when people updated profiles once a day, but not once peers can like a photo seconds after upload.
- Apply it uniformly, including session and login state: logging out in one tab should invalidate all open tabs, which improves privacy and security on shared devices.
- New challenges: connection and reconnection management, and state reconciliation. The app must update correctly after long gaps (a laptop lid closed for days).
- Reconciliation also applies to pre-rendered pages. Data sent with the initial page sits on the wire until scripts load, which is effectively a disconnection, and the first script connection is a session resumption.

chunks.heading: Control data exchange: retry, queue offline, protect in-flight data
chunks.text:
With AJAX, WebSocket and EventSource, the client can manage the server conversation, which the original link-and-form web could not.

- Show connection state. If the UI promises automatic updates, tell users when it's disconnected and when it is reconnecting.
- On disconnect, store pending data in memory or, better, `localStorage` and send it later. With ServiceWorker, apps can sync in the background even when closed.
- Handle timeouts and errors and "retry on behalf of the user." Tell the user only about persistent failures.
- Treat some errors specially: an unexpected `403` may mean the session was invalidated, so prompt a login screen.
- Prevent accidental interruption of the data flow with `beforeunload` handlers and by intercepting in-app link clicks to show your own modals.

chunks.heading: Don't break history, enhance it
chunks.text:
Without the browser managing URLs for state changes, JS apps can break expectations that plain hyperlinks gave for free.

- Call `history.pushState` or `replaceState` for transitions such as infinite pagination, which many apps skip.
- "Fast Back" (a term from Daniel Pipius): treat Back as an app-level button, render the cached previous page instantly, then apply live-data updates and tell the user what changed.
- Watch for cases outside your control: server-rendered HTML later modified on the client can come back stale after returning from a third-party site.
- Remember scroll position. He tested Twitter and Facebook feeds and found both exhibited "scrolling amnesia."
- Some state is volatile and tied only to a history entry. In a comment tree with collapsible subtrees, collapsed state may persist on Back but a fresh link visit should show everything uncollapsed.

chunks.heading: Push code updates as well as data
chunks.text:
"Pushing data without pushing code is insufficient." A page refresh used to reload both, so a live-data app also needs live code, especially when a tab can stay open a very long time.

- Reasons: breaking backend API changes require client updates, otherwise clients misread data or send incompatible formats; and a self-updating UI removes the user's reason to refresh.
- Mechanisms: with a server push channel, emit a notification when new code ships. Without one, append a version number header to outgoing HTTP requests so the server can compare it to its latest version, decline the request and advise the client.
- Some apps auto-refresh when the page is not visible (Page Visibility API) and no form inputs are filled in.
- Better is hot code reloading: swap individual modules on the fly instead of refreshing. Keep the architecture modular so a component update doesn't restart, say, the socket connection.
- This works best when behavior (code) is separated from data (state) and the UI is rendered from state, as in React. If state lives in the DOM or listeners are wired by hand, swapping code is far harder. He points to Dan Abramov's react-hot-loader.

chunks.heading: Predict behavior ("negative latency")
chunks.text:
His seventh principle is that a rich app can anticipate input to beat latency.

- Simplest form: start fetching data when the user hovers a link so it's ready by click.
- More advanced: analyze mouse trajectory to detect when the pointer is heading toward a button and prefetch before the click (he links a jQuery "I know where you are aiming" example).
- His conclusion: keep the web's hyperlinked-pages building block, load code, style and markup progressively as users navigate, and use JavaScript to add speed and interactivity without losing the web's original strengths.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Guillermo Rauch explains how defining a UI as a pure function of state (as in React) lets designers and programmers share one protocol. By rendering every state as a visible artboard, you can measure completeness, discover missing states, and improve estimates.

chunks.heading: Pure UI as a pure function of application state
chunks.text:
- Guillermo's core idea: define an application's UI as "a pure function of application state." A pure function can be replaced by its return value without changing program behavior (`concat('hello', 'world')` can be swapped for `'hello world'`).
- Applied to a GUI, the function returns an abstract representation of widgets or markup (a virtual DOM), not real DOM elements. It maps parameters to output.
- When parameters change (a new video, a user action), the function is called again and the view updates.
- The programmer no longer specifies the transition from state A to state B. He argues you only describe what A looks like and what B looks like, discretely.
- He frames this as a benefit of the programming model React enables, rather than of React's feature list.
- Footnote: comparing libraries by features is inferior to examining the model they impose on the programmer. The model tells you how code will fare as the product matures and the team grows, and where the technology will evolve.

chunks.heading: Designers already work this way: artboards and styleguides
chunks.text:
- Guillermo argues UI designers have been intuitively "programming" this way, arguably more directly than programmers.
- The rise of mobile forced designers to think about screen sizes, and artboards became the de-facto standard for showing how a UI renders per configuration.
- His example: the Socket.IO dashboard on desktop vs mobile is the same `dashboard()` function called with different parameters, e.g. `dashboard({ width: 375 })`. He notes that with layout data available in the function, CSS media queries can be redundant.
- Styleguides, such as GitHub Primer's buttons, are the same idea. The base function is `<button>` and its parameters are `class="btn-sm"` or `disabled`, which can be combined (`btn-sm btn-outline`).
- Declarative CSS and HTML suit this well.

chunks.heading: The VideoPress rebuild and the hidden size of the state space
chunks.text:
- Context: he redesigned and rebuilt VideoPress, the WordPress video platform. He dropped the Flash dependency for HTML5 `<video>` and added new functionality.
- He designed the main player states in his design tool: video converting on the backend, removed due to DMCA, connection or server error, not G rated so the viewer enters their age, playing but no further data received, and hovering the progress bar.
- Key warning: underestimating the state space is easy, because the experience is "just watching video." Every other state looks exceptional, like an error, so it's tempting to reduce it to "just `<video>` and a few extra divs."
- He offers this as an explanation for chronically poor software estimates. If the magnitude of the work isn't clear to the developer or designer, let alone to people outside the process, accurate prediction is impossible.

chunks.heading: Implementation as rendered artboards driven by JSON
chunks.text:
- The implementation mirrored the design workflow. He broke the design into small view functions that render to HTML artboards.
- Because the functions map data to UI, he wrote a simple JSON file listing the params for each state. Example: a "Thumb tooltip" view with entries for Default, Custom offset (30px) and Custom offset (left edge), each with width, height and tip position params.
- Each rendered view got a `[+]` icon to edit the invocation parameters live. He could drag numbers to resize the player and see behavior beyond the designer's breakpoints (iPhone, iPad). He compares this to fuzz testing.
- For image parameters he added a link that pulls a random image from imgur.

chunks.heading: Design vs discovery, and what discovery found
chunks.text:
- He separates two interleaved phases. Design is taking available data and coming up with its representation; the outcome is reasonably well specified. Discovery is the expansion and evolution of that input: uncovering new states and ideas during the process. Even very experienced designers go through this loop.
- Parameter permutations are potentially infinite, so only some combinations can be considered at design time.
- Concrete discoveries:
  - The tooltip over the progress bar grew to 6 representations. The tip triangle had to be split in half near the player's edges, and a state was needed for when the thumbnail grid hasn't loaded.
  - Light images clashed with the blurred-thumbnail conversion progress bar. Adding shadows made it work across a wide range of photos.
  - Implementation surfaced the video download stalling completely (the MediaElement `stalled` event) as a state neither designer nor developer had considered.
- He says the designer-developer communication becomes a clear protocol: the mockup is requested again with the extra parameter `{ stalled: true }`, and the TODO list expands with responsibilities neatly divided.

chunks.heading: Measuring completeness, progress and complexity
chunks.text:
- If you define 20 distinct states and 10 are rendered on screen as HTML, the implementation is 50% done. This makes completeness directly visible.
- Contrast with a jQuery payment form: a 200 on success, a 400 on failure, and handlers that show or hide `#msg-error` / `#msg-success`. The only way to know both branches are correct is to execute the code.
- That is hard in practice. Apps must answer questions like "what if this network call is taking too long?", "what if the response doesn't come back?" and "what if the server returns an error?" Reaching the form may itself require specific login state, role, privileges and profile data.
- Mapping the application this way measures complexity as well as progress: too many steps, too many screens, inconsistency.
- Visualizing how the map grows over time shows how accurate initial assumptions were. If much of the map is discovered late, the project was improperly scoped or understood, which explains why it's taking longer to ship.

chunks.heading: Where the workflow leads
chunks.text:
- Short term: designer-programmer communication improves dramatically by becoming "well technically delineated."
- Longer term, he extrapolates to a future where going from sketch to design to implementation is far more accessible to anyone with an idea, a "growing convergence" of designer and programmer roles.
- The goal of an app is the creative representation of data a set of users cares about.
- He notes there is still repeated effort translating ideas from mind to medium, and expects tools to follow as understanding of the process improves.
- Closing line: "Lorem Ipsum has had a good run. Let's replace it with data." Design with real data instead of placeholder text.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Rauch recaps his first year building ZEIT: Now (immutable one-command deploys), World (free DNS), Hyper (an extensible terminal) and Next.js. He explains the product philosophy behind each, plus ideas on accessibility, universal code style and being wrong about reactions.

chunks.heading: Building ZEIT: now, Hyper, Next.js (2016)
chunks.text:
Guillermo started ZEIT in November 2015 with Tony Kovanen and Naoyuki Kanezawa. He chose to launch with "people you love and respect" as a hedge against the personal risk of founding a company. The mission: "empower the individual. At home or inside companies and teams. Go directly to production without barriers." The aim is cloud deployment that is simple, instant and global. In his view, "a cloud where you choose regions is not living up to its name."

By January 2017 the team had grown to 8 people.

chunks.heading: now: one-command, immutable deployments
chunks.text:
Announced in April 2016, `now` deploys any project with one command. It takes a `package.json`, `Dockerfile` or static files, builds them in the cloud and serves them under HTTP/2.

- Each deployment is immutable and gets its own unique URL (e.g. `rauchg-blog-hhafwnefgw.now.sh`).
- The same system covers development, staging and production. You deploy to build and test, and "stage" by sharing the link with co-workers or clients before going live.
- Going to production is a single `alias` command (`now alias <deployment> rauchg.com`), with zero downtime. He used this to publish the blog itself.
- Milestones by end of 2016: 2 billion+ requests served, 40,000+ deployments, and usage nearly doubled in the last two months of the year.
- Adopters included government, health care, non-profits, tourism, education (hackathons, Ivy League classrooms), many Fortune 500 companies, and parents teaching kids to code.

chunks.heading: ZEIT World: removing the DNS/SSL bottleneck
chunks.text:
Guillermo calls dealing with SSL certificates, domains and DNS records "very tedious," for individuals and for teams. He has seen too many companies that depend on one specific person or team for this. Such processes "kill productivity and create invisible barriers for product engineers," and people get used to them.

- ZEIT World is a free global DNS solution.
- When `alias` is used with a new domain, ZEIT checks whether it uses its nameservers. If so, it configures the records automatically.

chunks.heading: Hyper: the terminal as a web-tech platform
chunks.text:
He sees the CLI as a combination of elegance and productivity.

- Elegant because most CLI programs follow the Unix philosophy: they do one thing well, compose, are easy to replace, and resist bloat.
- Productive because "text is king": low-bandwidth, fast to input, searchable (he cites `ctrl+r`).
- Hyper is the "Atom of terminals": open source, built and extended with web technologies on Electron. URLs can render as sandboxed `<webview>` tags.
- Milestones: 300,000+ downloads, 13,000+ GitHub stars, 300+ plugins and themes. It launched on Windows and Linux after macOS, and beat native terminals on some benchmarks.
- Plugins explored new CLI directions: HTML rendering, charts, status lines.

chunks.heading: Next.js: server-rendered React, minimal setup
chunks.text:
Next.js is a minimalist framework for universal React apps. He describes it as bringing back good ideas from PHP: no setup, start from the filesystem, automatic routing, and pre-rendered HTML on the first hop instead of a blank page.

- Start with `./pages/index.js` exporting a component, then run `next`.
- Each page is a webpack entry point, so each section becomes its own bundle based on its imports. No more shipping "several megabytes of JS code with each page."
- React's declarative model allows `<Link>` prefetching in the background via a ServiceWorker, which is why zeit.co and his blog feel snappy.
- Positioning: a generalization of the site vs app paradigms. Sites pre-render markup and load code lazily; apps download everything up front and feel faster afterwards. Next.js does both.
- He says it enables the "7 principles of rich web applications" he wrote about in 2014.

chunks.heading: Developer-experience details he adopts
chunks.text:
- **Addressable errors:** his only essay of 2016. Whenever he writes an error to a terminal or console, he attaches a URL, inspired by React's warnings. Instead of users Googling error messages, they land on a resource that can be updated over time and commented on.
- **Gradient default avatars:** hash the customer UID, take `mod 360` as the HSL hue, and spin evenly around the cylindrical HSL space to find harmonic colors. This makes multiple accounts easy to tell apart.
- **Universal code styles:** he now uses `standard` for JavaScript (no semicolons) and was initially skeptical. He is glad to spend no time debating style and wants this mindset applied to every language his teams use.
- **Emoji reactions:** he first expected them to be an annoying gimmick, especially for work. He now calls emojis "one of the best tools for conveying nuance and emotion" in text, since reactions add information to a channel without clutter and let people share how they feel instead of staying quiet.
- **Accessibility:** inspired by a talk from IBM Fellow Chieko Asakawa, he argues accessibility drives invention (braille went digital before consumer e-books; the telephone grew out of work for the hearing-impaired; the blind community adopted internet forums early). His conclusion: "No excuses anymore for disregarding accessibility!"

chunks.heading: Ideas about networks, unpredictability and humility
chunks.text:
- **The Earth is a brain:** the effectiveness of this "mega-brain" depends on how well individual "sub-brains" communicate. His example is Terence Tao solving the Erdős discrepancy problem after a stranger's blog comment (Uwe Stroinski). The whole is greater than the sum of its parts, so an individual's role is diminished.
- **Unpredictability:** citing Nick Szabo's "rolling singularity," people "can't generally predict what's going to happen next in markets or which new startups will succeed in the long run."
- He expects fast, free, unrestricted internet to have an outsized impact.
- **Interface vs reality:** from Donald Hoffman, perception is a set of evolutionary "hacks." His takeaway: "don't mistake the UI for the reality of the computer behind it."
- **"True enough":** he is drawn to accepting an inherent messiness in explanations. "True enough is as true as can be gotten."

chunks.heading: Bitcoin as a battery
chunks.text:
He answers the objection that proof-of-work is wasteful. If a system has no trusted third party, it must be anchored to a universally verifiable reality, and physical energy expenditure provides that. The cost of running Bitcoin is the exact cost of a system that trusts a network with no privileged nodes.

Via Chandler Guo, he adds a second incentive: if you produce surplus electricity, "Bitcoin mining is your battery." He cites Adam Back's framing of Bitcoin as a universal element representing proof-of-joules spent.

chunks.heading: Side projects
chunks.text:
- **thoughtcomplete:** autocomplete for your thoughts, built on the Twitter API. It came from the observation that there are only about `2 * 10^46` meaningfully different English tweets, so people keep making remarkably similar observations and puns.
- He sees npm as the closest thing to a Library of Babel for code: need a module to compare versions? You find all the possible ones.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Rauch argues that building anything means accepting tradeoffs and letting things drop (design, docs, tests), but efficiency is the exception. Once people experience a faster workflow or system, going back is nearly impossible, and even knowing a faster option exists creates an inexorable pull. He illustrates this with fast search, deploys in seconds, and his own experience as an immigrant.

chunks.heading: Efficiency is the one thing you can't forego
chunks.text:
Guillermo argues that life and engineering are full of tradeoffs, and that you have to learn to let some things drop to the ground to make progress. Examples he gives: de-optimizing email and meeting availability to hit a deadline, shipping a new company with a weak website design, or shipping a new app without documented APIs, thorough code comments or lots of tests.

His core claim is that one thing is different: once you are used to a certain level of efficiency in a task, system or environment, "it's extraordinarily difficult to forego it."

- Everything else (polish, docs, tests, design) can be traded away for a while.
- Efficiency, once experienced, can't be given up without it feeling like a "backwards change."
- He calls it "a quality worth fighting to preserve" and puts it "at the top."

chunks.heading: The "backwards change" test: why efficiency is sticky
chunks.text:
Guillermo uses a simple thought experiment to show the effect.

- Googling is a task you repeat every day.
- Imagine switching to a browser that takes 200 milliseconds to render search results instead of 20 milliseconds.
- It would be "almost impossible to justify such a backwards change" in your daily routine.

The general lesson for product builders: a faster, lower-friction workflow becomes the baseline, and users (and builders) will resist anything slower, even by small absolute amounts, when the task is repeated often.

chunks.heading: You don't need long exposure; knowing something faster exists is enough
chunks.text:
He says you don't have to live with superior efficiency for long to feel the pull. Merely knowing that "greener and more efficient grass is out there" does the same thing.

- Example: at your job, deploying an app to production takes hours.
- A colleague deploys in seconds (he links to ZEIT's `now`).
- Once you know that, you feel its "inexorable pull."

Implication: once a faster way is visible to your users, team or competitors, the slower way loses its justification. This is the logic behind building products around dramatically better speed of a core workflow, such as deploys.

chunks.heading: Efficiency applies to any system, not only software
chunks.text:
Guillermo says the effect is "by no means limited to programming." He illustrates with his own experience as an immigrant to the United States.

- He spent tireless hours assembling the evidence and paperwork required to become a legal resident.
- It took only "one or two visits" for him to know the effort and bureaucracy were worth it.
- Back in his home country he was no longer his "same productive self." Every process felt painfully slow: getting a bank account, incorporating a company, ordering food, hiring a plumber, the plumber's work, how the plumber got paid, and the plumber's punctuality.

Takeaway: the efficiency of the surrounding system (banking, incorporation, services, payments) shapes how productive people can be, and people will pay a large one-time cost to move into a more efficient environment.

chunks.heading: Einstein on why efficient systems emerge
chunks.text:
To support the point, Guillermo quotes Einstein's impressions of America from *The World As I See It*:

> "What first strikes the visitor with amazement is the superiority of this country, in matters of technics and organization. Objects of everyday use are more solid than in Europe, houses infinitely more convenient in arrangement. Everything is designed to save human labour. Labour is expensive, because the country is sparsely inhabited in comparison with its natural resources. The high price of labour was the stimulus which evoked the marvelous development of technical devices and methods of work."

Guillermo endorses this as his favorite trait of the country: the high cost of labor drove technical devices and methods that save human effort.

His closing logic: if it is hard to part ways with a more efficient web browser, "imagine how hard it is to leave behind a more efficient country!"

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Rauch's year-end essay argues static-first (Jamstack) architecture wins on speed, availability and safety, and that deploy-per-push preview URLs are replacing code review as the center of team collaboration and QA. It also collects product and engineering heuristics: resist settings, treat slowness and flakiness as signs of being wrong, demo often, and optimize team velocity.

chunks.heading: Static sites as the default, with servers moved off the hot path
chunks.text:
Guillermo argues that in 2019 the JAMstack (client-side JavaScript, APIs, Markup) kept growing, and that his favorite part is the assumption that markup is static. His case for static:
- **Globally fast:** deploy hoists all static assets to a global CDN. Removing the server also maximizes availability by cutting or eliminating cache misses.
- **Consistently fast:** "O(1) TTFB", meaning stable, predictable latency to the first byte, because no code, servers, sockets or databases are involved.
- **Always online:** servers go down and need complex rollouts, while static files are trivially cacheable. The odds of being paged over a static asset a CDN can't serve are "basically zero".
- **Faster and safer to roll:** no pods to rotate, containers to shut down, signals to handle or liveness probes to configure.
- **More secure:** serving the same markup and code to all users gives a drastically simpler security model.

On dynamic needs, he says servers "are not going away, but they are moving around and hiding."
- **Static Site Generation** moves servers off the hot path by computing the response ahead of time. Anything that could go wrong goes wrong at build time (availability), you compute once and reuse (less database/API load), and the HTML is fast.
- **Client-side JS and APIs** run later and allow "effectively infinite dynamism".
- When the set of pages is too large to pre-compute at build time, he suggests pre-computing the most critical public pages and doing the rest asynchronously.

chunks.heading: Next.js in 2019: a hybrid framework with per-page granularity
chunks.text:
Guillermo says Next.js grew to power Hulu, Tencent News, Twitch, AT&T and Auth0. He credits its all-in-one coverage of JAMstack, from a static landing page to very large sites to fully dynamic apps.

- The "secret sauce" is the simple `pages/` system, inspired by `cgi-bin` and throwing `.php` files in an FTP webroot. A page is just a React component; the simplest app is `pages/index.js` serving `/`.
- 2019 additions:
  - Dynamic path segments such as `pages/r/[subreddit].js`, with no configuration or custom server.
  - Pages with no server-side data props build to plain static `.html`.
  - Static data props fetch data at build time and "explode" dynamic path segments into many discrete pages.
  - `pages/api/myApi.js` defines a serverless function, most likely a JSON API.
- Mapping to the stack: J is client-side JS via React Hooks, A is `pages/api`, M is pages with no data dependencies or with static data deps.
- He stresses being "uncompromising" about backwards-compatibility: SSR is still fully supported and "no apps have been harmed".

chunks.heading: Deploy previews, the deploy URL and testing against the real thing
chunks.text:
Guillermo says Vercel's goal is to let teams instantly build and deploy JAMstack sites with no servers or infra to configure. Deploying anything from a bare `index.html` to Next.js, Gatsby or Gridsome starts with one command, `vc`, which returns a preview URL. The platform bundles CI/CD and a global CDN.

- **From code review to deployment preview:** he sees a transition away from code review toward preview. Code review (especially speedy review) still matters, "but nothing beats teams collaborating by sharing URLs to the actual sites that are being worked on."
- With the Git integration, every `git push` gets its own live deployment URL. The model makes deployments "orders of magnitude faster" to build, deploy and serve than servers or containers.
- **The deploy URL as center of gravity:** each preview is a real, production-like environment, so instead of mocking assumptions you test "the real thing". The most natural e2e test is visiting the URL and sharing it with customers, co-workers and your manager.
- The GitHub app does not just register a "Check" like other CI providers; it says "this is a deployment, here is the URL". Checks then run in parallel against that URL:
  - Browser testing of user journeys
  - Screenshot testing to prevent visual regressions
  - HTTP assertion testing of APIs and pages
  - Manual QA with designated reviewers who approve the PR

chunks.heading: Reliability: flaky tests, microservices and "everything is code"
chunks.text:
- **Flaky tests mean flaky UX:** developers are too quick to blame tools and press restart. The question to ask is what if it had been a customer instead of an automated test: would they have had a flaky experience, and would it be OK to tell them to press F5?
- **Serverless means infrastructure that upgrades itself:** his preferred defining trait. It covers OS upgrades, OpenSSL patches and Node.js runtime bumps, and is especially valuable for databases, where he is glad not to deal with upgrading stateful infrastructure.
- **Microservices increase complexity and reduce availability:** splitting into services removes guarantees the compiler or runtime gave a unit, turning it into a distributed system, and an extra network hop can only make things worse. Citing Kevin Mahoney's example, if C depends on A (0.8) and B (0.95), C averages 0.8 × 0.95 = 0.76, with a worst case of 0.75.
- His remedy is to make serverless functions "monolithic": statically bind each function's dependencies (Next.js API routes and the Go compiler do this) and avoid unneeded service hops.
- **Everything is code:** apply a config change the way you'd ship code. Review it, roll it gradually, and "mistrust it, just like you mistrust code."
- **All code is wrong:** assume most of it is. He endorses "if it's not fast and reliable, then it is wrong". Slowness is an off smell that makes users doubt the product, quoting Craig Mod: "Speed can be a good proxy for general engineering quality."

chunks.heading: What "native" means, and building cross-platform apps
chunks.text:
Guillermo says the word "native" has always bothered him, since people agree native apps are optimal but not on what native is. He proposes: "an app that behaves to the quality standards of the platform it's deployed to", which he calls platform fidelity rather than native code.

- That explains Electron's success: a well-engineered Electron app (he cites Slack's rewrite) delivers native fidelity regardless of language.
- Platform fidelity requires access to platform APIs, which makes mobile web "apps" a non-starter, especially on iOS Safari. He says this has nothing to do with performance or JS and HTML, but with being unable to deliver what a real app can do on the platform. One example he gives is the dynamic viewport that shifts as toolbars appear and disappear.
- React Native can reach full platform fidelity, with good performance via solid engineering (he cites Discord) and no API constraints. Like Electron it offers one development experience, a universal language, shared modules and components, seamless updates, faster deployments and iOS plus Android support.
- On SwiftUI: it is exciting, but RN, like Electron, "has a tremendous economic advantage".
- He suspects native mobile apps' performance comes less from native code generation and more from a rich standard library of well-optimized UI components. He draws the same parallel with Go's stdlib versus Node.js plus npm.

chunks.heading: Product design lessons: settings, inputs, demos and speed
chunks.text:
- **Settings are for successful products:** great products usually start with a dead simple onboarding that minimizes or eliminates options. His rule for startups and product management is to "absolutely resist adding options until substantial evidence of success without them exists."
- **Inputs should look like inputs:** he cites a study of 600 participants, 2 designers and 1 researcher confirming this, and points out that Google does it too.
- **Notion as the fanciest data structure:** quoting Joel Spolsky that "the great horizontal killer applications are actually just fancy data structures", he explains why he fell in love with Notion in 2019.
  - Its structure is a mutable, realtime graph of documents made of known blocks.
  - The key ingredient is direct manipulation, which requires the topology to be "completely transparent and obvious to the end user".
  - The sidebar exposes the document graph as trees you arrange yourself, and block types are trivial to create, edit, rearrange and combine.
- **Get busy demoing:** he marvels at the "product-improving and life-improving power" of frequent demos, noting they were essential to creating the iPhone. His advice: "Don't be afraid to ~~fail~~ demo."
- **Game engineering as inspiration:** React drew on how game engines get rendering performance. From a talk on Marvel's Spider-Man, he highlights careful planning around the platform's well-understood limits. Web tooling mostly only suggests limits (webpack warnings, Lighthouse and WebPageTest scores, Google rankings, the Amazon 100ms rule), whereas AMP is a systematic answer where slow experiences are very hard to create. He is optimistic about Chrome's Never-Slow Mode as a more general version.

chunks.heading: Trends Guillermo bets on: NoCode/LowCode, WebAssembly, QUIC and team velocity
chunks.text:
- **NoCode and LowCode are real:** the less code you write, the easier it is to maintain and the less likely it is wrong. He cites Next.js, SWR and zero-config deployments as examples. SWR in particular: "What you do in one line of SWR, you tend to do in a few dozen lines of Redux."
- He expects LowCode tools (React, Vue, Svelte) to keep gaining traction by making it succinct to share UI and behavior as components or hooks. He also expects visual tools to rise that bring those primitives together, including reusable components from a canonical system or a global shared library, and predicts the two camps will collide.
- **WebAssembly:** with sandboxing disabled it can match 95% of native code speed, better than he anticipated.
- **QUIC (HTTP/3):** Uber deployed it at scale and saw a 50 percent latency reduction from the 50th to the 99th percentile.
- **Shared CDN caches are dead:** browsers partitioning caches busts the idea of sharing React or jQuery via a common CDN URL.
- **Team speed over individual speed:** he endorses Google's open-sourced engineering practices: "optimize for the speed at which a team of developers can produce a product together," rather than individual coding speed, with an emphasis on speedy code review.
- **Zoom:** it went public, and its differentiator was that it "works better".

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Guillermo Rauch argues that testing is an investment judged by return and risk, and that modern infrastructure now makes E2E tests the best return. Per-push preview deployments plus headless browsers on serverless compute make prod-like staging and fast, cheap tests possible. He demos a Vercel, Checkly and GitHub workflow set up in minutes.

chunks.heading: Why Guillermo prioritizes end-to-end testing
chunks.text:
- Writing tests is an investment, judged by its return and its risks, including opportunity costs. There is "too much of a good thing" when time goes to tests instead of features.
- He cites Google's SRE book to make the same point about reliability: past a certain level, extra reliability hurts. Extreme stability "limits how fast new features can be developed," raises cost, and shrinks what a team can afford to offer.
- His 2016 guideline favored integration tests with "not too many" tests. In 2020 he argues for also prioritizing end-to-end (E2E) tests for the critical parts of an app, because that reduces risk and gives the best return.
- The case rests on focusing on the customer first, which he sees as the best way to run a business and to judge software quality.

chunks.heading: Why the conventional testing pyramid can be inverted
chunks.text:
- The conventional pyramid (Martin Fowler's) puts E2E at the top because it is slow and expensive. Guillermo asks what happens if those two costs go away.
- Modern deployment workflows plus serverless testing can "fully revert" the pyramid.
- He names two objections to E2E: staging is hard or costly, and running the tests is slow or expensive. Infrastructure now answers both.

chunks.heading: What can't be caught "in the lab"
chunks.text:
- Cloud software is deployed to dozens of operating systems, mobile devices, browsers and networks of varying stability and performance. The environment keeps changing as apps depend on more hosted services and third-party APIs.
- A fancy compiler or type system won't help if the site fails to load in Chrome because the right HTTP headers weren't sent for `.js` files, or if a feature isn't compatible with Safari.
- Quality goes beyond correctness. It also includes reliability (staying correct over time) and performance (doing the right thing quickly).

chunks.heading: Instant, prod-like staging: a deployment per push
chunks.text:
- With Vercel, every git push is deployed and given a URL. This is cost-effective through incremental computation, where static files and serverless functions are mostly reused from deploy to deploy.
- Deploys are stateless, so resources are used only on demand and scale with traffic. Vercel can keep deploy history forever, like GitHub keeps code history.
- Instead of one shared staging server, there can be "millions of concurrent 'staging' environments."
- "Staging" is in quotes because the tests run against real production infrastructure. That has reliability benefits:
  - Some browser features are only enabled over SSL.
  - Having every production feature on, like brotli compression and HTTP/2, reduces outage risk.

chunks.heading: Making E2E fast and cheap
chunks.text: - Puppeteer (Chrome's headless browser) combined with serverless compute that scales to thousands of concurrent executions makes E2E "both fast and cheap." He points to a Stanford paper (gg) as an example of that scaling.

chunks.heading: The Develop -> Preview -> Test workflow, step by step
chunks.text:
He demonstrates it on his open-source blog (`rauchg/blog`) with Vercel, Checkly and GitHub:

1. Define an E2E check in Checkly asserting the browser title always contains "Guillermo Rauch". It fails at first, as expected. Checkly gives full access to the Node and puppeteer APIs, with no setup or scheduling ceremony, since you write inside the function that gets invoked.
2. Install the Checkly GitHub app and, under the check's CI/CD tab, link it to the repository.
3. Create a branch that adds the `<title>` tag, deliberately misspelling his name.
4. Open a pull request. Within seconds Vercel deploys, a headless browser acts as a visitor, and the error is exposed on the PR.
5. Push the fix. The check re-runs automatically. Then merge, and merging to master deploys to `rauchg.com`.

- He stresses there was zero additional configuration: "Vercel supplied a URL, Checkly tested it, GitHub was notified."

chunks.heading: Continuous testing as the answer to complexity
chunks.text:
- Checkly can run tests from multiple locations around the world and invoke checks over time, not only at PR time.
- He quotes Leslie Lamport: a distributed system is one where "the failure of a computer you didn't even know existed can render your own computer unusable."
- His conclusion: as systems depend on ever-changing platforms and other cloud systems, "continuously testing just like our users do is our best bet to tame the chaos."

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Rauch explains Vercel's $40M Series B and the seven tailwinds behind its growth: obsessive customer focus on the frontend, hybrid SSR/SSG, running code everywhere, measuring real user experience via Core Web Vitals, collaborative previews, and openness beyond Next.js.

chunks.heading: Vercel is frontend focused
chunks.text:
Guillermo argues the most customer-obsessive way to build a web product is to focus on the frontend.

- Every customer interaction passes through the frontend: first contact with the brand, every purchase, signup, article and form submission. Each one is a chance to "impress, delight, perform, be accessible and memorable."
- He borrows from Jeff Bezos' Day 1 letter: "obsessive customer focus is by far the most protective of Day 1 vitality."
- Frontend is where technological and artistic differentiation lives. Backend is becoming "increasingly commoditized, turnkey and undifferentiated," whereas it used to be built entirely from scratch.
- Vercel's customer focus is a double challenge: delight the developer, and give them the platform to delight their own customer.

chunks.heading: Zero configuration and defaults that serve end users
chunks.text:
- Next.js pioneered zero configuration in the React space, so developers can focus on their product.
- It was not only developer experience. Next.js shipped preconfigured essentials for users: out-of-the-box server rendering for fast page boots and SEO, code splitting, production bundle optimization and minification.
- Guillermo's point: a better developer experience, backed by good defaults, lets frontend developers succeed in production.
- Cited proof: Next.js powers Apple and TikTok.com.

chunks.heading: Hybrid rendering and incremental adoption
chunks.text:
- Being customer focused means not being dogmatic: "meeting the customer where they are" and enabling incremental adoption of new technology.
- Four years before the post, Next.js made contrarian bets: multi-page over single-page apps, server rendering (SSR) over spinners, and dynamism everywhere rather than only on the client.
- Static site generation (SSG) later added the option of pre-rendering pages and caching them at the edge.
- His conclusion: pure server rendering was not enough and pure static (Jamstack) is not enough. Giving developers SSR and SSG "on a per-page basis" is what works.
- Next.js keeps evolving while maintaining backwards compatibility.

chunks.heading: Computing everywhere
chunks.text:
- JavaScript runs everywhere: the build process (SSG), the origin (SSR), the edge and the client's device. Vercel embraces this "everywhere computing model" rather than "serverless."
- Flow: a Git push triggers a build, where frameworks like Next.js pre-render pages before any user requests them.
- The build can also output serverless functions alongside static assets, which run on demand for more personalization and dynamism.
- After the page boots, React adds interactivity, realtime data fetching and caching (he links SWR), and animation.
- Apps are pushed automatically to a global edge network with "no management, no overhead, no configuration and… really fast page loads."

chunks.heading: Realistic performance: Core Web Vitals over CDN latency
chunks.text:
- A CDN is a key ingredient but "only represents a minor contribution" to a fast site. HTML download time from the edge is "just the tip of an entire iceberg."
- Backend teams can read p99 and p999 times from a dashboard. Frontend teams were tempted to say "my page loaded in 42ms" from CDN latency or PoP counts, which misses the real experience.
- Measuring frontend quality was hard because nobody knew what to measure. The breakthrough was Core Web Vitals from the W3C Web Performance Working Group and Google: LCP, CLS and FID. They capture how fast content appears, how little the page jitters, and how fast it reacts to input.
- These became a Google search ranking signal starting May 2021.
- Two strategies to prepare:
  - Austerity: drop chat widgets, analytics, ads, GDPR popups and all JS. He jokes you might as well shut down your business.
  - Address reality: for example, optimize oversized, slow images with the Next.js image component.
- Instead of relying only on synthetic Lighthouse tests, Vercel's built-in Analytics computes a "real experience score" from actual visitors' web vitals. Hashicorp uses it to hold itself to performance goals.

chunks.heading: Collaboration through preview deployments
chunks.text:
- Development should not be confined to `localhost:3000`, bespoke VMs or a monolithic staging server.
- Every branch and PR, and every proposed content change, gets a shareable link served from the same serverless infrastructure as production.
- Clients, teammates "and robots" can visit it to give early feedback or report bugs.
- Decoupling frontend from backend lets non-coders contribute:
  - Marketing or technical writing teams: connect Next.js data fetching functions to a headless CMS.
  - Product teams: integrate a feature flagging system to decouple deploy from release.

chunks.heading: Openness and where Vercel goes next
chunks.text:
- Next.js is the "lighthouse framework," but Vercel is designed to be completely agnostic to it.
- Capabilities any framework can use: pushing and updating static pages without rebuilding the whole site, previewing proposed data changes, serverless functions, image optimization and the analytics system. He names Svelte, Nuxt.js and Gridsome.
- Vercel's mantra until then: Develop → Preview → Ship. He commits to making it the most delightful process, with top performance at every step, computation everywhere, and help with the "iceberg of frontend complexity."
- Next step is adding "Iterate": a mindset of experimentation coupled with constant feedback, helping teams "discover what to develop next."

chunks.heading: Series B and business context (Dec 2020)
chunks.text:
- Announced a $40M Series B led by GV, with Greenoaks, Bedrock, Geodesic and existing investors Accel and CRV. It followed the April 2020 Series A.
- In 2020 alone Vercel added Airbnb, The Washington Post, Trip Advisor, Scale and Hashicorp as flagship customers.
- He frames the post as seven tailwinds behind the acceleration: frontend focused, fast for everyone, hybrid, everywhere, realistic, collaborative and open.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Guillermo Rauch announces the Vercel rebrand and $21M raise, and explains the thesis behind it: the backend is commoditized, so value has moved to the frontend. He lays out three bets: components as the primitive, deploy-preview URLs as the collaboration primitive, and speed by default.

chunks.heading: Vercel's thesis: the frontend is the new opportunity, and the workflow is the product
chunks.text:
- Guillermo argues the backend has been "commoditized by cloud infrastructure, Kubernetes and off-the-shelf APIs," so the most interesting new modernization opportunities have shifted to the frontend.
- The frontend is where enterprises create products and content that attract users and drive revenue.
- Jamstack (JavaScript / APIs / Markup) lets the frontend split from the backend, so site development moves faster and independently. He cites Google, Facebook and Microsoft (Microsoft Docs is 100% Jamstack) as proof.
- Vercel's mission: "the ultimate workflow for developing, previewing, and shipping Jamstack sites."
- Accel's Dan Levine framed the opportunity as Vercel being "like AWS for frontend developers," with a designer and developer-first approach separating winners from losers across market categories.
- Announcement context: re-brand to Vercel plus $21M in funding from Accel, CRV and angels including Jordan Walke, Nat Friedman, Pete Hunt, Jessie Frazelle, Soleio and Naval Ravikant.

chunks.heading: Components are the right primitive for the frontend
chunks.text:
- Demand for richer frontend experiences pushes teams toward component and design systems: "Your button should look the same on web, mobile and desktop, and even your emails."
- Guillermo notes people used to talk about selector engines and the DOM until React introduced the component primitive. Other frameworks define components, but React pioneered the trend.
- He, Tim Neutkens and Naoyuki Kanezawa co-created Next.js on the belief that React was powerful enough to be "the full engine for the frontend," so people could do everything with React rather than a single component.
- Product-positioning stance: Vercel aims to be the one-stop shop for any component-based technology a team adopts (Vue, Nuxt, Svelte, Angular, Glimmer), not just Next.js users.
- He frames Svelte and Vue as compelling frameworks attacking different problems, such as reducing client-side JavaScript, and says "Vercel as a platform wants to support them all."

chunks.heading: Deploy preview beats code review: URLs as the collaboration primitive
chunks.text:
- Guillermo's diagnosis: the push-and-review workflow is too complicated. Teams burn cycles configuring CI/CD, setting up Jenkins, picking a CI vendor and a CDN vendor, and getting them to talk, "ensuring the Rube Goldberg apparatus stays coherent."
- Vercel's breakthrough was realizing the preview deploy URL is the superior abstraction. It works like a CMS preview, but is achieved by integrating with Git and deploying on every push.
- Benefits he lists:
  - Anyone (marketing, sales, legal, engineering) can review by receiving a URL over chat.
  - It redefines the whole process from idea to QA, because you test against the real thing.
  - It "eliminates the entire staging process."
- Every deploy URL gets automatic HTTPS via Let's Encrypt, so sharing is secure and testing happens in a production-like environment.
- Without SSL, teams find security warnings after deploying, and browsers disable modern features such as Bluetooth, webcam and microphone on non-SSL sites.
- His framing: "Sounds like a pretty basic evolution, but it tears down so much complexity and makes frontend teams so much faster!"

chunks.heading: Speed as the core value: performance for users and for teams
chunks.text:
- Guillermo's claim: "If you're creating a modern frontend nothing matters more than great site performance for the user."
- Google Lighthouse scores measure frontend performance across multiple dials and strongly influence SEO ranking.
- Vercel's pitch is a global edge network and a perfect Lighthouse score out of the box on every deploy, without teams thinking about the CDN or serverless internals.
- Mechanics he describes: each URL deploys to every edge in the world, static assets are cached and compressed with top codecs (Brotli built in), and sites are optimized for performance metrics that are hard to test locally.
- Speed is also about the team: bring the developer experience closer to the cloud and make iteration "easy and fast by default."

chunks.heading: Positioning and going-to-market stance
chunks.text:
- Narrative structure he uses: establish a market shift (backend commoditized, frontend is where value is), then name three megatrends the product is built around (components, preview URLs, speed).
- Open source as strategy: he calls the journey "open at its heart," pointing to Next.js, "much like the platform it builds on."
- Framework-agnostic distribution: supporting every component framework widens the funnel beyond Next.js adopters.
- Calls to action are simple: join the movement and follow the company on Twitter.
- Closing framing: "We are still in the early days of a new beginning for the Web. A Web that's faster for end-users and easier to build for developers."

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Guillermo Rauch explains why Jamstack on an edge network differs from a server with a CDN on top: framework builds can hoist the results of computation to the edge. Pre-render as much as possible once at build time, share it across all users, and let the framework pick the optimal output per page.

chunks.heading: Static hoisting: pushing computed results to the edge
chunks.text: Guillermo argues that Jamstack CDNs differ from "a server with a traditional CDN on top" because they can do more than host and cache static assets: they can **hoist** them. A traditional CDN treats the origin as "an opaque black box". A Jamstack network lets you push content directly to the network, and frameworks can be designed to exploit that.

chunks.heading: Hoisting as a compiler idea, applied to architecture
chunks.text:
- In JavaScript, hoisting means declarations are moved to the top of a scope, so calling `b()` before it is defined still works.
- In compiler optimization, hoisting means code that is static or invariant is moved outside a loop. His example: in `sum[i] = i + (b + c)` inside a 100,000-iteration loop, `b + c` is loop-invariant, so an optimizing compiler moves it out and it behaves "as if you had written it outside of the loop yourself".
- He extends the same idea to architecture: Jamstack makes it possible to hoist the results of computation to the edge, right next to visitors.

chunks.heading: Pre-render as much as possible
chunks.text:
- A core tenet of Jamstack is to "pre-render (pre-compute) as much as possible", which gave static site generation its prominence.
- The key shift: computation that would have happened later in the request's timeline moves to the build phase. It is performed once and shared by all users.

chunks.heading: Edge-aware frameworks: how Next.js does it
chunks.text:
- Since Next.js 9, `next build` automatically outputs the optimal asset per page (entrypoint), via automatic static optimization.
- Next.js 9.3 refined the static-site generation hooks and introduced incremental static generation for appending pages. Next.js 9.5 made incremental static regeneration stable for updating them.
- He says Next.js makes hoisting the static parts of a site or app to the edge "a breeze". The output type depends on the data fetching strategy the developer uses:
  - ○ Static: automatically rendered as static HTML, with no initial props.
  - ● SSG: generated as static HTML plus JSON, using `getStaticProps`.
  - λ Lambda: server-side rendered at runtime, using `getInitialProps` or `getServerSideProps`.

chunks.heading: Worked example: how vercel.com is built
chunks.text:
- The homepage, which he calls the company's "cover letter", is built statically as `index.html` and pushed to the edge "for maximum speed and reliability".
- `/api` functions are exported as serverless (lambda) functions, created by placing files in `./pages/api`.
- Blog posts are generated at build time by querying an API with static site generation hooks, so they are hoisted to the edge like the homepage. The build output showed `/blog/[post]` with about 100 paths.
- The dashboard is "super dynamic in nature", yet it is a static HTML page that fetches data securely from the client side using React Hooks (SWR).
- Takeaway: even a highly dynamic app can ship a static shell at the edge and fetch only the dynamic data on the client.

chunks.heading: The conclusion he draws
chunks.text:
- CDNs and static hosts have existed for a long time, but only now can content be pushed to the network itself, with frameworks optimized for it.
- With optimizations like static asset hoisting, he says websites are "faster and more reliable than ever before".
- His recommended starting point for a Jamstack site or app: Next.js, deployed to the Vercel edge network.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Guillermo Rauch announces Vercel's $102M Series C and lays out three priorities: build an SDK for the Web around React and Next.js, lower the barrier to collaboration, and focus on the end-user. The core lesson for platform and tooling builders is that you serve two users, and the end-customer's experience is the ultimate fitness function.

chunks.heading: Series C framing: what Vercel is building and why
chunks.text: Guillermo announced a $102M Series C (June 23, 2021), following the Series B the previous December. He states the vision as: "a global realtime medium for both creators and consumers, where all friction and latency are eliminated." He names three uses of the money: build the SDK for the Web, lower the barrier of entry, and focus on the end-user.

chunks.heading: The Web has no SDK, so Next.js is the starting point
chunks.text:
- Guillermo points out that, unlike other software platforms, the Web never shipped with an SDK or Standard Development Kit.
- New browser APIs keep arriving, but the developer still has to assemble them into an "engine" for every new project.
- He sees the resulting diversity of tools as what makes the Web innovative and dynamic. He also sees it as a major obstacle when companies rush to reinvent themselves digitally.
- Next.js is positioned as the meaningful starting point for building great pages, open sourcing "the lessons learned from the giants of the Web" (he cites Next.js 11's conformance work).
- He notes Next.js grew organically, as developers explained and recommended it to one another.

chunks.heading: React as a durable building block
chunks.text:
- React was then 8 years old. Guillermo calls it "a durable abstraction and building block."
- He calls its longevity "a narrative violation of the common wisdom that 'frontend frameworks are changed every week.'"
- Next.js is built on that foundation rather than on a new rendering paradigm.

chunks.heading: Lowering the barrier to contribute
chunks.text:
- Vercel already gave developers global infrastructure to deploy and scale frontend projects. Guillermo lists remaining collaboration friction:
  - Setting up and maintaining your developer environment
  - Integrating it into Git for continuous integration
  - Manually pushing and waiting to share progress with your team
- His view: the Web is not a read-only medium. "Each Web browser is simultaneously the consumption and creation mechanism."
- Product response: Next.js Live, meant to let everyone contribute to the Web, whether pitching an idea or an edit, as an experienced developer or a new designer, from a local editor or the browser itself.

chunks.heading: A platform company has two users
chunks.text:
- Guillermo argues a platform and tooling company has two users, acknowledged or not:
  1. The user of the tool (the developer)
  2. The user of the output of the tool (the end customer)
- However many downloads Next.js gets and however delightful the dev experience, "the customer is king."
- Stated fitness function: "Our primary fitness function is your success for your customers."
- Goal: visitors may not know how a page is built, but if it is delightful and fast, "they ought to think it was powered by Vercel."

chunks.heading: End-user performance is designed in
chunks.text:
Guillermo's examples of end-user performance baked into products:

- **Next.js origin:** born from the insight that React as a Single Page Application put rendering burden on the user's device that should have been on the server.
- **Vercel Analytics:** prioritizes a Real Experience Score calculated per device, rather than listing traffic stats or TTFB latencies.
- **Pre-rendering** at build time or via Incremental Static Regeneration: takes CPU cycles out of the page-serving equation entirely, removing latency for the end user.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Guillermo Rauch lays out Vercel's strategy for the next decade: infrastructure should be an output of frameworks, the web is shifting from pages to agents, and the cloud should deliver solutions (PRs, fixes) instead of alerts. He argues the AI web must stay open, with model choice and open protocols rather than one closed mega-app.

chunks.heading: From pages to agents: the cloud's next unit of software
chunks.text:
Guillermo argues the web's first wave was pages, and the next is agents. Pages are fast, dynamic, personalized, and page speed correlated closely with conversion, which Google rewards with rankings, creating a flywheel of "more business, more conversion, more organic traffic". Customers like Under Armour, PetSmart, DoorDash, Nintendo and Porsche partner with Vercel to work backwards from the customer experience while the infrastructure is automated away.

His claim: "Pages got us here, but agents will get us there."

- An agent is "just" a piece of software that performs a bunch of steps on your behalf, intelligently, and delivers an outcome. His example: Google AI Overviews acting like "someone" who opens 10 tabs, reads, compares and visualizes for you.
- Unlike pages, agents are not usually synchronous and are never static. They can think for seconds, minutes, hours, and soon days and weeks.
- Agents don't follow rigid fetch-and-render instructions. They can write their own code and create tools on the fly.
- He believes every organization and individual should be able to create and deploy their own agents, keeping the web's freedom to "own a domain and deploy to it".

chunks.heading: Traditional Cloud vs AI Cloud: how each layer changes
chunks.text:
Guillermo maps each cloud layer to an AI-era equivalent, and says traditional services "are foundational, they're not going away":

- Static and semi-static UI, one-shot responses, become fully dynamic and generative UI with streaming responses.
- Framework for UI and pages (React / Next.js) becomes framework for AI and agents (the AI SDK).
- CDN of pixels (CloudFront) becomes a CDN of tokens (AI Gateway).
- Compute for human-written code (EC2) becomes compute for agent-written code (Vercel Sandbox).
- Foreground compute, quick and CPU-bound (Lambda), becomes background compute, long-running and IO-bound (Fluid).

He also notes the "hello world" of yesterday was a page and today it is an agent. The interface used to be clicking through UIs; now it is prompting, or just doing work behind the scenes.

chunks.heading: Framework-defined Infrastructure and the "React of the Cloud"
chunks.text:
Guillermo says Vercel was born from his 2015 frustration that the cloud offered infinite compute, yet the pixels on the web weren't getting better, nor was crafting them. The cloud's burden of physical data centers was inherited in digital form: DevOps, K8s, VPCs, CI/CD, IAM, CDNs, IaC. "The time you should have spent on the pixels... was spent on the configs."

- Vercel led with developer experience: frameworks and tools that generate the infrastructure on deployment.
- The analogy is React, which treats the DOM as the output of state and data. Vercel aims to be "the React of the Cloud", where hyperscaler primitives are outputs, not things to manipulate directly ("jQueryed").
- Framework-defined Infrastructure (FdI) is the mechanism: CI/CD, compute clusters, CDNs and caching systems are provisioned automatically, like a "cloud compiler" that turns code into optimal infrastructure.
- Frameworks serve two purposes: abstracting platform complexity by codifying expert best practices, and on Vercel, automating infrastructure.
- Traction he cites: Next.js had 500M downloads over the past 12 months, more than in the entire 2016 to 2024 period. Vercel is crossing 1 billion application deployments and powers two of the top 20 highest-traffic web properties (OpenAI and The Weather Company), while also serving 1-person companies making millions in ARR.
- His guiding principle: "it's always Day One."

chunks.heading: From problems to solutions: the self-healing cloud
chunks.text:
Guillermo splits the software lifecycle into build and run. FdI gave autonomy in build (write, test, prepare for production). Run is where code serves users and things "go wrong, slow down, or altogether break", and he believes AI will deliver the next level of cloud autonomy there.

- An AI Cloud should "monitor, optimize, secure, and repair itself, without human intervention".
- Today every application at scale pays gigantic costs collecting telemetry and observability data and surfacing it in dashboards, "hoping that humans will open them, prioritize issues, and fix them by hand".
- His rule: an AI Cloud shouldn't hand you problem after problem (alerts, 5xx errors, latency spikes, traffic anomalies). It should give you solutions: pull requests, recommendations and automated actions. It should "repair and optimize, not merely inform".
- Vercel's examples: the Firewall Agent responds to threats and provides investigations and mitigation strategies to human operators; the Code Review Agent analyzes every pull request by running it in a secure sandbox, emulating a skeptical expert colleague, a thorough "vibe check".

chunks.heading: Keeping the AI web open: model choice, open protocols
chunks.text:
Guillermo warns the choice is to give up the web and proxy all data and intent through one closed mega-app, or to reinvent it in the open. The web's beauty is that anyone can own a domain, deploy to it and link to anyone, with "no app review process", no "platform fee", and open, documented protocols and formats.

- The first AI wave has been dominated by closed models, proprietary SDKs, protocols and centralized interfaces.
- His alternative: a web of agents instead of a single agentic interface, and model choice instead of a single model SDK.
- Vercel's contribution is the AI SDK, which abstracts over providers and aims for better developer experience than vendor-specific SDKs. The `ai` package is the second-largest AI package on npm by downloads, behind only `openai`, and notably provider agnostic.
- He points to open protocols as the foundation of the new web: MCP for connecting agents, the Agentic Commerce Protocol for commerce, and the Agent Client Protocol for coding.

chunks.heading: Building for developers and their agents
chunks.text:
Guillermo says users increasingly rely on agents to solve problems and expect more intelligent experiences. This changes the job of framework and devtools builders: "our job is no longer to empower and delight developers, but also their agents."

- Developers themselves offload problem-solving to agents, so tools must serve both audiences.
- The product goal is surfacing insights and solutions, "not endless UI or problems".
- He frames this as an opportunity for everyone, developers or not (he points to v0), to reinvent the web on open foundations.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Rauch argues learning to code is a messy, discontinuous process, sped up by open source, online communities and hacking competitions. Using Izhal and code golf as examples, he shows these games teach transferable problem-solving (reverse engineering, debugging blind, trial and error, perseverance), and he recommends learning through fun and friendly competition.

chunks.heading: Learning by hacking: Izhal and early exposure
chunks.text:
- Guillermo says there was no single moment he "learned to code". It was a discontinuous process of ups, downs, impostor syndrome, months of voracious learning, then months of distractions.
- Decisive factors he names: exposure to open-source (Linux), online communities (IRC and forums), and hacking competitions.
- Izhal.com was a hacking game: start at Level 1 and hack a made-up system to reach each next level. It had a forum for hints, a level shown as flair, and a public leaderboard.
- Level 1 was solved by viewing page source and finding an HTML comment with the next URL. Difficulty climbed to disassembling binaries and writing key generators.
- He argues it taught problem-solving skills rather than coding itself: reverse engineering a system and "unusually effective debugging" with very little information, and it did so very quickly.
- He recommends beginners try similar challenge sites and suggests content creators experiment with this model for new educational materials.

chunks.heading: Why he recommends learning by having fun
chunks.text:
- His closing advice: there have never been as many ways to learn to code (bootcamps, free YouTube videos, expensive courses, exclusive chatrooms), but he suggests "learning by having fun, overcoming obstacles and a healthy dose of competition with your friends".
- He frames code golf and hacking tournaments as the alternative to formal curricula.
- He would not start a beginner on JS1k. He sees it as useful for setting aspirations of what you could one day do and for marvelling at the expressive power of JavaScript.

chunks.heading: Code golf, JS1k and the expressive power of JavaScript
chunks.text:
- Code golf is a game whose goal is to reduce code as much as possible ("golfing").
- JS1k was a yearly tournament: make the coolest possible demo in 1K (1024 characters) of JavaScript. It is not returning for 2020.
