- He cites his friend Román Cortes, for many years one of the most successful JS1k contestants. Román's 2013 runner-up entry is a heavily compressed program that still runs fine in any browser seven years later, and Guillermo embedded it in his Next.js-powered blog post.
- Román's new hobby, code-golf.io, inspired the post. It offers challenges at all difficulty levels across several languages, and solutions are submitted in the fewest characters.
- He noted that results are remotely verified, so the game is sound and complete with no easy way to cheat. That made him curious about secure code execution, a topic he had studied over the years.

chunks.heading: Reverse engineering an unfamiliar environment
chunks.text:
His method when probing code-golf.io's sandbox, with no manual:

- Start with the question "What is this system executing?" (a function? who invokes it? how?).
- Throw an error to read the stack trace. The trace was too short for Node.js, which ruled Node out, and it revealed the code was read from `/tmp/code.js`.
- Enumerate the global object. `globalThis` existed, indicating a very recent JS environment, and the first member was `print`. `console.log` did not work, so he kept using `throw` for inspection.
- With `print` he enumerated the whole environment. Finding `Realm` hinted at how sandboxing was implemented.
- He notes `print` adds a newline, so he needed `write` to solve the Quine challenge.
- He says this brought back the feeling Izhal gave him in 2002: starting from very little and figuring things out, "like learning to code again".

chunks.heading: Solving the Quine challenge: iterating from 27 to 24 characters
chunks.text:
A Quine is a program that prints its own source. Writing one requires thinking recursively; writing the source as a string leaves you "one layer removed from success".

His iteration path:

- First working solution: use `read` on the file found earlier (`/tmp/code.js`) and `write` the result. It used 27 characters. He called it a "completely unsatisfactory, partial" victory because leaderboard leader primo had 24.
- Second approach: a function that prints its own source via function-to-string introspection. It used 30 characters. The gap to the old approach was 3, and he needed 3 more to match primo, so he abandoned it. He was still encouraged that another path existed, and documented attempts in Notion.
- Back to the first approach, compressing the path: relative `code.js`, `/tmp/code` without extension, `/tmp/code*`. None worked.
- Enumerating an `os` object revealed Unix-style syscalls. Using `chdir` with a relative path pushed him to 39 characters, but confirmed he was in a regular Unix-like filesystem.
- He then worked out the default working directory, guessed `/`, and made `tmp` relative, removing the leading `/` for one character.
- Still 2 characters short, he reasoned the only removable pair was the parentheses. He recalled JavaScript's tagged template literals (popularized by styled-components) and dropped the parentheses to match the 24.
- Result: his "one and only contribution" was a permanent "4th 1st-place" on the leaderboard.

chunks.heading: Principles for tough problems
chunks.text:
- Seeing others' demonstrated results drives him: "inspired by what other had demonstrably accomplished", as on the forums back in the day. When primo's 24 showed it was possible, he kept going despite believing nothing was non-essential.
- Apply multiple "search" strategies and choose the most promising one; drop a path when the remaining gap is too large (his 30-character attempt).
- Document attempts as you go (he used Notion).
- Expect trial-and-error and perseverance. Each failed path (path shortening, `chdir`) still taught something that later helped.
- Skills he says matter throughout his career as a programmer: figuring out unfamiliar environments and systems without a manual, iterating, and perseverance.
- He compares the small win to CI: "green just… feels good".

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Takeaways from Rauch's a16z speedrun fireside chat. Open source is a fast test of product-market fit, early focus beats unbounded ambition, and in the AI era choosing what to build (and what to dismiss) is the real edge. He also covers hiring for proof of work and communication, and cutting distractions from your product's story.

chunks.heading: Open source as a speedrun to product-market fit
chunks.text:
- Guillermo treats open source as a filter. The two hardest startup problems are getting people to know you exist and building the right thing, and open source stress-tests both at once.
- His framing: "I've always thought of open source as a speedrun to product-market fit, because if people don't use it when it's free, when it's easy to consume, when the code is available, then you probably should be working on something else."
- He accepts the downside that openness makes replication easier, especially in the age of agents. His counter is that the best open source projects extend into broader platforms, and success surfaces new problems to solve.
- Example: Next.js is only a sliver of the cloud problem enterprises actually face, which is where Vercel's business sits.
- He says founders stall because they worry about the future too early: "What stops entrepreneurs in their tracks is that they worry too much about what's going to happen in the future. In reality, they don't even have product-market fit yet."

chunks.heading: Unbounded vision, ruthless focus (the "bicameral mind")
chunks.text:
- Guillermo describes a "bicameral mind": a bold, boundless long-term vision, paired with extreme discipline about what gets built on any given day.
- With three people in the room, unbounded ambition destroys you if it dictates the roadmap: "When you're getting started and you're three people, if all you do every day is unbounded ambition and building two hundred million different features, then you've fucked up."
- Early Vercel tried to make everything deployable: every language, runtime and framework, even databases.
- He forced the question "where are we being truly excellent?" The answer was the front-end layer, a new kind of managed service that didn't exist yet.
- He credits that narrowing with the difference between building something no one would pay for and building something worth hundreds of millions.
- His blunt counterfactual: "If I had continued doing everything, I would have made a company that made zero dollars. Literally zero dollars."
- Why focus pays: "Discerning buyers want the best of each class of problem. They don't settle for the second-best solution."

chunks.heading: In the AI era, choosing what to build is the edge
chunks.text:
- When AI makes everything buildable, the temptation is to build everything. Guillermo argues that is backward: when every problem is shallow with enough tokens, picking which problems deserve attention becomes the competitive advantage.
- He warns that many founders are already over-building: "A bunch of you are probably already over-building massively because you notice that you can just prompt it and it'll do it. But the discernment of what problems are worth solving could be one of your biggest differentiators."
- Good use of AI at Vercel: an agent working overnight on a JavaScript optimization that made the platform 20-40% faster for customers.
- Bad use of AI: rewriting internal HR tools.
- He sees the CEO's job as increasingly about helping the company decide what is worth investing in when everything is possible.

chunks.heading: Hiring for proof of work and how people package ideas
chunks.text:
- Guillermo looks for people on the rise rather than people who have already arrived: those shipping high-quality work, especially with AI tools.
- He pays attention to something most hiring managers ignore, which is how candidates communicate what they built: "Sometimes the reason I reach out to people is not just what they built, but how they communicate it."
- Example: he cold-DMed a developer after seeing a novel approach to a well-known UI problem, which also came with a new way of packaging and explaining the contribution.
- He ties this to a broader product philosophy, comparing it to Apple's unboxing experience: the website, the store, the feeling of lifting the lid, with every layer thought through.

chunks.heading: Cut the noise from your landing page and positioning
chunks.text:
- He criticizes "slop landing pages" from startups, such as a screen recording of the founder's entire desktop.
- What he sees in them: a dock with two hundred applications, a full browsing history, two hundred plugins.
- His rule: "Delete all the things that are not your thing, because they're an excuse for people to get distracted."
- The principle is to show only what is yours, and make the packaging as intentional as the product.

chunks.heading: Choosing what to dismiss is a competitive advantage
chunks.text:
- Guillermo argues that in a world where every new tool and framework generates instant hype, saying "no" is underrated: "Silicon Valley has this sharp edge of people just get so f***ing excited about everything. And some of those things are worth dismissing. Choosing what you dismiss can also be a competitive advantage."
- He never outsources judgment. He downloads products, signs up and uses them firsthand. "If I don't fully understand it myself, it's very hard for me to actually build conviction."
- His two-phase process:
  1. Experiment broadly.
  2. Set a high bar for what you actually bring to market.
- When something clears that bar, he goes all in: post it everywhere, email it, present it.
- He warns against confusing the excitement of experimentation with the conviction required to ship.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Guillermo Rauch explains how v0 reached 3M builders by obsessing over reliability, how AI products ship with built-in metrics, and why ChatGPT became a top signup source for Vercel. He argues customers are increasingly agents, and that the web is moving from dynamic to generative, ephemeral software.

chunks.heading: Why v0 is built for reliability and taste, not just generation
chunks.text:
- Guillermo says AI products come with built-in metrics. Copilot's completion acceptance rate is one big number (51% one week, 52% the next), so a team always has a compass for iterating.
- For v0 the signals are whether people deploy what they generate, what happens to the app afterwards, and whether the code works and renders correctly.
- He treats reliability as the core quality bar: "You want to come in, you create a generation, it has to work." v0 trained its own custom code application model that sits in front of the frontier model, plus fine-tuning, all in service of reliability.
- Users of AI coding tools have a shorter fuse than traditional developers. If something fails, they flip the table, so he wants outputs that work 99.99% of the time.
- Taste is embedded in the model. Example: on iOS, the Safari theme bar should match the page background color. Before, that took frameworks and education plus hoping people upgraded; now it can be taught to the model and applied to every generated landing page.
- He calls this "the next thing after frameworks." Frameworks created a "pit of success" for people who fit them. A model can deliver that guidance to a far broader set of people than the single-digit-to-low-double-digit millions of developers.
- To keep improving, he analyzes categories of customer errors and asks "could a model have solved this problem?", then turns each one into an eval.

chunks.heading: Expanding who builds: dev-adjacent users and prototypes replacing pitch decks
chunks.text:
- Guillermo noticed early that ChatGPT was very good at React and Tailwind, so Vercel embraced it instead of ignoring or fearing it. He saw LLMs as a generational leap "more general than a framework" that opens the top of the funnel to "every person on the planet."
- v0 (text to app or front end) has over 3 million builders, with high engagement and retention, and Fortune 10 companies on the enterprise tier.
- The biggest discontinuity is that AI coding tools attract dev-adjacent people: designers, marketers, "basically anybody with a keyboard." His joke: instead of yapping into your team chat app, yap into v0 and create more value.
- Prototypes are replacing pitch decks. You used to raise a seed round to build a first prototype; now founders arrive with a working front end because the cost is so low. You can go through hundreds of prototypes before settling on an idea.
- Vercel's user base doubled year over year at zero extra cost, which he credits to AI opening the top of the funnel.
- His advice for newcomers: people entering software today leapfrog the previous generation because they have access to everything learned collectively.

chunks.heading: ChatGPT as a lead and signup channel
chunks.text:
- Vercel shared that signups sourced from ChatGPT have been growing exponentially.
- Cause: the AI SDK playground lets Vercel query multiple LLMs side by side. Over time they saw that asked for the best way to deploy a React app, the models often choose Vercel, due to training data (opinions, writings, GitHub issues).
- Anecdote: at the AI Engineer conference in San Francisco, people at the Vercel booth said ChatGPT had told them to use Vercel.
- He says this changes marketing: people used to find Vercel through a podcast like this one; now they go straight to "your AI buddy."
- AIs still ground themselves in search for fresh information, so he tells customers to keep ranking high and publishing good content.
- Content needs to change: people ask questions rather than type keywords. Vercel thinks "LLM first" in how it publishes, and FAQ-style content may help because it matches questions one to one.
- Agents need their own representation of a site: llms.txt is the static version, and MCP servers are the next evolution, letting agents talk to other agents.

chunks.heading: Building dev tools: two customers and the developer experience trade-off
chunks.text:
- Vercel started from his pain bringing a cutting-edge site online: configuring cloud infrastructure from scratch and bridging tools and infrastructure (which led to Next.js). The test was always "I want to bring my idea online immediately."
- Strategy: developer experience as a Trojan horse for automating the cloud, rather than courses or certifications.
- He obsessed over the number of characters and steps between a user and the "a-ha" moment, down to creating a folder, creating a file, and exporting a first React component.
- Advice for dev tool founders: you have two customers, the developer and the developer's end user. Start from the end user and work backwards.
- Navigating the tension: a feature can delight developers (+10 happiness points) while leaving their users unhappy two quarters later. He got this wrong early, for example with extra config flags or relaxed operational limits like "unlimited" quotas, which hurt operational excellence.
- His exercise: visit a newly launched AI product as an end user, judge how it feels, then work back to what powers it.
- With AI, the customer is now also the agent the developer wields. He asks whether APIs should change to favor LLMs as users. Short, succinct APIs (like Stripe's dot notation) still matter, but LLM strengths and weaknesses will shape runtimes, languages, type checkers and frameworks.

chunks.heading: Agents: expert agents, synchronous vs asynchronous, and a separate entry point
chunks.text:
- Framework: "virtual co-workers." Vercel will have virtual designers, marketers and developers. These are expert agents, and he expects millions, if not hundreds of millions of them.
- People start with broad tools (ChatGPT, Claude) then move to domain experts. Examples he cites among Vercel customers: OpenEvidence (healthcare, sourcing frontier data) and GC AI (legal).
- A digital-native company reinvented today would likely have an agentic interface rather than a SaaS dashboard.
- Two types: synchronous agents (ask and get an answer, like ChatGPT or an AI IDE) and asynchronous agents that work longer, collaborate with other agents and humans, and return an artifact such as a website, a pull request or a confirmation message. His example: tell an agent from bed to fix a problem and come back with a PR.
- Front ends still matter on both sides: the output artifact and the input, capturing attention with an ergonomic entry point.
- Agents are their own modality and are hard to merge into existing products. That is why Vercel created a separate app, v0.dev. He notes Google faces the same choice, hence "AI mode" sitting beside Maps and Images.
- Two classes of users: people building apps (conversational onboarding, v0) and people building platforms (experienced developers with GitHub repos, who use Vercel and roll up their sleeves). He compares v0 to Waymo: ideally no human operator, with an eject path to Cursor or VS Code if needed.
- He now uses v0 almost exclusively for his own coding because he is obsessed with time from idea to online.

chunks.heading: Making a company AI-native: prototype, product, then whole business
chunks.text:
- His tweeted path: no AI, then an AI prototyping team, then an AI product team, then every company is an AI company, applying the lessons to the rest of the business.
- Support AI is the lowest-friction entry point for established companies. Vercel went further by building an expert model in its own technologies (Next.js, React, the web).
- v0 serves two roles: it feeds Vercel's support (vercel.com/help reuses that intelligence) and lets customers get access to the expertise of the CEO and CTO at scale, since Vercel has over 100,000 customers and cannot offer broad professional services. He calls AI a "human amplifier" and a "token factory" for the business.
- Next: apply AI to firewall, security and observability. Instead of reporting 500 errors, an agent opens a pull request with the fix.
- On self-driving infrastructure he says Vercel is "practically almost there." During a Google Cloud and Cloudflare outage, v0 could diagnose from logs and observability data which vendor was the cause.
- The payoff of the developer-experience work: if agents fall into the pits of success of the frameworks, you no longer have to convince developers.

chunks.heading: Generative, ephemeral software and security by construction
chunks.text:
- The web went from static to dynamic, and now moves from dynamic to generative. Vercel's years of work on streaming and dynamic sites (like Amazon-style just-in-time recommendations) was repurposed through Fluid Compute for apps that stream from LLMs.
- He fights the idea that an app is a permanent thing. He criticizes the Mac DMG-and-drag-to-Applications ritual ("this is your puppy now") and the latency of app stores.
- He is "Team Web" and "Team Fully Generative Software forever": "Everything will be ephemeral." He now has an aversion to searching for software because generating it can beat the latency of finding and installing it. If generation keeps improving in quality, performance, security and reliability, installable and procured software is "an unwinnable battle."
- For developers this means building agentic platforms where each user may get an app generated on the fly, with v0 possibly becoming the generation engine.
- Security: he believes LLMs will produce code that is secure by construction, especially in safer languages like Rust and TypeScript, and that the next Heartbleed won't happen in a world of AI-written code. He cites an LLM-found Linux kernel use-after-free bug and Vercel's own evals of frontier models against a real vulnerability.
- v0 prevents about a thousand vulnerabilities per day (such as shipping database secrets in client-side code) compared with what the LLM would otherwise ship, because Vercel's infrastructure primitives let it guide generation.
- He wants QA agents that constantly test critical paths (sign up, buying, downloading), noting the AWS CTO's line that "everything is failing all of the time." He cites failed onboarding flows he hit while testing speech-to-text apps.
- Timeline: the biggest transformation of the web in about five years, perhaps three, with "kingdoms collapse" for companies that don't adapt and AI-native companies rising quickly.

chunks.heading: Mindset: few strong beliefs, clean slate, long-term view
chunks.text:
- He encourages not holding too many strong beliefs. When people say "AI can't do this," he tries to be on the side of AI, because the situation changes in 3 to 9 months.
- He thinks from a clean slate: everything is up for grabs, including which tools a new startup procures first. He picks on chat apps as likely to be disrupted.
- Habit: most weekends he starts something from scratch on Vercel, to dogfood the platform and ask what friction can still be removed from idea to application.
- He calls AI "underhyped": even if progress froze, the value and number of entrepreneurs building would be huge, and it is a platform shift that requires rewiring your brain. He values AI as a place to ask any question without embarrassment.
- He takes such a long-term view that little seems overhyped, since "all software will be AI."
- He says Vercel hires fast typists, and uses speech-to-text tools like Superwhisper and Wispr Flow himself.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Guillermo Rauch explains how Vercel dominated one niche (front-end) before expanding, why Next.js stays open source while the infrastructure is the business, and how v0 turned English prompts into apps and hit $4M ARR in about 11 months. He also covers staying hands-on as a technical CEO and why teams will get smaller.

chunks.heading: Why Vercel went from a general deploy platform to a focused front-end cloud
chunks.text:
- Guillermo started Vercel to democratize web quality at the level of Meta, Google and Amazon. In his words, the cloud "felt like you needed a PhD" and open source tools like Kubernetes and React took months to assemble.
- His first mistake was being too general. The company "was trying to deploy everything under the sun." It started working when he focused on the front end, where his expertise lay.
- His rule: "Being a jack-of-all-trades doesn't work in this world. Both developers and the most discerning enterprises just want the best product in the category."
- He calls it dominating a niche. Be world-class at one thing first, then expand outward.
- Many founders think the first version of the product has to match the size of their ambition. Vercel's ambition was to disrupt all applications, but it started "world-class and small."

chunks.heading: Expanding by letting customers pull product out of you
chunks.text:
- Guillermo says he "had it upside-down in the beginning" and thought he had to give developers everything.
- His better approach is "to establish a dance with a customer." Give them enough that they love the product, and then "they should be the ones pulling product out of you."
- Developers kept asking for a database and more back end on Vercel. For years his answer was "we're not ready yet." Now Vercel is ready, and he describes the shift as going from a front-end cloud to a developer cloud.
- Next.js stayed tightly coupled to the business for the first 6-7 years. Vercel also supports other front-end frameworks, such as Svelte, used by Logitech and IKEA.

chunks.heading: Open source framework plus paid infrastructure: how the business model works
chunks.text:
- Next.js has no direct revenue. Guillermo says he never considered doing it differently: "Open source for me has always been my life," and a proprietary framework "just doesn't make sense."
- Vercel gives away the programming model (Next.js) and charges for the heavy lifting of running it: global infrastructure, security, DDoS mitigation, and staying up through traffic spikes.
- He argues open source hits diminishing returns on infrastructure. Most of that engineering is operational (monitoring, upgrades, rolling systems, staging), and "Vercel doesn't need to be open source."
- His principle is "infrastructure has to be an output of the application." Most companies start from the infrastructure, and Vercel inverts that.
- The comparables he cites are GitHub (URLs to code), Databricks (open source Spark plus a highly optimized cloud engine) and Snowflake and Datadog. Pricing follows usage: a small app pays little, and an app that takes over the world pays more.
- The AI SDK follows the same pattern: open source, no direct business model, and growth from about 100,000 to almost 1 million weekly downloads in about a year. The goals are developer adoption, feedback, brand and learning, with the bet that people deploying later will choose Vercel.

chunks.heading: Preview URLs as a collaboration feature
chunks.text:
- He built Vercel around "keystroke to live application," measured in milliseconds. He wanted to cut a weeks-long process to a developer running `git push`.
- Every Git branch automatically gets an ephemeral, secure preview URL. He says he underestimated how valuable this would be: companies value even more the ability for developers to collaborate with everyone else in the organization.
- Preview URLs let you test on a phone before shipping. One ecommerce customer has 90% mobile traffic and uses the URLs to "have the developers face reality."
- His example of the alternative: a large bank still schedules 12-person meetings so one person can screen share a feature.

chunks.heading: How v0 grew and why it changed Vercel's funnel
chunks.text:
- v0 turns English prompts into working web apps. He describes it as "not code first. It's code last."
- It launched as a research preview in September 2023. It took 10 months to reach $1M ARR, then 14 days to $2M, then 20 more days to $4M. He says he has never seen a trajectory like it and that it was making hyperscalers run out of GPU capacity in their largest regions.
- It is a "startup within a startup," built by a team of fewer than 10 people, entirely on the public Vercel platform. Guillermo checks that the team is "not allowed to cheat" by asking infra for special provisioning, which proves the platform has "no graduation risk" (customers outgrowing it).
- v0 widens the top of the funnel from a couple of million developers to potentially hundreds of millions of people. Signups are "through the roof" and application creation has roughly quadrupled.
- v0 output beat his own hand-built personal blog on responsiveness and accessibility.
- v0 is not a new foundation model. It combines state-of-the-art models with evals, benchmarks, prompts, RAG and AI-tailored design systems. This encodes the Next.js and React teams' preference data and taste, which lets him "scale myself" instead of sending experts to every company.
- His prediction is that Vercel's expertise will be exported through AI, and other companies will build their own "v0 for X" (CAD, email, medicine) using the AI SDK.

chunks.heading: Using v0 in sales and as a collaboration link
chunks.text:
- Sales reps screenshot a prospect's legacy website, drop it into v0, and show a high-performance rebuild during the call. It replaces a "trust me bro" pitch.
- He says this shortens sales cycles and raises customer trust and delight.
- Customers now collaborate by sharing v0 links rather than documents or words. This extends his earlier aim of making people collaborate through links.
- v0 also makes migrating legacy frameworks to Next.js easier, which removes a sales hurdle (customers who want to move but cannot spare dev time).

chunks.heading: Security and enterprise trust
chunks.text:
- Vercel's rule is zero configuration and secure by default. Because it hosts the application, it has to filter out 100% of malicious traffic instantly, unlike a pure CDN that only filters.
- He credits crypto customers (Solana, large NFT companies) with forcing Vercel to harden security and DDoS mitigation. Vercel responds within seconds, while he says competitors sometimes take minutes.
- Whenever a new technology wave arrives (crypto, AI), startups tend to build on Vercel, and that is also how it enters large enterprises: they acquire the disruptor. A shared Next.js and React stack speeds integration: "you copy-and-paste some files into another repository."
- As of this conversation: $100M annualized revenue in May 2024, 80% year-over-year growth, developer usage more than doubled over the past year, and about 550 employees.

chunks.heading: How he runs the company as a technical CEO
chunks.text:
- He believes CEOs, especially technical ones, "can and should be involved in every aspect of the business," including closing deals, sales compensation, roadmap and pricing.
- He stays informed by using the product himself (v0, Vercel), talking to customers and the developer community, and hiring people with technical backgrounds who have used Vercel. Executives are expected to understand the customer and product deeply, so no time goes to briefings.
- His role with executives is "the bridge to reality": bring customer stories, give high-quality feedback, and require that "you have to be able to use our product to demo our product."
- His principle: "as a CEO you have to understand." Delegating with confidence comes from understanding, not from outsourcing the labor.
- He sees companies becoming more transparent and optimizing information flow rather than creating silos.
- He expects smaller teams: more products, reaching more people, built by fewer people, as AI writes code and infrastructure is abstracted. He says the "marginal cost of software production goes to zero," and cites Open Operator, built by a Vercel customer within 24 hours of OpenAI's Operator launch using v0, cloud browser infrastructure and open models.

chunks.heading: Summary
chunks.text: Guillermo Rauch explains how Vercel grew from a developer-first open source framework into an enterprise platform. He covers building beyond the developer champion, starting sales from customer success, closing deals before features like SSO existed, and using security as a differentiator.

chunks.heading: Developer love gets him in, enterprise needs keep him there
chunks.text:
- Guillermo built Vercel's approach on open source Next.js, then asked what a company needs to pay for on top of the framework: a platform, collaboration workflow, and enterprise features.
- Next.js was designed by borrowing from the largest sites on the internet. He started with server rendering, "what google.com was doing for search and what facebook.com was doing for newsfeed."
- Vercel's pitch spans three phases: develop (open source Next.js), preview (a URL for every change or code push, for team feedback), and ship (an edge network that automates cloud infrastructure).
- He says the real-time feedback loop has been the throughline since launch: changes appear in the browser without a refresh, now targeting around 10 milliseconds from keystroke to screen.
- Browser-based development (Next.js Live) lets anyone be hyperlinked into editing a project collaboratively in single-digit seconds, instead of losing a day or weeks to environment setup. He doesn't expect developers to work only in the browser, but says quick copy changes and pair debugging suit it.

chunks.heading: Growing past self-serve signups into enterprise
chunks.text:
- He says he used to be obsessed with thousands of signups, then started caring what people were using the technology for. He didn't want it to stay a tool for quick tests or side projects.
- Self-serve interest was growing and working. He chose to look at the early experiments inside large companies and ask how to grow them "into much more than just a handful of developers being excited."
- The shift in thinking: beyond making things fast for developers, arm developers with "features, substantiations, materials, documentation, integrations, and workflows that the rest of the company needs" to turn an experiment into "the lifeline of the company."
- Customers named in the conversation include the Washington Post, Airbnb, IBM, Staples, McDonald's, and the Grammys (Vercel hosted the 2022 Grammys, a couple of years after its first paid customers).
- He frames enterprise as mission-aligned. Vercel's goal is to make the web faster for developers and end users, and "without that enterprise arm, I think we would be leaving a lot of business on the table."
- Enterprise rollout also drives seat expansion. Without it, a product "might get stuck at just one team within a company."

chunks.heading: Think two layers past the developer who adopts you
chunks.text:
- His advice to tool founders: your early adopter is a developer, but that developer has stakeholders and users beyond them. "If you just think one layer in you're going to get stuck." Think one layer in, then two layers deeper.
- Imagine those conversations and requirements, and then simply ask: what does your company need to use more of the product?
- He says to talk to procurement, the security questionnaire owners and the CSO, "even if they're not yet even buying your product." Knowing their questions and concerns gives "the right frame to build scalable products in the future."
- Developers stay valuable as advocates. Executives turn to developers and ask what will make them happy and what the company should buy.

chunks.heading: Building sales: start from customer success, then add account executives
chunks.text:
- Vercel's sales function grew out of customer success, not the other way around. It started with the support team and a recognition that customers fall into categories with different levels of "demand/anxiety/tolerance for failure."
- Some customers need to know every possible roadmap direction, ask detailed questions constantly, and want priority in the queue when stuck. The support team guided companies through successfully rolling out the technology.
- The first account executives came next. Their job was to help companies understand the landscape, compare offerings, and see why Vercel is the better long-term partner, which meant selling more of the vision of where Vercel will be.
- He rolled this out slowly so the team could learn what worked. Vercel hired its first CRO and developed customer success and sales together, using those conversations to find gaps in documentation and in how customers are serviced.
- Why a sales motion matters: some companies "will just not even entertain the technology if they cannot talk to sales." Developers may avoid sales, but the company as a whole wants to know who it's partnering with.
- Enterprises also want more predictable pricing than serverless usage-based models offer, and they want a person on the phone for when they have issues or "need to make my next big step."

chunks.heading: Selling features that don't exist yet
chunks.text:
- Before SSO, Vercel had already landed many enterprise customers. He says demand was strong enough that his team worked with customers' security teams and internal champions to align roadmaps.
- The pitch was candid: "You really need our product. We've made it really secure. We have a lot of the foundations... But we do recognize that the SSO feature is missing." He told customers the partnership with WorkOS was coming, and offered to work on it together.
- He says roadmap conversations with enterprises are often this kind of close collaboration. He had assumed Vercel would just ship products from its R&D labs and "lead the way."
- Looking back, he says Vercel "could have done even more business" had it partnered with WorkOS earlier. Customers who compared the SSO onboarding to other tools' integrations loved it.
- He argues enterprise features offer room for delight too. "It's not just all like real time react components. It's also delighting all the other stakeholders."

chunks.heading: Reconciling developer-led and enterprise buyers
chunks.text:
- He describes two buyers with opposite preferences: developers want self-serve and usage-based pricing, while enterprise buyers want predictability and a phone call. Vercel runs one motion for the scalable, bigger customer.
- Security and SSO are a "clean differentiator" of which bucket a customer falls into. Corporate security was a top-three priority for Vercel's own security team once the company passed 100 people.
- Enterprise deals move slower than a developer picking up a product they like that day, but "the impact just goes up dramatically." He cites doing tens of billions of requests a week as the leverage Vercel brings to its own providers.
- Enterprises evaluate guarantees "years down the line," including security and infrastructure. Developers pick whatever solves the immediate situation.
- On the risk of drifting from developer experience (he cites Heroku's website as an example others have drifted), he acknowledges the tension: a more secure system can add friction. He is "confident that we can still retain an excellent DX over time while we have a successful enterprise business."
- His reasoning: enterprises increasingly buy developer experience too, since they want teams to enjoy daily tooling. He points to Stripe, which made developer productivity a focus of its go-to-market and educated the enterprise world about its value.

chunks.heading: Enterprise roadmap: security, access control and isolation
chunks.text:
- Security is his top enterprise priority. Vercel sits at the entry point for healthcare providers, fintech, multimedia companies and e-commerce stores, so enterprises need a lot to succeed at scale.
- Investments named: role-based access control, more granular controls, and corporate identity and access management.
- He wants to give security teams a way to understand the system from the outside: data flows, activity, auditing, and what endpoints exist and what data flows through them. The aim is "to lead with great solutions rather than try to be reactive to security questionnaires."
- Supply chain attacks are a concern for customers anxious about what gets deployed. Role-based access control helps companies see and control what ships to their ".com" sites. He notes the platform was conceived so everyone can make changes instantly, and says the two worlds can be reconciled.
- Isolation is the longer-term goal: Vercel as a company's own developer platform with full control in isolation from others. Vercel is massively multi-tenant at ingress, but he sees ways to isolate workloads and give enterprises more ownership.

chunks.heading: What he'd tell his past self
chunks.text:
- Be aware of your taxonomy and schema early. He cites a joke tweet: if you sell guitars, don't name the table "guitars," because you may sell drums later. Call it "items," then "sellable things," because you may sell services.
- Learning your future requirements (for example from podcasts like this) doesn't mean obsessing over them, but you can lay basic infrastructure from the start.
- Take security seriously early. He gives the example of a company with a centralized identity provider from the start, which can grow from 100 to 200 to 500 people "and not have to like deal with like five different IDP systems."
- Use vendors that provide enterprise features out of the box rather than reinventing them. He says most startups and internet companies "have a long way to go on this security space."

React has become the 'linux kernel' of modern software development. The industry has broadly standardized around its 'syscall interface', from vendors shipping hooks or components as their SDKs, to LLMs being trained to generate it.

The metaphor holds further. Today, Linux is mostly used in the form of distributions that bundle it. Most users are oblivious to what kernel version they're even running, because they're interested in a working operating system with all the necessary tools to be productive, as well as an app ecosystem, support, and security patches.

A lot of people start using React by (sometimes unknowingly) assembling their own 'distributions' aka frameworks. This is akin to checking out the Linux source, running `make vmlinux`, then re-assembling the operating system by hand. I think this is a very cool thing to learn and do, and early in my career I'm very thankful I bootstrapped my own Linux systems with projects like LFS and Gentoo. It built character 😆 and foundational knowledge.

If you're building a product or a company, I strongly recommend you pick a distribution, not assemble one. Next.js is the most popular, but naturally many others have emerged: TanStack, Remix, Astro, Waku to name a few great ones, built by passionate, expert "kernel" engineers.

I strongly believe AIs will create *more* secure, more correct, and more performant software than humans. 

The “vibe” in vibe coding should speak to the creative direction style, rather than the quality of the output. This is certainly our goal with @v0, prevent slop at all costs. 

Agents don’t get tired, so they’ll make fewer mistakes. It’s too easy for a human today to forget to auth an endpoint. To not apply operational limits and quotas. To forget to escape and validate untrusted input. 

Interestingly enough, our CTO @cramforce recently discovered a serious vulnerability in an open source project. It involved a lack of sanitization of potentially malicious payloads in a quite subtle, unsuspecting line of code. After our responsible disclosure to their team, I found the PR that introduced their bug and ran it through a few models. Almost all frontier coding models correctly identified the high risk involved in the inlining technique used to pass data to the browser.

It’s extremely common for human programmers and human reviewers to let these issues slide. That PR was written and reviewed by experts. The same applies to every other important area of software quality. We humans might lapse, rush or simply not know enough and not ship enough tests, accessibility, caching & other performance optimizations… Agents won’t forget or be lazy to ship enough instrumentation and alerting so that they themselves can get paged when the site is down.

It won’t happen overnight and this future will require the coordination of both AI and traditional software engineering techniques, including frameworks, infrastructure and security-as-code… but it will come.

@v0 has now prevented LLMs from writing vulnerable code in 16,200+ generated applications. Concretely, it's prevented *sixteen thousand* token leaks, from AI api keys to database compromises.

How does this work?
• From a threat model perspective, v0 doesn't take LLM code for granted. We consider all code potentially incorrect or adversarial.
• Next.js makes a strong distinction between server-side tokens and client-side tokens, which are `NEXT_PUBLIC_` prefixed.
• v0 analyzes `NEXT_PUBLIC_` usage and warns the user. Because we have support for server-side code execution, the code can then be easily moved to Route Handlers / Server Actions / etc by the AI.

Further, when v0 deploys to @vercel, server-side code becomes secure Functions that run in isolated sandboxes and read encrypted environment from our built-in secure vault.

We're continuing our research and investment into guardrails so that v0 users can ship with confidence. Our goal is to make v0 generated applications more secure than human-written ones. Shoutout to @ido_pesok for laying the groundwork in this area.

Prompting is thinking. The sharper your thoughts, the better the prompts, the better the outputs. Engineering and design are headed into a world where most of the output is produced by prompting, if not all.

The way we interview engineers has already been trending in this direction. At Vercel, we don’t care if you memorized every API and module. When we look at your coding, we assess the quality of your thinking and collaboration. It’s more so an evaluation of your “thinking tokens” or reasoning trace. My prediction is that the demand for great thinkers will remain unabated. It’s unclear if we’ll call them engineers or if it’ll matter, because these people will have a lot of full stack impact on the whole business, as they’ll have access to prompt their way to any successful outcome.

A good reminder for builders is that someone adopting your product happens in two moments. 1️⃣ awareness 2️⃣ low-friction first use. People use products when they *need* them.

As an example, someone pitched me their pre-release “ai-native photoshop” the other day. I went to the site and roughly got the idea. It helped that the product itself was the website so I understood the idea faster by messing with it, rather than marketing fluff.

However, just now I actually had a use case. I was astonished by how good this thing is. It worked first try and I’m now entering the “holy shit” phase. 

The first time I used it was the awareness development moment. If the product builder expected a successful “session” then, he would have set himself up for disappointment.

The second moment was the crucial one. Users’ attention spans, propensity to go through yet another tool, signup, etc are very low. That second moment needed to be flawless and it was.

Incidentally this is why you need to really pick your battles with product surface and optimize for quality. Had that second moment not been successful, I don’t know if I would have tried it again for a while. Anecdotally, people seem to do an “exponential back off” with products they’re disappointed by. They won’t try you again next week, they’ll try you again in a few months, maybe after another awareness moment in between.

The classic @rabois startup wisdom is that at software companies you need two kinds of people: 

▪️ barrels: rare, high-leverage individuals in a company who can take an idea from start to finish

▪️ ammunition: talented specialists (engineers, designers) who execute excellently but need direction and ownership to be effective

In the AI age all the leverage belongs to the barrels. The tools are getting so good they can now effectively take any idea to reality for the right barrel. The ammunition is LLM tokens and parallel agents.

Models are like EC2. If your entire product is to re-expose EC2 as-is, you'll likely be in a tough business.

But: if you write software on top of EC2, now you're part of the cloud economy. As an analogy, if we go by the @redpoint's InfraRed Cloud Infrastructure index, $600B+ of public company value has been created on top of cloud primitives by 23 cloud companies¹

And that's just public companies, only a fragment of the entire cloud value chain.

I believe the AI cloud economy is going to be much larger. The model is a very important base layer, but there's an immense amount of value to be added on top to ship great products. (In fact, if anything, we've seen that the model layer is fluid and uncertain, having changed or upgraded models probably a dozen times at @v0).

People will want to buy AI applications and agents that solve useful, concrete and domain-specific problems. That are secure, reliable, have a high quality bar, mitigate errors and minimize slop. Models alone are not enough.

Yesterday at @vercel we took an important step towards enabling this future with a foundational piece of our AI Cloud platform: the AI Gateway. It's never been easier to access these new foundations. The best part: we're partnering with the best labs and inference providers in the world to give you day0 access to new models and increasingly affordable and faster tokens.

DIY agents today are more reliant on the forward-deployed engineer model. It’s hard for Enterprise companies to go from 0 to 1 on agents on such a fast moving space.

This is what we want to unlock with @aisdk and the @vercel AI Cloud. The cloud won in the first place because companies have very business-specific problems. There’s a sales meme “don’t mistake busy-ness with business” that points to the fact that you might take pride in spending lots of time in meetings, sending emails, making phone calls, but at the end of the day you have to close business.

All successful agents have 3 key components:

🧠 Brain → model, harness (logic)
👐 Hands → tools, computer, browser
🗃️ Files → memories, skills, repos

The 'easy' way is to throw all these in 1 stateful computer (a Mac Mini)

Like, you run 𝚌𝚕𝚊𝚞𝚍𝚎 or 𝚏𝚡 in your mac, you keep it running all day with 𝚌𝚊𝚏𝚏𝚎𝚒𝚗𝚊𝚝𝚎, it has storage, and CLIs and apps installed.

But if you want to cost-efficiently run agents in the cloud, you actually start breaking down these parts.

🧠 The harness can run in Fluid compute. To make it reliable across restarts, rollouts, crashes, you make its event log durable using Workflow.

👐 The hands can be a dedicated browser fleet like Browserbase/Kernel, a computer like Sandbox, and even more efficient lightweight tools like just-bash.

🗃️ 🆕 What was missing was a way to also decouple storage. Imagine you want to run a memory consolidation cron job every night ("dreaming"). You can read/write to the files directly without 'booting up' the agent's full computer.

Today we're introducing the perfect companion to Sandbox: Drives. We shipped the computer for agents, now we're giving you the 'external disk' you can attach at will. It's early, and we'll be expanding capabilities here quickly.

Btw, breaking apart the agent into these independent parts not only optimizes costs in a big way, it also *massively* improves security and auditability. I'd argue you can't even run a secure agent otherwise!

We placed a bet 10 years ago that everything would be computer.

Next.js started out as a server-side rendering framework, introduced incremental page generation, and doubled down on personalizing the web. At the time, the dogma was that servers weren’t needed. You were supposed to make everything static.

First we set out to prove that computers in the cloud, or servers, didn’t have to be *hard* for developers. With Vercel Functions, we made scaling compute in the cloud easy, fast, and zero configuration.

Now we’re proving compute can be cost-efficient, especially for AI workloads. Since launching https://t.co/Mfqozf4JBi 5 weeks ago, we’ve seen 68% of our invocations seamlessly adopt our new compute paradigm of “serverless servers”. Customers are seeing up to 85% cost savings 🥹.

I’m extremely excited about what’s coming next. Our computers, from our dev servers, to our build infrastructure, to our functions, will increasingly be in the hands of Agents, rather than humans alone. I anticipate the vast majority of @vercel deployments will soon be made by an agent of some kind, like @v0 or @windsurf_ai and @cursor_ai.

I can’t wait to see the next wave of applications we *all* ship on top of these foundations.
